content.rendered:
People don’t receive as many letters as they used to: email has largely replaced physical mail. And when an envelope does arrive, often the content has been written not by anyone we’ve ever met, but by the marketing department of a company keen to sell us some exciting new product or essential service. Despite such mail coming from a stranger, however, it uses our name to give the impression that the sender knows us and our needs personally: “Dear Mr Smith, I thought you’d like to know about our latest widget, and I’m writing to tell you all about it because I believe it will transform your life” – or words in a similar vein.

We know that there is an element of insincerity in communication like this: the letter has been generated automatically by a computer; there is no real person involved who knows us and genuinely wants to help us. In this article, we’ll see that Jesus’ knowledge of us is very different from the superficial knowledge of the marketeers.

Zacchaeus

In Luke’s account of Jesus’ visiting Jericho, we are introduced to a man who we might think was far from the Kingdom of God:

“And there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich” (Luke 19:2). 1

1 Bible quotations are from the ESV UK.

It is likely that a typical working day for Zacchaeus would entail cheating his fellows in order to generate revenue for the Roman authorities – lining his own pocket in the process. The crowd’s description of him is probably fair:

“He [Jesus] has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner” (verse 7).

In reality, however, this man was closer to the Kingdom than most of those around him.

Jesus explains to Zacchaeus that he must stay at his house. Zacchaeus responds with joy, and his repentance is matched with action:

“And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, ‘Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold’” (verse 8).

We, too, are called to respond joyfully to Jesus’ invitation, making changes in our lives that reflect true repentance and dedication. The happy conclusion is expressed in Jesus’ pronouncement:

“Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (verses 9,10).

As far as we know, Jesus had never met Zacchaeus before this incident. But notice that Jesus addresses him by name:

“And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, ‘Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today’” (verse 5).

Jesus’ familiarity with Zacchaeus is not like the use of our names in the junk mail that we receive through our letterboxes. Far from it: Jesus knew Zacchaeus well. He knew that here was someone in need of salvation, ready to respond to an invitation to let Jesus into his life.

Zacchaeus was probably surprised when Jesus used his name. It is not every day that a first-time acquaintance calls out to us with such personal knowledge of who we are. But Jesus said that he knows all his followers in this way:

“the shepherd of the sheep … calls his own sheep by name and leads them out … and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice” (John 10:2-4).

Let’s look at two more episodes in which Jesus addresses people by name.

Simon Peter

After Jesus shares bread and wine with his disciples on the night of his betrayal and arrest, he makes a wonderful promise to them:

“I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke 22:29,30).

The disciples may have felt rather proud to hear such words describing their high place of honour in the future. However, the very next thing that Jesus says would surely have caused Simon Peter’s thoughts to tumble back down to the here-and-now:

“Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (verses 31,32).

And then:

“I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me” (verse 34).

How do you imagine Jesus saying that first phrase – the twofold use of Simon’s name? Perhaps Jesus followed the first “Simon” with a knowing and loving sigh, then said “Simon” again, and this led into his explanation that Simon was about to go through a few very difficult hours. It is clear from the recorded words that this was not a rebuke from Jesus. How wonderful it is that, in the same statement, Jesus provides comfort for Peter by explaining that he has already prayed for him, and that Peter will ‘turn again’ and be a strength for his fellow-disciples. In effect, Jesus is reiterating his assurance that Peter will be in the Kingdom, despite his imminent threefold denial of his Lord.

Jesus knew Simon Peter inside out – not just his name, but his strengths and flaws too. Later on, when Peter had fallen asleep in the garden, Jesus again shows his deep and sympathetic understanding of Peter’s nature:

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41).

Mary Magdalene

On the morning of his resurrection, Mary Magdalene speaks to Jesus without immediately realising who he is:

“she turned round and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus” (John 20:14).

Then Jesus uses her name:

“Jesus said to her, ‘Mary.’ She turned and said to him in Aramaic, ‘Rabboni!’ (which means Teacher)” (verse 16).

Jesus identifies himself by using her name! It’s almost as if he were saying, “I know you. It’s me. It’s the one you’ve been longing to see. Here I am. I’m alive.”

How would you feel?

Remember Jesus’ words about his flock:

“he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out” (10:2,3).

Jesus knows all of us – not just Zacchaeus, Simon and Mary, but us too. And Jesus’ sheep follow him and know his voice:

“When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice” (verse 4).

Supposing Jesus were to use your name, how would you feel?

Would it be a surprise, as it was for Zacchaeus? Do we not expect Jesus to know us personally? It shouldn’t be like that: we should know that our relationship is close enough for him to know our name – and much more about us.

Would we be troubled? Perhaps we would fear that we were about to receive a well-deserved rebuke from the Lord. That is not how Jesus spoke to Peter. Gentleness, not harshness, was the tone. Jesus is saddened by the weakness of our humanity.

When we hear Jesus’ voice – and we will, when the Kingdom is established – it should surely be as it was for Mary. We will be hearing the one whom we had longed for but hadn’t dared to expect. The one whom we already knew well, but had never seen face to face, will be addressing us.

But, meanwhile, what does it mean to be truly one of Jesus’ sheep?

The good shepherd

“I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me … and I lay down my life for the sheep” (verses 14,15).

Jesus is the Good Shepherd. We know what that means. There are many references to shepherds in the Old Testament that point forward to this: God as shepherd, David as shepherd, corrupt rulers as evil shepherds. Most famously, Psalm 23 describes how “The Lord is my shepherd”. God feeds and revives and protects from enemies, and blessings abound in His house for ever. What is true of God as shepherd is true of Jesus too.

Jesus said that the shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. We’re reminded of the attention paid in the parable to the one lost sheep amongst the hundred.

“If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them has gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go in search of the one that went astray?” (Matthew 18:12).

This is no casual “I care about you” from the shepherd: he focuses all his attention on finding the sheep that has gone astray. And Jesus says that he goes further than the shepherd in the parable: not only was he prepared to go to great effort to search for the “lost”, but he was willing to lay down his life to provide salvation.

We should understand, however, that, as well as Jesus’ being willing to do something for us, there is an obligation on us to respond. Ponder for a moment the fact that Jesus says that the sheep follow the shepherd “for they know his voice”; and “my own know me”. If we are truly part of Jesus’ flock, then we will listen actively to what he says, and this will result in our knowing him and following his example.

Peter listened to the shepherd

Jesus tells Peter that, after his denial of Jesus, ultimately he will strengthen his brothers:

“And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

It seems that Peter listened to these words, absorbed them and acted upon them. Later in his life, he writes this to his brothers and sisters:

“Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to Him who judges justly. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed. For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:21-25).

The word translated “returned” here is the one translated “turned again” in Luke 22:32. Peter had learned from his experiences, had meditated upon them in the light of what Jesus said to him, and as a result knew his Lord more deeply. He had witnessed first-hand the way that Jesus suffered and died for his sheep.

When we share bread and wine with our brothers and sisters, we remember the Shepherd who knows his sheep by name and whose sheep know him. He is the Shepherd who is prepared to make every effort to find us and restore us to the fold when we go astray, and the one who laid down his life for his sheep.

title.rendered: Archaeology and the Bible: Do they conflict?

excerpt.rendered: Question of the month Many believers will have felt a certain excitement on encountering tangible evidence of people and places

content.rendered:
Question of the month

Many believers will have felt a certain excitement on encountering tangible evidence of people and places mentioned in the Bible: perhaps catching their breath on their first glimpse of Temple Mount, or blinking in the daylight as they emerged from Hezekiah’s Conduit into the Pool of Siloam. Such excitement can be experienced in Gentile lands, too. Countless Christian tour groups have lingered in the Great Theatre at Ephesus to ponder the events of Acts 19, or on the Areopagus (Mars’ Hill) to reflect on Paul’s words to the Athenians. Those unable to travel overseas may not have been greatly disadvantaged; close to home, for some of us, there is the British Museum’s outstanding collection of artefacts associated with the Bible, about which whole books have been written: the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser, the Taylor Prism, the Nabonidus Stele – all these, and many more, are of direct or indirect significance for our appreciation of the Bible. We have turned to them enthusiastically for evidence that the Bible is true.

For all such material, we owe our thanks to biblical archaeology. From the mid-nineteenth century, this discipline has shed significant light on the world of the Bible. Many early archaeologists were searching for evidence that the Bible is reliable, being men and women who believed that it contains an accurate record of people and events from times past. We should be grateful for these people, and for the fact that they were permitted by God to do their work at a time when general belief in the Bible was in decline. Some have speculated that the timing was not coincidental.

A reason to believe?

It should be stated, however, that archaeology is not why we believe the Bible. Whilst it is satisfying to see tangible evidence of biblical places, events and even named individuals, this is not the faith that justifies us from our sins. When the Thessalonians “turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God, and to wait for His Son from heaven” (1 Thessalonians 1:9,10), 1 they did so because they heard the preaching of the apostles and “accepted it … for what it really is, the word of God, which … performs its work in [those] who believe” (2:13). Paul and his fellow apostles persuaded people to believe by the force of their inspired words. As part of their mission of preaching the gospel, we never read of them inviting their Gentile hearers to consider archaeological remains in the Holy Land.

1 Bible quotations are from the NASB 1995.

In our enthusiasm for biblical archaeology, therefore, we should be careful about the claims that we make for it. We should not forget that there are far more biblical places and people for which there is no archaeological evidence – yet we ask people to believe in them too. We must not be selective in our approach to this topic. Our witness to the Bible will quickly lose credibility if we gloss over the absence of archaeological evidence for some of our claims.

Contradictory evidence

This can become more of an issue for us when archaeology seems to suggest that the Bible is untrue. There are plenty of people who would claim to be able to provide such ‘evidence’. Amongst those prominent in biblical archaeology today is the Jewish professor Israel Finkelstein, who has stated openly that archaeology in Israel does not support the Old Testament accounts of the Israelites’ wilderness journey, their conquest of Canaan, the building of Solomon’s Temple, and so on. Such testimony quickly takes on a sinister aspect. If Jews cannot prove their occupancy of the Land in ancient times, then what right do they have to it now? Regrettably, biblical archaeology has become part of the fraught politics of the region.

What, then, should be our approach if we are asked why we believe in the Bible despite archaeological ‘evidence’ which seems to suggest that it is untrue? Here are a few approaches that I have found helpful – and a ‘worked example’ which strengthened my own faith.

  • Does it really matter? No one will ever prove the Bible right or wrong from archaeology alone. The conviction that God’s Word is true is acquired in other ways. At the end of the day, whether or not the archaeology of Israel meets the current assumptions of archaeologists is not a major concern for us. It is not something on which God has asked us to take a position.
  • Are we reading the Bible carefully enough? Sceptics have claimed that the arrival of a new culture (the Israelites) in Canaan, especially on the scale described in the Old Testament, ought to be evidenced by archaeology. In fact, God’s people took over much existing ‘infrastructure’ on their arrival. He had promised them the use of “great and splendid cities which you did not build, and houses full of all good things which you did not fill, and hewn cisterns which you did not dig, vineyards and olive trees which you did not plant” (Deuteronomy 6:10,11) – all Canaanite in origin. There is a clear biblical explanation for any lack of evidence of major culture change at this time.
  • Are we looking in the wrong period? It is not always easy to reconcile the conventionally accepted chronology of Old Testament history with information contained in the Bible. Those who start with the assumption that the Bible is reliable have sometimes been able to challenge the scholarly consensus. For instance, the alternative chronology of ancient Egyptian history proposed by the ‘nonconformist’ Egyptologist David Rohl, whilst not exactly finding universal favour, has been sufficiently challenging to some of his peers. His argument, set out in his book A Test of Time, is worth considering.
  • Is the evidence hidden? Some have doubted whether certain Canaanite cities really existed where the Bible says they did. However, if these cities have been built over by later towns (as some have), making archaeological exploration impossible, then no evidence for their existence is ever likely to be found. Such ‘absence of evidence’ is not ‘evidence of absence’.
  • Has all the evidence been lost? Some Canaanite cities were entirely destroyed by the Israelites, leaving no evidence that they ever existed. When the Canaanite king of Arad fought against Israel, “Israel made a vow to the Lord and said, ‘If You will indeed deliver this people into my hand, then I will utterly destroy their cities.’ The Lord heard the voice of Israel and delivered up the Canaanites; then they utterly destroyed them and their cities” (Numbers 21:2,3). There are no remains of these cities to be found.
  • Has the evidence not been found yet? It sometimes takes time for biblical archaeology to ‘catch up’ with the Bible itself. The size and grandeur of the ancient city of Babylon, the historicity of the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, the existence of ‘politarchs’ (Acts 17:6,8) and other local officials in the cities of the Roman Empire – all these things were once doubted by scholars on the grounds that there was no archaeological evidence for them. Over time, however, ample evidence was unearthed. Those who doubted the Bible were proved wrong.
  • Are we looking in the wrong place? The Bible does not always give us as much information as we might like about the location of some of the places it mentions. It can be hard to know exactly where to look – and, as the example below shows, easy to discredit the Bible by misinterpreting the evidence that is found.

These points will not deal comprehensively with every alleged discrepancy between the Bible and archaeology. But they may give us lines of approach. We should also keep in mind the marked contrast between the incomplete evidence that is, by definition, the best that archaeologists ever have to work with, and the complete canon of Scripture that has been preserved. We are not really comparing like with like.

Susa: a case study

Let us consider a worked example, in which archaeological ‘evidence’ that seemed to contradict the Bible was later abandoned entirely. I say much more about this example in a new book, At the Citadel in Susa: Ancient Iran and the reliability of the Old Testament, to be published by the Christadelphian Office in July, God willing.

In Susa (or Shushan, KJV), the western Iranian town of Shush, we meet King Ahasuerus of Medo-Persia, his beautiful queen Esther, and her uncle Mordecai. Historians knew of this place not only from the Book of Esther but also from Greek and Roman sources. By the nineteenth century, however, Shush was a tiny, insignificant village, and its connection with the Bible had been forgotten. There was no firm evidence where the biblical Susa was – or even whether it had existed.

Archaeological investigations began at Shush just over 200 years ago, led by people who believed the Bible to be true. Inscriptions identified the site with certainty, and the ancient city’s general layout was established, including certain details that matched the Bible’s record – for example, the clear distinction between the upper “citadel” (Esther 1:2,5) and the lower “city” (3:15). Within a century or so, work had located other features that the Bible describes: the royal palace, the three distinct courtyards of this palace (2:11; 4:11; 6:4), “the king’s gate”, where Mordecai refused to bow to Haman (3:2), and “the city square”, through which Haman led Mordecai on horseback (6:11). This was all very encouraging for Bible believers.

New doubts

But not everything at Susa was so reassuring. Interpretations of some early findings called into question the information recorded in Esther. For instance, archaeologists concluded that the entrance to the palace throne room was to the south, and that the king’s throne therefore also faced south. As no southern wall to the throne room was found, it was assumed that in this direction lay a large, open terrace. This did not match the details of Esther 5:1, which states that the king’s throne was “opposite the entrance to the palace”, where Queen Esther was seen standing “in the inner court of the king’s palace in front of the king’s rooms”. The Bible’s description of the throne room appeared to be inaccurate. However, later work on the throne room unearthed a threshold. There had been a door and therefore a wall here after all; the earlier archaeologists had simply not done enough digging. And the throne room was confirmed to be very close to the palace’s residential section, as Esther 5:1 also says.

But now there was a second problem. Between the southern doorway of the throne room and the residential section of the palace there was not a courtyard, as described in Esther 5:2, but a short corridor. Again, time provided a solution. More sophisticated archaeological techniques revealed that the southern door of the throne room had in fact opened outwards; this door was therefore the exit, not the entrance. As before, it had simply required more work to clear up the alleged discrepancy with the Bible.

Then a third problem emerged. Immediately beyond the actual entrance to the throne room (now known to be on the north) was not the king’s palace, as Esther 5:2 says, but an open space. Now what were Bible believers to think?

A biblical solution

Elsewhere in the palace lies a small suite of rooms accessed from a courtyard directly to the north. Findings pointed to this being the most private section of the royal apartments. Over time, archaeologists came to realise that at the very centre of this suite of rooms, in what they named ‘the King’s Chamber’, there was probably a second throne, which had a direct line of sight to the adjacent courtyard. At last, all the information fitted the description in Esther 5:1,2. The throne from which King Ahasuerus “extended to Esther the golden sceptre which was in his hand” never was the one in the large throne room on which the archaeologists had concentrated for so long; it was the one in the king’s private apartments. The integrity of Scripture was upheld.

We cannot expect every perceived discrepancy between archaeology and the Bible to be resolved as neatly as this. But the fascinating feature here is of ‘evidence’ that appeared, on three occasions, to disprove the Bible, having to be completely reinterpreted as further investigations took place. The story of archaeology at Susa is the story of the steady endorsement of the truth of the Bible. Scripture was vindicated – just as we would have expected; for, unlike some of the conclusions of the archaeologists, the Word of God does not change.

excerpt.rendered: Another aspect of holiness is being ‘set apart’ by God for His purpose. Paul was a man who knew first-hand

content.rendered:
Another aspect of holiness is being ‘set apart’ by God for His purpose. Paul was a man who knew first-hand the grace and purpose of God. As someone who was “called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God” (Romans 1:1), God had a special plan for him which would be revealed through a dramatic encounter with the Lord Jesus.

Before he was known as Paul, “servant of Christ Jesus” (Romans 1:1), he was Saul of Tarsus, a pedantic Pharisee and religious extremist who tried to destroy the Christian church (Acts 8:3). He was still “breathing threats and murder” against Christians when he encountered Jesus on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:1).

A voice from heaven called out his name: “‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’” (verse 4). These seven anguished words transformed Saul’s life in an instant. Through tormenting Christians, he
was crucifying Christ all over again. In deep remorse, Saul repented of his past and became a follower of Jesus.

In Greek, ‘Saul’ means ‘asked for (from God)’. Before he was even born, Saul was singled out by God to be an apostle. In Hebrew, his name means ‘prayed for’. I’m sure Jesus Christ prayed for Saul to
repent, in the same way he prayed for Simon Peter (see Luke 22:31,32).

After being ‘set apart’ by God for his first missionary journey, Saul became known as ‘Paul’ (Acts 13:2-9). ‘Paul’ means ‘small’ or ‘little’. With this name change, Paul’s character also dramatically transformed from prideful persecutor to humble preacher.

The life of Paul demonstrates how God can call anyone to be holy, even the very worst of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). Holiness isn’t about being perfect – holiness is responding to God’s call and taking on the name of Christ. Called by name. Called to repent. Given a new name.

Have you responded to God’s call and repented through baptism? Then you have been given a new name: Christian. With this new, holy name comes a new life and purpose. This purpose, as Christ tells Paul, is to be a ‘witness’ to others (Acts 26:16): showing the same grace, love and mercy which the Lord has shown you.

excerpt.rendered: Sometimes we can fall into thinking that because holiness is God’s characteristic, we aren’t like Him. Even if we tried

content.rendered:
Sometimes we can fall into thinking that because holiness is God’s characteristic, we aren’t like Him. Even if we tried to be holy, that sounds like an awful lot of discomfort and effort. Does that sound familiar? Those thoughts can creep into our mind if we have a wrong image of holiness, so it is essential for us to look at what holiness really means for us.

I’d like to pose the following hypothesis: Even though God is holy, complete, completely perfect, and perfectly separate from sin, holiness is not unreachable for us. All the words I just mentioned are commonly used interchangeably for the word ‘holy’. Visualise them in your mind as a precious jewel – something perfect in the way it’s made. When you look at it, you can’t help thinking it is complete. This jewel is incredibly valuable and therefore something you would keep separate, apart from influences that could cause damage or harm to it.

Now imagine you are that jewel. That’s what God means when He says: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). You are precious in His eyes! How can we be holy? Stay away from those harmful influences. Show that you are special. Stay separate. In practice, that involves having the following:

A HOLY HEAD
The most crucial part about being holy in your head involves your thinking. What do you plan? What do you prioritise? What do you dwell on? Who do you think about? Holy thoughts don’t look for
opportunities to serve self. The holy mind seeks to glorify God in everything: “my brothers and sisters, always think about what is true. Think about what is noble, right and pure. Think about what is lovely and worthy of respect. If anything is excellent or worthy of praise, think about those kinds of things” (Philippians 4:8, NIrV).

HOLY HANDS
Holy hands refer more to what we are doing physically. Jesus Christ had perfectly holy hands. With them he blessed the children, he reached out to the outcasts of society. He was not defiled by their uncleanness; he brought them the help they needed, and so made them complete. He prayed, maybe even with his hands uplifted. His holiness came from a closeness to his God, and therefore being separate from sin. We can follow that example and use our hands to do what blesses and does good to those around us. Holy hands don’t follow bad habits, lead people (including ourselves) astray or craft distracting false idols. They don’t try to get as close as they can to sin.

A HOLY HEART
In many ways, the holy heart is the trickier challenge because a holy heart is not directly visible to the outside world. A holy heart is set upon what is right – working towards God’s kingdom. In your heart, your secret place, you can keep what you treasure most. Is God in that secret place for you? Or is your heart filled with things you would be ashamed of saying in front of your Lord Jesus? “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Luke 12:34).

Does that make you feel like you will never measure up? The good news is that “it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). Paul goes on to say, “Do all things without grumbling or disputing, that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labour in vain” (verses 14-16).

It is worth it, because one day – on that day of Christ’s return – we will see the Holy One, face to face.

excerpt.rendered: If you were asked to choose which is God’s most unique attribute, what would you say? Imagine you had to

content.rendered:
If you were asked to choose which is God’s most unique attribute, what would you say? Imagine you had to choose between grace, love, holiness and compassion. Many would opt for either grace or most likely love. But the most unique characteristic is actually holiness. It is God’s defining characteristic; it’s a term the Bible uses to define His goodness and power. Now that should make us think, ‘What is holiness?’

The Hebrew word is ‘qodesh’, which literally means ‘set apart’. However, that has been somewhat misused and misinterpreted. People can take this to mean that they should not associate with anything or anyone and so they become very insular. Jesus was the “holy one of God” yet he associated with many – so it can’t quite mean that we should live as hermits.

Holiness is very difficult to explain but a simplified description could be ‘being perfect and pure in every way’. God contrasted His ‘complete perfection’ with our imperfection by telling Moses to remove his sandals because he was standing on “holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). Isaiah in his vision was told: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD” (Isaiah 6:3). Not just ‘holy’ but three times holy! It’s as if I said that I saw a man who was huge, huge, huge – you’d know this was a very big man. That is what God is like – He is pure in every way.

God wants us also to be “perfect and pure in every way” and says in Leviticus, “be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). The whole of Leviticus is about becoming perfect or holy as the children of Israel were about to enter the land God had prepared for them. He wanted them to reflect His perfection. But to help them understand that they were impure He made them go through rituals to remind them of their position and state. The difference between God (holy) and mankind (unholy) was stark. God cannot abide impurity and will consume it – hence the frightening power of God is emphasised in the Old Testament.

In the New Testament the emphasis changes. Jesus Christ touches the impure; he associates directly with the unclean, but instead of repelling them he transfers his holiness to them. He heals the infected,
he cleanses the unclean. It’s as if he is making them ‘pure’ and that is the message to us. We cannot become holy on our own, it is our Lord who can cleanse us and therefore bring us near to God.

Holiness is God’s characteristic which we cannot attain on our own; it is only through the touch of Jesus that we can come into His presence.

content.rendered:
The days were long, the work was hard; there was much opposition and she felt discouraged. She did not want to do this kind of work, nor labour in the place where it took her. How she longed to be in a better place, working with those with whom she felt a kindred spirit, working with the one she loved! She felt downcast at her insufficiencies and failures, which were not helped by her difficult surroundings.

Difficult times

Have you ever felt like that? Day follows night, night follows day, and time seems to slip away as we do the things that we always have to do. Life can seem like an endless cycle of having to spend our time occupied in the things of this temporary life, trying to cope with the failures, disappointments and trials that are our lot, trying not to be consumed by it all.

The Bride feels like that; this is where her longing lies. She wants to be with her Beloved, to work with him and to experience his love, but she has a big problem. While thinking of him, she feels inadequate and unworthy of him:

“I am dark … like the tents of Kedar … Do not look upon me, because I am dark, because the sun has tanned me” (Song 1:5,6). 1

1 Bible quotations are from the NKJV except where otherwise stated.

Like the goatskin tents in Kedar that were blackened by the hot sun: this is how she sees herself, afflicted due to the stresses of life. She has to work in her brothers’ vineyards, and not that of her Bridegroom. She does not see herself as a beautiful bride, prepared for her “altogether lovely” Bridegroom (5:16) – she is very conscious of his perfection and beauty. The contrast with herself is painful.

A beautiful city

We too feel unworthy of our Bridegroom. We are very conscious of our failings, compared with the beauty of his character and his complete obedience to his Father’s will. Yet he does not regard us as we see ourselves; his words reveal his wonderful thoughts:

“Like a lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters” (2:2).

“Behold, You are fair, my love! Behold, you are fair!” (4:1).

“You are all fair, my love, and there is no spot in you” (verse 7).

“O my love, you are as beautiful as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem … Turn your eyes away from me, for they have overcome me” (6:4,5).

Tirzah means ‘delight’. It is thought to have been a beautiful city built on a high, commanding position. Jerusalem is the most beautiful of cities – in prospect if not in history. The Bridegroom views his Bride with wonder as he sees her even now in great beauty. His love for his multitudinous Bride overwhelms him. She knows that she is flawed, but he does not see her so. How comforting to know that he sees us as the people that we will become, not the failing people that we are now! Who do we want to be? To have a clear vision of ourselves in glory is a help to us now, as we seek to be worthy of our Bridegroom.

Disaster – yet blessing

The Bridegroom did come to his natural Bride, but she did not open the door to him: “I have taken off my robe; how can I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how can I defile them?” (5:3). So Israel refused their Messiah, who then left them: “I opened for my beloved, but my beloved had turned away and was gone” (verse 6). This was a disaster for those in Israel who refused to believe in him; yet it meant hope for all people of the world who will accept him and seek to obey his commandments.

Our beloved Bridegroom went away to prepare a place for us, but he did not leave his Bride alone. He gave her “the Spirit of truth” (John 14:17). This Comforter would teach the apostles many things and bring to their remembrance all the things that he had said to them (verse 26); they would go into all the world and preach the gospel. This gospel message would reach down through time to the present, still-waiting Bride. The Lord Jesus knew all this, and even when he was about to be arrested and suffer a cruel, agonising death, he prayed for us too:

“I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word; that they all may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I in You; that they also may be one in us …” (17:20,21).

We have this prospect of glorious unity with the whole family in heaven!

The glorious Bride

“‘Come, I will show you the bride, the Lamb’s wife.’ And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God, having the glory of God. Her light was like a most precious stone, like a jasper stone, clear as crystal” (Revelation 21:9-11).

How breathtakingly beautiful! This is the amazing destiny of the presently flawed Bride of the Lord. How comforting it is to know that we will soon hear these wonderful words:

“Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away; for lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. The fig tree puts forth its figs, and the vines are in blossom; they give forth fragrance. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away” (Song 2:10-13, RSV).

This is the beautiful picture that we can hold in our hearts. When the going is hard and problems seem overwhelming, we can take out this picture, examine it, see ourselves with our Bridegroom in glorious unity and holiness, and gain strength to continue. With the beloved disciple John we say, “Even so, come, Lord Jesus!”

content.rendered:
This article leads us to think about the love of God. But first, a little self-analysis.

Imagine, if you will, a large hairy spider, crawling towards you; you can see the hairs on its legs, and it seems to have an evil intent. Its bright little eyes are fixed on your toe, and all the stories about arachnophobia, tarantulas and black widows are running through your mind. Or, if you like spiders, think of snakes or scorpions or whatever makes your hair stand on end just thinking about it. If none of this troubles you, think wasps.

Now, brush that vision away from your mind and think of a playful puppy coming towards you, or a kitten, or whatever you find most appealing. You want to put your hand out and touch those soft ears, to respond to that welcome.

You have probably noticed that you have experienced very different reactions to these different scenarios; yet all are God’s creatures, all are amazing. We can learn something about our ‘love’ from these imaginings. Our love is, naturally speaking, reserved for those things and people that we find attractive, appealing, lovely. So our love is evoked by those things outside ourselves, and our loves, likes and dislikes determine our reactions.

God is love

God’s love is not like that, and there is an essential difference. Although the Lord God is our example, nevertheless His love will always have a quality about it that we find hard to emulate. God does not love because He finds things or people lovely or loveable; He loves them, not because He sees in them some priceless attribute or some great worth or beauty, but because He is God, and He loves as a light shines. The Apostle John tells us that “God is love” (1 John 4:8,16) 1 – that is, love is of the very nature of God. It is not just extravagant language; it is true and real and amazing. God’s love is not evoked, not drawn from Him by what is outside Him, but comes from within Him; it is of Him; it is an inescapable facet of the person of the Almighty.

1 Bible quotations are from the ESV.

His love is extended to whatever is, not reserved for the lovely or the loveable. God loves as a light shines. A lightbulb shines from within itself – we know that there is electricity flowing into it through wires attached, ultimately, to the power grid, but apparently the bulb is the source of light. It is not a mirror reflecting another light, it is not illuminated by another; in a completely dark room, when you switch on the light, the light springs forth and floods the whole room with light which reveals all that is there. The love of God is like that; it springs from Him, it pours from Him and all men receive its warmth. Some respond in faith and find that the love expressed in creation has a greater parallel in the spiritual realm, in the person of the Lord Jesus, and in all spiritual blessings in him. Some do not respond and are immeasurably the poorer.

Not pretend love

God’s love is not a pretence. He does not just pretend to love us; He is not acting love. It is perhaps surprising that such a thought could even arise, but it does because that is how we often behave. We mimic an emotion because we think we should. We wear a mask. Our natural inclinations are far from the pattern of the Lord; selfishness and self-centeredness are our natural characteristics, and it is the lifetime battle of discipleship to replace such impulses with the fruit of the Spirit.

In the meantime, we often wear a mask. It is not suggested that there is anything wrong with wearing this mask; we have no other option. It is part of Christian discipline. Perhaps, by God’s grace, when the mask is finally removed, it may be found that underneath we have conformed, in part, to the pattern of the Lord. But the Lord God is not like us. He is without hypocrisy; in Him there is no pretence; He really is love, and He loves as a light shines. In the words of Paul in Romans, “hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts … God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:5,8); “… nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (8:39).

Boundless love

Our love has constricting bounds. It is often a poor and compromised emotion. His love is pure and boundless. So, His love is not put off by those things that would surely destroy our love. His love is not only for the loveable and the lovely. He can love a sinner, such as you or me. He is not pretending; He really does love, even when we are neither loveable nor lovely.

It is not that the Lord is unaware of how we really are. In Scripture leprosy is selected as a parable of sin (see Leviticus 13:1-3). Leprosy infects the very core of a man; it runs in the blood; there was no cure – even today it is a persistent disease; it pervades the whole body; it influences every area of living; shows itself in every manner and at every moment. It is the perfect parable of a man in sin. So there is no question that God knows us through and through; understands our hearts; is not deceived by our mask.

And yet He loves us; loves us enough to give His own Son to die for us. And this parable (leprosy) guards against another danger: once we realise that God loves us, it is a small step to think to ourselves, “Then I must be loveable, there must be something in me that God finds attractive”; and it is another small step to say to ourselves, “So I really deserve God’s love.” Nothing can be further from the truth, and the leprosy parable needs to live in our minds.

God loves us because He is God, and loves as a light shines. “God so loved the world …” (John 3:16). At first thought, that may seem surprising; the word “world” has many negative connotations in Scripture. The same writer says, “Do not love the world” (1 John 2:15) – the same word. In John 3:16, where Jesus spoke to Nicodemus, he could have said, “God so loved the saints, or the believers, or His children”; but no, “God so loved the world” – all without exception.

Resisting God’s love

Now of course, God is also righteous; when a man or woman resists His love and ignores His Word, the principles of righteousness will frustrate the love of God, and adverse judgment is the inevitable end. Righteousness will not allow an unrepentant sinner to live indefinitely; but note that even then God’s love prevails. The oblivion of death is a kindness. In death there is no pain, no remorse, no consciousness of anything; it is a kind end for one who might have feared much worse. That is why the false doctrine of eternal torment in the fires of hell is entirely incompatible with the character of God, the love of God. God loves as a light shines even upon those who, sadly, refuse His salvation.

But if a man or woman will turn in humility and faith, then the Lord is gracious and His love is extended freely and bountifully. “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that He loved us and sent His Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10); “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God” (3:1).

Where is our love?

Where are we in this matter? Where stands our love? Perhaps somewhere between the two? We retain our natural impulse to love the lovely, and only the lovely. Yet, by the grace of God, and the influence of the Word, we are learning the love of God. Our love and care begin to overcome any adverse reaction. We learn to forgive, because we have been forgiven, and that we might be forgiven. We begin to see beyond the unpleasantness of human nature to the potential of a converted soul. Perhaps we see in our own hearts the unloveliness of a fallen nature, but perceive also glimmers of change as the love of God is spread abroad in our hearts.

The Lord Jesus also showed in full measure God’s love in all its glory. Under the Law of Moses, the leprous man would have made the Lord Jesus unclean. Now it was reversed: the Lord Jesus made the man clean (see Matthew 8:2-4). And Jesus touched him. He could have stood apart, perhaps touched him after he was cleansed; but no, he touched him as he was – one who may not have felt a human touch for a very long time.

While we were sinners

It was while we were still sinners that the Lord touched us. The Lord Jesus also loved those who were unattractive, spurned, rejected. He was moved with compassion, not revolted by the sight of the leper with his hideous distortion and disfigurement. He did not shrink back, as we might, from the deranged. He shared his Father’s assessment and condemnation of sin – and died for sinners. His love also was as a light shines. We also seek to be so, however falteringly, so Paul counsels us: “May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ” (2 Thessalonians 3:5).

God who calls himself ‘Father’, who revealed Himself in the Lord Jesus, and then told us not just “This is My Son” but “This is My beloved Son” – the Son of My love – sacrificed that love and sent him to die on the terrible cross to be the Saviour of all who will turn in faith and love. And it was not because we are loveable, or lovely, but because He is God, and His love shines as a light.

So, brothers and sisters, in the words of Jude, “keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life” (Jude verse 21).

There are many wonderful features of our faith and our community – blessings handed down to us both in terms of our doctrinal and practical understanding from Scripture, and the way the community is organised and structured. This piece, though, is about a different distinguishing feature of ours – not quite as unusual, perhaps, but crucially important nevertheless, and one which underpins every aspect of our fellowship. It is our approach to Scripture.

The right foundation

Our Statement of Faith rightly rests on a Foundation Clause which states that the Scriptures are our only source of information about God and His ways, and that they are wholly inspired. Ours is a revealed religion. We do not look inwards into ourselves to introspect and thence deduce the truth; we know spiritual truth only on an ‘outside in’ basis, because God has chosen to intervene in the world to reveal it to us. It is “to the law and to the testimony” that we must turn to understand what is what regarding the big realities of life – not to developing church tradition, to authoritative leaders, or to claims of direct revelation from the Holy Spirit.

“The Foundation – That the book currently known as the Bible, consisting of the Scriptures of Moses, the prophets, and the apostles, is the only source of knowledge concerning God and His purposes at present extant or available in the earth, and that the same were wholly given by inspiration of God in the writers, and are consequently without error in all parts of them, except such as may be due to errors of transcription or translation.” (2 Timothy 3:16; 1 Corinthians 2:13; Hebrews 1:1; 2 Peter 1:21; 1 Corinthians 14:37; Nehemiah 9:30; John 10:35)

Flowing out of this comes a whole approach to Scripture. “Why do we always have to read the Bible?” our children might ask, sometimes in exasperation! “Why do we listen to so many talks and do all that Bible study?” Of course there is a danger that study and knowledge can become ends in themselves; that we focus on the letter and not the spirit; that we over-intellectualise our faith; or that we spend so much time studying that we don’t get out there enough to actually do the Word of God in real life, or tell other people about it. And yet, alert to those dangers as we must be, the fact remains that the Word of God is prime. How could we not read it? How could we not study it for all we are worth? God has spoken, after all, and just one of His words must outrank a million of ours.

The whole counsel

Coupled with this is a ‘whole counsel of God’ approach to Scripture. We read and value the whole thing, Old and New Testaments alike, and see it as one unfolding revelation of God, consistent with itself and deeply interconnected. Ours is not an approach which lays the Old Testament to one side, slightly embarrassed, and preferring not to talk about it. We reject the notion of a bloodthirsty, angry God in the Old Testament who finally educates Himself to become ‘clean and nice’ in the New. Instead, we meet a consistent God of infinite depth and beauty in both Testaments, a God of mercy and of judgment, a God who confounds and challenges our expectations of Him and refuses to fit into the boxes that we sometimes subconsciously try to make for Him. Of course it is true that there are different periods in salvation history, that ritual observance of the Law is not required today, and that God’s perfect revelation of Himself in Christ is utterly transformational and once-for-all. But it is a revelation that was planned from the very beginning, and which is spoken of and foreshadowed throughout the Old Testament. It is no accident that the New Testament begins by taking us immediately back to Abraham and to David; this is no less than we would expect.

Our view, then, is that all Scripture is inspired and profitable; that it was God not man who was speaking in times past to the fathers by the prophets. We reject that the older records are the ideas of primitives. Our approach to Scripture is holistic – we look for connections, for Bible echoes, for foreshadowings, for eternal principles that run consistently through Scripture. We seek to understand one scripture in the light of another. When we want to understand a topic, we don’t latch on to one verse and interpret it irrespective of whatever else the Bible might say on that or related subjects; rather, we try to see each passage in the light of the bigger scriptural picture, carefully looking for those overarching themes and connections.

Why do we do this? What is our license for approaching Scripture in that way? There are at least three reasons, each of which could be expanded on at length:

  • By specific statement. The Scriptures (Old and New Testament) claim to be God’s inspired Word, breathed out by Him, pure words and true, our “thus saith the Lord”.
  • By example. Jesus and Paul and the other New Testament writers quote and use Old Testament Scripture in a way that shows that they believe it to be completely reliable and absolutely authoritative. As Jesus said, “the scripture cannot be broken”. There is also testimony within the New Testament about itself (for example, Peter considering Paul’s writings as ‘Scripture’).
  • By inductive proof. When we read the Scriptures this way, it simply works, and in a way which constantly delights and amazes – we find connections we didn’t expect, types and symbols we hadn’t considered, beautiful symmetries and consistencies. The Bible is probably the most connected and interwoven (‘intertextual’) book there is precisely because it is all one Word of God!

Alternative approaches

For Christadelphians, then, it is entirely normal to be studying a passage in the New Testament, for instance, and to expect to turn back to the Old for additional insights and background, or to put what one part of Scripture says about a topic against what another says, or to think about how a teaching in one place meshes with another important biblical theme.

We might well take this for granted; it seems so obvious that we would read the Scriptures that way. Why would anyone do anything else? And yet it is relatively uncommon! There are churches who scarcely consider the Old Testament at all. Even for supposedly ‘whole Bible’ churches, statistics often show that disproportionate time is spent on New versus Old (sometimes in ratios of 15:1 or worse), and the Bible as a whole is less well understood. This can lead to a lack of balance because only one aspect of a subject is considered, or because the Old Testament background to a topic is not brought sufficiently into the mix.

Similarly, it can be a real eye-opener to discover how differently the Bible is approached in scholarship. Many assume an ‘evolutionary’ model in which a certain writer couldn’t have said something at a certain date because (it is claimed) no one had thought such a thing by that point in history. Everything is considered in human terms and limited by (often unnecessary) human assumptions. It is assumed that doctrines develop over time as writers get more sophisticated (thus, it is claimed, John has a more ‘developed’ Christology than the other evangelists, so must have been much later in the assumed inexorable journey towards the doctrine of the Trinity).

The conception that writers, infallibly guided by the Holy Spirit, are bringing together different facets of the truth which are meant to be placed together and seen in the light of one another to bring us to the whole truth of God on a topic is not necessarily common. Instead, wedges are driven between biblical writers (“James thought this, but Paul’s view was different”; “Zechariah’s perspective was different from Haggai’s …”). Nowhere is this clearer than in the wedge that is classically driven between Jesus and Paul, with Jesus sometimes seen as some kind of charismatic Galilean rabbi and Paul as the great (although sometimes confused!) theologian and founder of Christianity as a world religion. But this is a terrible mistake. Jesus was able to come and present the uncompromising and transformational message that he did precisely because he knew that the Apostle Paul and others, also guided by the Spirit, would come afterwards, and further and more fully explain the significance of what he would accomplish – and how it all grew from those essential Old Testament roots. In God’s great design, the whole thing was always meant to be a unity.

So what?

This heritage of our holistic approach to Scripture is a very special and precious thing. We say this not to congratulate ourselves, but to take a moment to appreciate what we have (after all, we didn’t invent it; we’re just trying to embody the attitude to Scripture that Jesus and the apostles had). It comes naturally to us because this is how we’ve always done it, and we might take it for granted. But in the wider world it is not necessarily ‘normal’ at all, and one of its consequences is that, on some matters and passages, our exposition will be different from that of those around us: we will hopefully have a more broad-based, deeper-founded ‘whole-Scripture’ approach to our exposition than others will sometimes take.

We might think that it doesn’t matter what approach others take to Scripture because we are not operating in that environment. But non-Christadelphian Bible teachers, writers, bloggers and podcast-creators often study under those other frameworks and (often subconsciously) operate under their assumptions. It’s now easier than ever for us to come across this material and not necessarily realise the differences. Sometimes, even amongst ourselves, we may be tempted to deemphasise or devalue some parts of Scripture, or to say, “Shouldn’t we just focus on the teachings of Jesus?” Of course we absolutely should focus on them, but we shouldn’t just focus on them! We should remember that Jesus’ words are themselves tethered to, built upon, and expounded by the rest of Scripture.

Let us appreciate, then, what we’ve been gifted in looking at and studying the whole of Scripture. Never let us be guilty of snatching at passages and atomising Scripture into a set of independent (and, for some, contradictory) teachings about this or that. Rather, let us continue to treat each passage as part of a beautifully connected, intricate and endlessly fascinating whole of wide and eternal relevance. No ‘Jesus versus Paul’ for us, but rather Jesus illuminating Paul, and Paul illuminating Jesus – and all the other biblical writers too! – with our Lord God in heaven as the greater Author behind all those wonderful and necessary component parts of the Bible He has blessed us with.

content.rendered:
The word of God wasn’t just theoretical for Ezekiel. Being a prophet for the Almighty affected his life directly. Not only were his words to be signs to the people around him, he himself was to be a sign to them (Ezekiel 4:3; 12:6,11; 24:24,27). That would not have been easy for Ezekiel. His actions were to stir people and to cause them to ask questions, making them ready (or at least readier) to receive his message.

In chapter 4:1-3 Ezekiel is instructed to enact the siege of Jerusalem (since the book is pretty much chronological, we assume the siege was still in the future; see 1:3, 8:1, 24:1,2). Not only are the people told what is going to happen to Jerusalem, it is portrayed as a picture before them.

Then Ezekiel is told he must lie on his left side for 390 days (4:4,5), each day being representative of a year of punishment for the house of Israel. Once this is done, he then has to lie on
his right side for 40 days to bear the iniquity of Judah too. This is another one of those puzzling passages where one wonders how this worked; we’re talking about more than a year! Did
he lie there 24/7 or did he go home at the end of the day and return in the morning? Either way, the work of a prophet affected him personally.

In the following chapter Ezekiel is told to cut off his hair. People usually only cut off their hair for a vow or for cleansing (Leviticus 14:8; Numbers 6:18), because it was considered a shame (Leviticus 21:5; 2 Samuel 10:4,5). In Ezekiel’s case, the hair represented the Jews and again he was to act out what was going to happen to them. Looking at the ‘timeflags’ in 1:2 and 8:1 which are 14 months apart, I wonder if this enactment with the hair happened while he was lying on the side.

It makes you wonder what the people thought of Ezekiel. Did they think of him as a freak? Later on God warns him that the people are talking about him, that they listen to him, but that they won’t do as he asked (33:30-32). It was just mild entertainment to them!

In chapter 12 he again acts out what would happen to their compatriots back in Jerusalem. He was to expect questions from his audience (verse 9). The explanation (verses 10-14) is remarkably accurate – check its fulfilment in 2 Kings 25:4-7. But the worst hit for Ezekiel comes in chapter 24. As a sign to the people around him, Ezekiel’s wife dies (verses 15-24). Why would God do this? And how could Ezekiel bear it? But he did (verse 18).

Ezekiel’s life as a prophet was anything but easy, but he put up with it. He endured all the hardships for the LORD’s sake, having faith that God had promised something better. What are we willing to put up with for the sake of our faith?

content.rendered:
There is a strange inconsistency about modern attitudes to the abilities of people in ancient days. This is a generation when postal deliveries get slower and slower. Yet there is a marked tendency to talk in a patronising fashion about the limitations of inter-communication in the time of the apostles. No telephone, radio or newspapers! No railways, no fast ocean vessels, no motorways!

Even so, for all their technical limitations, the people of the Roman world were not fools. The Empire was equipped with a superb network of roads on which couriers were ceaselessly coming and going. Duplication of documents was a well-organised business, and here were even lending libraries. Some hints of this busy efficient systematic way of life peep out in the epistles of Paul. They show that from the very earliest days, the growing church made full use of the facilities of inter-communication in order to forge bonds of fellowship between widely separated ecclesias.

Good News Spread Abroad

There are two excellent examples of this in the epistles written by Paul to the Thessalonians. So far as indications go, these short letters were written from Athens or Corinth only a very short time after Paul had left Thessalonica. It is very unlikely that a period of more than six months had elapsed from the time of his first preaching there to the writing of these letters. Yet he was able to say: “In every place your faith to God-ward is spread abroad; so that we need not to speak anything (about you)” (1 Thess. 1:8).

Thus within the short space of a few months ecclesias everywhere (e.g. Philippi, Galatia, Antioch, Judaea) had heard the exciting story of the Gospel’s progress among the Thessalonians. Already, far and wide, the faith and zeal of those new converts was talked about. There was no need for Paul to indulge in any publicity on their behalf! “For”, he continued, “they themselves (his correspondents in various places) report concerning us what manner of entering in we had unto you” (1:9); that is, as the next words show, the sincerity and enthusiasm of the reception of the message there filled Christian correspondence to all parts. The implication seems to be that some letters received by Paul even brought him “news” about his own missionary work in Thessalonica.

Even though Paul himself “need not speak anything” about progress in Thessalonica, he apparently did; “we ourselves glory in you in the churches of God” (2 Thess. 1:4) – a further indication that the apostle found time to keep other parts of the Christian world posted about Gentile eagerness for the Gospel.

It was the same regarding other churches also: “I thank my God through Jesus Christ for you all, that your faith is spoken of throughout the whole world”, he wrote to and about the ecclesia in Rome. It was more to be expected that the progress of the Gospel in Rome would be known and talked about everywhere, for that great city was the hub of the empire. Even so, the words provide an additional bit of information about the network of communications which made the ecclesias of the first century almost as close-knit as those of the twentieth.

A Faithful Minister

The epistle to the Colossians provides another example. ‘We heard of your faith in Christ Jesus, and of the love which he have to all saints”, Paul wrote to them (1:4). The words imply a detailed knowledge of the pattern of their ecclesial life. Evidently this news had come through Epaphras “our dear fellowservant, who is for you a faithful minister of Christ; who also declared unto us your love in the Spirit” (1:7,8).

Indeed, Epaphras was only one of a splendid team of young men, who evidently put themselves entirely at the service of Paul and his Gospel work. When Epistles and Acts are combed over, the list of dedicated workers who gave themselves to the Lord in this way is tremendously impressive. It is also shaming to the church of the present day, which with a tenfold increase in the number of its missionaries would still be ill-stocked. The list includes: Luke, Mark, Timothy, Tychicus, Aquila and Priscilla, Erastus, Trophimus, Titus, Crescens, Artemas, Apollos, Zenas, Onesimus, Jesus Justus, Epaphroditus, Tertius, Demas (for a while); and it is unlikely that Phoebe was the only woman who played her part in this splendid work.

An even more emphatic demonstration of the efficiency of communication in the early church comes incidentally in Peter’s second epistle: “… even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given unto him, wrote unto you (there is much variation of opinion as to which letter this refers to), as also in all his epistles …” (2 Peter 3:15,16). Charles Begg, Regius Professor of Ecclesiastical History at Oxford (1910), commented on this: “There is nothing surprising in these words. Under the Empire epistolary communication was as easy as it is now, though the speed of conveyance was not quite so great. It is not only possible, but probable, that St. Peter received every one of St. Paul’s Epistles within a month or two of its publication” (Int. Crit. Comm. on Peter and Jude). Evidently our brethren of the early days knew a good deal about each other, even though widely separated.

This fact makes all the more telling the argument regarding the early church’s doctrine of fellowship to be drawn from the Seven Letters to the Churches. Sardis was “dead”; Laodicea was “wretched and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked”; Ephesus had “left its first love”; Pergamos tolerated “Balaamites” and “Nicolaitanes”; Thyatira had in its midst a “prophetess” who seduced the Lord’s servants. Yet Smyrna and Philadelphia, both highly commended and warmly encouraged, are given no reminder of their bounden duty to sever all connection with such corrupt ecclesias! The obvious inference is that the first century doctrine of fellowship did not require this kind of drastic action. Indeed, with complete knowledge of all the circumstances, Jesus described himself as the one “that holdeth the seven stars in his right hand”!

The answer usually given by self-confident separatists to this argument is: “But of course these seven ecclesias were not in touch with each other. Communication was not easy in those days, and so they were unaware of the lapses that were taking place. Had they been, of course they would have cut off these unworthy ecclesias”!

How well does such an argument stand up?

Harry Whittaker

Comment Upon Inter-Ecclesial Fellowship

In the above article Brother Whittaker has drawn attention to the question of withdrawal from ecclesias. It has happened more than once that a group of brethren or ecclesias has withdrawn from another ecclesia over what is in their opinion some error of doctrine or more usually of practice and then withdrawn from all other ecclesias who do not support that judgement, on the ground that the latter are involved in the sin of the first ecclesia. This is sometimes known as “block disfellowship” and clearly has no sanction in Scripture.

However, sometimes the circumstances are such as to challenge the judgement of other ecclesias and require their decision. To put the matter in perspective we offer the following extract from an Editorial Note on “Inter-Ecclesial Responsibility” (The Christadelphian, July 1945): “… ecclesias have a duty to make rules regulating their procedure in harmony with the principles of ecclesial life laid down by the apostles. And ecclesias are related to each other as members of the body of Christ. While the Lord rebuked each of the seven Churches for its faults, he added to each of the letters to the Churches that he that hath an ear should hear what he said, for what he said was intended for all to hear. The rebuke of one was a warning to all to avoid the evil rebuked. If an ecclesia is known to persist in teaching wrong doctrine, or in retaining in fellowship those who do, other ecclesias can only avoid being involved by disclaiming association. In matters of doubt, where it is a question of judgment of fact, ecclesial decisions must be respected, as the Guide and the Constitution provide. But when there is grave error in doctrine or practice, an ecclesia has a duty of loyalty to the Truth, and it is recognised among us that by the Truth is meant the definition of doctrine in the Statement of Faith. If an ecclesia fail in such loyalty, other ecclesias cannot co-operate without complicity. Harmony in essentials has ceased to exist, and behind a facade of union there is really disunity. Division is a sin when there is loyalty to Truth: when there is disagreement on fundamentals it is an evil to be endured with patience.”

title.rendered: Renew: a new digital service from the Office

content.rendered:
Over the past twelve months, a team at the Office has been working hard to create a new digital service called Renew. This will be a website (a web app), available, God willing, by the time you read this, to be followed by a mobile app (iOS and Android) in the second half of this year. Designed to be a unique repository of Christadelphian content, on initial release it will contain the magazine in an attractive readable format, along with CMPA books (and soon booklets) – but also audiobooks, and other, non-CMPA Christadelphian material such as podcasts and music.

Why call it Renew?

There are two key passages behind the choice of the name. One is Romans 12:2, which exhorts us: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind …” 1 The pressure and thinking of this world crowd in upon us all too readily in modern, digitally-enabled life; it can be hard to find a minute for spiritual reflection and the things of God. Our aim with Renew is to try to use technology for good by providing a powerful platform that is a real treasure-trove of biblical content from across the history and the breadth of our community. That includes Bible study and exhortation from some of our most able expositors of the past and present, but also audio content for reflection, meditation and worship – and, in time, perhaps other features, such as community news and events, daily Bible readings and other features.

1 Bible quotations are from the ESV.

A second passage is 2 Corinthians 4:16-18:

“So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.”

We are all ageing, and the pressures of this world, physical, emotional and ideological, can each take their toll. But if we can use technology as a tool that can help us in the process of spiritual renewal, by expounding the Word of God and promoting the deep fellowship that we share, then we should certainly try to do so. The real source of renewal, of course, is the Word of God that is able to transform our minds into the mind of Christ; but we can help one another in that journey by opening up the Scriptures for each other, and through encouragement and shared worship.

The story of the project

Renew began life a few years ago as an iPhone app focused on Christadelphian music, the brainchild of Brother Jason Robinson (Thousand Oaks, CA, USA). It amassed over 500 subscribers and was appreciated by many, particularly young people, as a convenient tool to access Christadelphian music from such sources as Jehoshaphat Music, the Manitoulin camps and elsewhere. But it was difficult to support single-handedly, and there was always a desire to expand into expositional and exhortational content, both written and audio. The Christadelphian Office has a rich repository of content, from the days of Brother Robert Roberts right up to the present. It includes excellent Christadelphian expositional writing, as well as powerful exhortational and practical articles. There is also youth content through Faith Alive, and a deep global connection through our ‘News and Work’ section and the Office’s function as a ‘central hub’ for the community.

Thus conversations between Renew and the Office began. The Office already had a digital subscription service (our Digital Library), but, whilst powerful as a vast repository of content, it was built using legacy technology, and the search facility – so crucial to an online library – was problematic. It was an easy decision to make, therefore: Renew would come under the auspices of the Office, and would be reconceived as a much fuller digital platform, in both mobile and web formats, able to provide both text and audio content (video is also possible, but that is not our current focus). It would aim to bring together the best of both legacy platforms while trying to avoid any obvious shortcomings, and it would give us the opportunity to build things in a modern, scalable way, using the latest technology.

Thanks to a generous ecclesial donation, the costs of developing the new app have largely been covered. This means that we were able to hire top-level technical talent on a part-time basis. Brother Luke Bennett (Nuneaton, Whitestone, UK), a former developer and chief technology officer, is contracted to the project on this basis, and is its technical lead. We also use a non-Christadelphian developer based in Nashville (TN, USA). Other members of the Renew team include Sisters Esther Ramcharan (Toronto West, ON, Canada) and Claire Robinson (Brant County, ON, Canada) and Brother Joshua Bryan (Glasgow, Kelvin, UK). Other members of the existing Office team are also involved, along with some of our volunteers helping out in various ways. We are grateful to them all. The project is overseen by Brothers Jason Robinson and Mark Vincent on behalf of the CMPA.

What is Renew?

Essentially, it is a repository of content (magazine articles, books, songs, podcast episodes and audiobook chapters) which you can subscribe to and access either through a website (technically a web app – renew.thechristadelphian.com), or through a mobile app (the latter, in iOS and Android versions, will be released later in the year, God willing). The website is available now. You can sign up, verify your email address and that you are Christadelphian-connected, and you are on your way.

This is a subscription service, and the available payment tiers are illustrated in the panel overleaf (there is also a free tier which includes free articles, music and podcasts, plus other content). Family subscription plans are also available, allowing several family members to have their own logins for a single monthly payment.

What’s included

Depending on the subscription tier that you select, available content on day one will include:

  • The full archive of The Christadelphian magazine (more than 40,000 articles from authors including Robert Roberts, John Carter, Harry Tennant and Dennis Gillett, as well as our writers from the modern era). We hope to make the archive of Testimony magazine articles available in due course.
  • All our CMPA books (over 220 titles), with booklets coming soon (preaching and community titles such as The Ecclesial Guide).
  • A large selection of Christadelphian music (over 500 tracks from sources like Jehoshaphat Music, plus choir recordings of all the hymns).
  • A vast collection of podcast episodes, including Good Christadelphian Talks from California, Wilderness Conversations from Sydney, the Faith-Works podcast from Adelaide (for young people, by young people), the Bible Feed podcast from the UK, and others. There will be more than 600 episodes available at launch.
  • Audiobooks – mainly CMPA books, but also some non-CMPA titles. There will be around forty titles at launch, both classics and newer titles, and we will be adding more over time.

God willing, all this is only the beginning. We have built Renew as a platform, designed to be easily expanded. We plan to launch more content and services over time, and will keep you updated about progress through the magazine, the app, via newsletters, email and social media.

A few key questions

I don’t want all this technology. Can I still get my print magazine as I always have?

Certainly. No one will be forced to migrate to Renew. You can continue subscribing to the print magazine month-by month as you are currently doing, if you wish.

I am a Christadelphian Digital Library customer. How will this affect me?

Ultimately, Renew will be a much more powerful and complete platform than the Digital Library. If you want to switch over immediately, you can do so – just subscribe to Renew, and then cancel your Digital Library subscription. However, we will be emailing all our Digital Library customers in May / June to help them to migrate.

Why don’t you launch the mobile app right away?

This is mainly about trying to keep things manageable by focusing on one thing at a time. We want to get as many people as we can using the website and subscribing in a manageable way, while we get everything finished on the mobile app. Then, when we are ready to launch the app, people will already have their logins and subscriptions in place, and will be familiar with how it all works.

I want to subscribe to Renew and I already have a digital subscription to the magazine.

If you can’t wait, then you can subscribe to Renew right away, and then cancel your other subscription when you’re ready. Alternatively, we’ll be emailing all our auto-renewing digital subscribers over the next couple of months with details of how to migrate.

I have a digital subscription to the magazine, but I don’t want to subscribe to Renew because I don’t need anything else.

Yes, for the time being it will be possible to stick with this arrangement. If we decide to change that, we’ll let you know.

I want to subscribe to Renew but I already have a print subscription to the magazine.

You can either (1) keep your print subscription and take out a Renew subscription on top, or (2) subscribe to Renew, take the print magazine ‘add-on’ within Renew, and then ask us to cancel and reimburse you for the remainder of your print magazine subscription.

I already have a login and a password for thechristadelphian.com e-commerce store. Do I need a different login and password for Renew?

They are two different systems with two different accounts. Of course, if you wish to use the same email address (and even the same password) for Renew, then you can do so, although the best advice is to use different passwords for different systems where possible, for maximum security.

So much is included – how much will it cost?

There are multiple payment tiers (including free) to cover every budget and requirement. For full details, see the details below.

An exciting future

If you would like to enrol right away, you can do so at renew.thechristadelphian.com for the early-launch version. It would not be surprising if there are still one or two rough edges here and there, so please be patient if that is the case. Or you may prefer to wait a month or two while we sort out any initial teething issues. We will keep you updated through our various communication channels. One key objective is to provide a good search experience. We will be powering this through modern AI techniques, but we will not have all that switched on and working on day one. This means that the search function is definitely one aspect that we expect to see improving as we go through the remainder of 2026.

This is a big project. If you have any feedback or issues, you can let us know either within the app / website, or via renew@thechristadelphian.com. We ask for God’s blessing as we embark on this new phase of our work.

Payment tiers

There are three paid plans, and three add-ons (all payable in other currencies too):
