  • Essentials. £3/month or £33/year. Includes all music and podcasts, current and previous twelve editions of The Christadelphian, at least twenty audio­books and forty books.
  • Deep Dive. £6/month or £66/year. Includes everything in ‘Essentials’, plus the last fifty years of The Christadelphian, and all audio­books and books, except the last five years.
  • Complete. £9/month or £99/year. Includes everything in ‘Deep Dive’, plus full archive of The Christadelphian, all audio­books and books, and additional archives to come.

The following add-ons can be applied to any of the paid plans:

  • Couples (one extra account in the same household). Add £1/month.
  • Family (four extra accounts in the same household). Add £2/month.
  • Print magazine (a physical copy of The Christadelphian through the post each month). Add £3/month.

excerpt.rendered: A popular proverb in Ezekiel’s day was, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on

content.rendered:
A popular proverb in Ezekiel’s day was, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (Ezekiel 18:2). It points to a general feeling amongst the nation of Israel that God was a vengeful God who was quick to punish people for their sins – and not only to punish those directly involved in a particular sin, but also their descendants.

In a way, we can’t really blame those who thought this. After all, time and again, they had heard that God “will by no means clear the guilty,” and will “[visit] the iniquity of the fathers on the children and the children’s children, to the third and to the fourth generation” (Exodus 34:7; see also 20:5; Numbers 14:18; Deuteronomy 5:9). They had also seen first-hand the application of the law – how practising adultery, idol worship, witchcraft and a long list of other offences was punishable by death.

Perhaps out of fear or a lack of understanding, they had focused on the severity of God without also acknowledging His kindness (compare Romans 11:22), for He also said that He “[keeps] mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin” (Exodus 34:7). Hang on! Does God forgive sins, or doesn’t He? No wonder the Israelites were confused!

It was time to set matters straight. Referring to the sour grapes proverb, God declared through Ezekiel: “This proverb shall no more be used by you in Israel” (Ezekiel 18:3). It was important for God’s people to understand that each person was responsible for their own actions. Perhaps there had been a growing sense of helplessness: ‘Our ancestors sinned, so we’re already doomed. The law is too difficult to keep. Why bother?’

Perhaps we sometimes think like this too: ‘Mankind has been struggling with the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life since Adam and Eve were alive. What hope do I have of doing the right thing? What’s the point in trying?’ God responds with another question: ‘Why choose death?’ (see Ezekiel 18:31). God really was giving them – and us – the choice to “turn and live” (verse 32). At the same time, it remains true that “the soul who sins shall die” (verse 20). We all sin, and the consequence is that we die. Digging deeper, we realise that grace is the only answer to this dilemma.

In Ezekiel 18, it is the “righteous” person that shall “surely live” (verse 9), but in Psalm 143:2 we read, “no one living is righteous before [God]”. Without God, righteousness is impossible, but we have a God who “[has] no pleasure in the death of anyone” (Ezekiel 18:32) and “desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). “It is God who justifies,” so, “who shall bring any charge against God’s elect?” (Romans 8:33). We are justified (made righteous) by faith, through the blood of the Lord Jesus Christ, and not by the works of the law (Romans 5:1,9; Galatians 2:16).

We sometimes forget that, as far back as Genesis 3, Jesus was revealed to God’s people. They didn’t know him by name, but little by little, he was revealed through prophecies, principles and allegories. Those who understood what this coming seed would do made for themselves “a new heart and a new spirit” (Ezekiel 18:31). They turned away from evil and tried their hardest to obey God. They chose life, and it will be God’s good pleasure to give it to them when Christ returns.

excerpt.rendered: When we read about a prophet, perhaps our first thought is of someone who makes predictions. But while that was

content.rendered:
When we read about a prophet, perhaps our first thought is of someone who makes predictions. But while that was part of a Biblical phophet’s role, there was more to it. The Hebrew word translated as ‘prophet’ in our English Bibles is often defined in lexicons as ‘spokesperson’ or ‘speaker’, so a prophet was someone who spoke as a representative of God.

A prophet’s message showed people God’s perspective, or revealed things perhaps known only to Him. For excample, although Ezekiel was living many miles from Jerusalem, he was able to see the idolatry and corruption that was going on in the temple there (chapters 8 to 11). This would have helped Ezekiel’s audience make sense of their circumstances. There were in exile because of Judah’s wickedness and the fact that this was still going on in Jerusalem showed that further waves of captivity were imminent.

It’s useful, therefore, to think about the initial audience of a prophet. Who were they? What were the particular circumstances of their time? What was the purpose of the prophecy in their time? Was it to encourage the faithful to stand firm perhaps, or to help people prepare for the judgements of God that were coming? Answering these questions first makes it easier to work out how these prophecies can encourage us today.

Even prophecies which are still to be fulfilled had a foundation in the events of the prophet’s own time. When we look at the prophecy of the dry bones, we dine that in its original context, it was a response to how the Jews felt at the time: “Behold, they say, ‘Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost: we are indeed cut off” (Ezekiel 27:10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 22, 25). Even though Tyre was soon going to fall, new military alliances would emerge from their former trading partners, and they too would ultimately face God’s judgements.

Some aspects of prophecy are timeless – they refer not to a particular period but are true in all ages. Take for example, Ezekiel’s visions of the glory of God. THis showed that God’s presence wasn’t limited to the temple in Jerusalem, but was to be found wherever God’s people were. Thus, the glory of God left the temple where people had turned their back on the true God, and was instead found with the faithful Jewish exiled in Babylon (chapters 1, 3 and 10).

title.rendered: Loving the LORD through every season

content.rendered:
“Seasons serve as powerful metaphors for the various stages we encounter in life.”

Seasons is an annual publication produced for sisters of all ages, with contributions from sisters from all around the world. This is the third book that has been produced in magazine style, and it features articles, uplifting interviews, thoughtful verses, moving poems (for example, “Dementia: where has my mother gone?”) and delicious recipes.

The book is written by many sisters who help the reader to find God in every corner and in every stage of life. It is written conversationally, and it feels as if each sister is talking directly to you – like a family member sharing her life experiences, providing helpful guidance and words of wisdom. Seasons demonstrates how each ‘season’ of life can bring you closer to God. Life is always changing, and we face different challenges in every season:

  • Spring: hope and beginnings.
  • Summer: growth and abundance
  • Autumn: harvest and gratitude
  • Winter: rest and reflection

I particularly liked the interviews with a number of sisters. They are written in the style of having a chat with them over coffee, and I felt that I got to know each of them personally. Here is a sample:

  • “Finding the light”: Bree writes about how she came into the Truth and what it means to her – how it affects her life and the comfort that the Bible gives.
  • “Season of youth”: a young sister from Esslingen in Germany, writes about seeking out her place in the world, meeting new people, making the right choices, and finding role models and spiritual mentors to help and support her in the Truth.
  • “Single season”: Diane addresses the challenge of feeling connected and relevant in the ecclesia. She suggests finding a task for which you can volunteer; contributing will help you feel part of the community.
  • “Mum of teens”: a sister from Adelaide in Australia recounts her experiences of having three teenage boys – the challenges, but also the opportunities, that arise as they grow up; and seeing her sons get to know others through youth camps, and gaining an enthusiasm for the Truth and learning God’s ways.
  • “Wisdom years”: a sister tells how she enjoys having time to help others, providing support and encouragement to young families. She offers important advice to younger sisters: try to put God first, no matter where you are or what your situation; always include God in all aspects of your life.

In addition to the interviews, at the end of each season there is a guided study of the Book of Ruth. This is divided into four parts:

  1. An introduction.
  2. “Elimelech’s choice” – his decision to leave the land of Judah with his wife and two sons, due to famine, and to live in Moab. This is contrasted with the life of Lot, who made a similar decision to dwell in Sodom.
  3. “Life in Moab” – the family were to stay for ten years in a land where the people were known for their idolatrous practices.
  4. “Naomi’s choice” – after her husband and two sons die, she decides to return to Judah with her daughter-in-law Ruth. They are welcomed back, and, acting faithfully, they are blessed by the Lord.

Amongst the many interesting articles, one on the sisters Mary and Martha stands out. They both love God, but they express their love in different ways. Mary loves God with her heart and mind, and Martha serves God with her actions. This article highlights the importance of prioritising and learning to find balance – understanding when it is necessary to spend time with God without distractions, but also knowing when we can be helping and serving others.

There are personal stories, such as Sister Kathleen Ritmeyer’s “Finding and living the Truth in Israel”. She is now at Cardiff ecclesia, but her story began as a Catholic in Ireland, before she became an archaeologist (and a teacher), working on the Temple Mount excavations in Jerusalem. Her knowledge of Israel and the Jews is extremely informative and interesting. She relives her experiences in Israel anecdotally – the people she met, and the places she went. We follow her journey: how she actively sought to find the Truth by studying the Scriptures with a like-minded group in Israel, and then met Brother Leslie and Sister Edith Johnson, who were living in Jerusalem. She read with them and eventually realised that they all had the same beliefs. Kathleen and her husband Brother Leen later moved to the UK.

Seasons includes a wide range of subjects covering all aspects of our lives and roles as sisters. I found the “Woman of valour” piece particularly helpful. It highlights the qualities of the woman who fears the Lord: she has compassion, speaks wise and kind words, and puts God first.

Having finished reading this book – which is beautifully illustrated – I felt blessed by the knowledge and the wisdom shared by other sisters. I know I will be going back to this book regularly to reread sections for uplifting thoughts and encouragement, as well as to try out some of the recipes.

Seasons. Edited by Sister Rebekah Dangerfield and Sister Rose Stone. Click here for more information and to purchase.

excerpt.rendered: Most speakers will know that sensation in the pit of the stomach when the hands of the clock point out

content.rendered:
Most speakers will know that sensation in the pit of the stomach when the hands of the clock point out that our time is up, the audience is getting fidgety, and we still have not finished our address. We can sympathise with the audience. We ourselves have often suffered from brothers who ‘go on too long’. But now it is happening to us, and we are helpless to do anything about it. We begin to perspire. We speak faster and faster to get to the end of our notes. We sit down with a heavy heart, feeling that we have failed again, and decide that we are never going to be a good speaker. We are just not cut out for it.

Cheer up! It has happened to all of us, especially when we first started speaking, and there is a simple and straightforward solution that will prevent it ever happening again. The answer has nothing to do with the quality of our voice, our ability to smile and look at the audience, the kind of notes we use, or the addition of visual aids – all these are irrelevant, in this context. We need to look somewhere else.

The ‘audience contract’

The length of talks is important. Here in the UK, exhortations are typically around twenty-five minutes in length, Sunday Bible talks forty to forty-five minutes, Bible class papers forty to fifty minutes, and fraternal gatherings are usually two talks of forty minutes each. Even though these times are not all the same, if a speaker goes much over them, then the audience can begin to grow resentful.

Someone once invented the concept of an ‘audience contract’. This suggests that, at the start of an address, the audience has a mental picture of how long it is expected to be. They ‘agree’ to sit and listen for this period. After it has gone by, they expect to be released. A similar situation is clear in school: a lesson has a fixed length, the bell goes, and woe betide the teacher if he tries to continue the lesson for another ten minutes! Christadelphians are more polite than schoolchildren, but they experience the same bad feelings if the speaker much exceeds his allotted time. Even though an evening talk is much longer than an exhortation, they do not begin to fidget after twenty-five minutes in the evening, because mentally they expect forty-five minutes. Indeed, if the speaker sat down after twenty-five minutes, they might feel uncomfortable, even cheated. So it is as well to respect these boundaries, if we want people to feel good about, and remember, our addresses.

The question is: How do we ensure that we keep to the time allotted? What is the secret of a ‘punchy’, crisp address? As already suggested, the answer has nothing to do with presentation. It is all a matter of preparation. Preparation is something that takes place well before we walk up the steps to the platform. It belongs to the study, the armchair when the family has gone to bed, the wet towel round the brain, long before the adrenalin begins to pump.

A matter of preparation

Before we start planning an address, we know how much time we should take. We also know that the address must have three parts: a beginning, a middle and an end.

The beginning is the Introduction, when we explain what we are going to talk about, why it is important, and the route that we propose to follow. This is a bit like the president reading out the agenda at the business meeting: people like to know what they are going to be listening to, and that it has a framework which has been planned out in advance – they feel more comfortable that way. So the Introduction is important – the audience needs time to have its appetite whetted, to see where things are going. It is not good practice to start the address by saying, “Please turn to Romans chapter 8.”

In between, and longer than the beginning and the end, is the middle – the Development, the section where we analyse, imagine, persuade or review, logically setting out our argument.

The address must also have an end – a Conclusion, where we look back at what has been said, pick out the key points, and think about how what we have learned might affect us in the future.

How many points to include?

Let’s get down to business. Let’s say that we are preparing an exhortation. This has a target length of twenty-five minutes. We need to set aside five minutes for the Introduction. We will also need five minutes for the Conclusion. This leaves fifteen minutes for the Development. Assuming that it takes five minutes to develop each idea or example, this means that we have time for three – and only three – points in our Development. So for exhortations, we have the ‘Rule of Three Points’ – three points will be our maximum, if we are to keep our contract with the audience. This is about right for an exhortation. Three points is a comfortable number to absorb and remember, and we are meeting to remember Christ, not to listen to an election address.

How many quotations?

Another point worth keeping in mind is the number of Bible passages we can fit into the time allowed. If the audience is asked to find and read many texts, the brain will become numb and the concentration dimmed. In practice, it is much more effective to look at a few texts, and spend enough time on each of them to understand them properly, than to race round the Bible on a verse-by-verse steeplechase. If we can select one good example to prove our point, and prove it thoroughly by reading the passage in its context and analysing it carefully, then what is the point of giving more examples? The extra ones will not add to the impact, and will probably diminish it through mental fatigue.

So, we should set a limit to the maximum number of passages we ask brothers and sisters to look up – say a ‘Rule of Seven Passages’. Seven is a golden number, and seven passages (a ‘passage’ would include the verses around the one we are working on) is probably as much as our brains can cope with at one time. In practice, we might even decide to concentrate on three passages, one for each of the three points of our exhortation, branching out from them where necessary to find, say, an apostolic comment on the Old Testament passage that we are looking at.

Out with the scissors

Now, let’s say that we have decided to take our theme from the day’s Bible readings, and it happens that one of the chapters concerns God’s mercy. We opt to make this the topic of our exhortation. The first step is to assemble a list of other Bible passages relevant to this topic. Some will come from the Old Testament, and some from the New. Some will be highly appropriate, and some will touch only vaguely on the topic. Now, this is the point where most brothers who go on too long go wrong. They feel compelled to include all the relevant passages – a comprehensive survey of Bible passages on God’s mercy. This creates a list of, say, twelve or so passages to get through, and inevitably in trying to look at them all, they run well over the fifteen minutes available for their Development.

What you must do, brothers, is to select the three best examples you can find and discard all the others. Remember, you need five minutes to adequately develop each point of your argument, and in an exhortation you have fifteen minutes in total. So, pick out the three strongest examples from your list of passages – say, God’s declaration of His name to Moses, Hosea as an illustration of His mercy to Israel, and Paul’s rejoicing over God’s mercy in Ephesians 3 – the choice is entirely yours, but make sure that they are the points that you feel most strongly about and can put over convincingly.

Write headlines

Next, set out these three points as ‘newspaper headlines’, and write your notes around them. Make a big headline for the Introduction: for example “INTRODUCTION – The quality of mercy”. Under this heading you will be introducing the subject, what mercy is, why we need it and why we must be merciful, and explaining that we shall be looking at three Bible passages on this subject.

Then write the three Development subheadings, just as if you were a newspaper editor: say, “DEVELOPMENT –

  1. ‘Merciful and gracious’,
  2. ‘They shall be My people’, and
  3. ‘The gift of God’s grace’.”

Now write the headline for the Conclusion: for example, “CONCLUSION – ‘Blessed are the merciful’ in practice.”

You now have three main headings (Introduction, Development and Conclusion) and, under Development, the three sub-headings which are your three points. Write your notes under these headings, and trim away any ideas or distractions which are not immediately relevant to the heading.

Be tough

You need to be quite ruthless. It is like packing for a cycling holiday. You have two panniers and a saddlebag. You assemble on the living-room floor a huge heap of items which you feel might be useful. Then you realise that they will not all fit in, and you reverse the approach. You pick up each one in turn and say, “Can I do without this spare toothbrush?”, “Do I really need three pairs of socks?” and so on, until you end up with only the truly essentials, which you can fit into the three bags. Be like that. Examine each idea that has sprung into your mind and say, “Does this truly belong to my theme? I only have five minutes – is it a really strong point?” If you have any hesitation, then scrap it. Only the best is good enough for God.

Tell them what you’re telling them

Finally, the time comes to climb the steps and give the address. You explain in the Introduction that you want to look at three examples of God’s mercy. Tell us when you start the first example, and when you have finished the first and are moving on the second, because we feel comfortable if we know where you are taking us, that we are in safe hands, and that in due course we will arrive at the destination. And when you get near to your Conclusion, give us a sign that you are coming to the end. Say, “And so we come to our last reference” (and make it your last!). As you come to your Conclusion, close your Bible, and speak slowly, leaning on the rostrum, for these are the words which above all you want the audience to remember – the main points of your address, and the action points for the future.

Bible classes and Sunday talks

Of course, the same principles apply equally to a Bible class address or Bible talk for visitors. Because we have longer, and the subject is more complex, then we may have four or even five sub-headings to our Development.

Let’s say that it is a Bible Class and we are expounding a chapter in an epistle. First, we read it through lots of times, in several different translations, until we see what the author is driving at. Perhaps we read a book or an article by a Christadelphian author who has already commented on the chapter. We look up maps. We make notes about the characters involved, or the towns visited, or the issues that troubled the first readers of the epistle. This is the first stage – the assembling on the living-room floor.

Now out come the editor’s scissors. First, we decide which are the four or five important points the writer of the chapter is making – his own ‘headlines’, where possible, the points where his inspired argument turns. Maybe we won’t have time to cover every verse, so we choose which we will concentrate on, the key ones, the ones that have a vital message for our hearers. We compose our own newspaper sub-headings for the four points of the Development. Then we write our notes under these headings, brutally discarding anything not directly relevant. Next, we need to write an Introduction, to put the chapter into context, explain the background, and tell the audience what we are going to cover in this address (remember, only five minutes for this – it is an introduction, and no more; some introductions take up half the address, which is very bad practice). Finally, we headline the Conclusion, and summarise the main points and their relevance for today.

Sticking to the rules

So, there we have it. No-one need go over his time. Fidgety audiences can be a thing of the past. It is all a matter of careful preparation, sticking to the ‘Rule of Three’ for exhortations and the ‘Rule of Seven’ for quotations, and trimming away anything that is not absolutely to the point.

“And the Lord said, who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of meat in due season?” (Luke 12:42, KJV).

May God bless your labours to prepare healthy, spiritual ‘food’ for our dear brothers and sisters, and strengthen their faith.

title.rendered: Should I use ChatGPT to help prepare my Bible Class talk?

excerpt.rendered: Question of the month Those of us who have tried ChatGPT or other large language model applications will probably recall

content.rendered:
Question of the month

Those of us who have tried ChatGPT or other large language model applications will probably recall the amazement at how powerful this technology is. Its ability to condense, synthesise and summarise, or to brainstorm and suggest new approaches and solutions, seems uncanny. And one of the intriguing things about it is that, at present, leading technologists seem somewhat unsure as to quite why the technology is so effective.

Powerful, but use with care

There seems little doubt that in both corporate and private life there are many powerful uses, with both futurists and present-ists grappling with how it will change the world; there are both extremely positive implications and potentially ominous implications. One of the things that we do know is that, despite how compellingly the output may read, it isn’t always accurate or free from bias; it needs to be fact-checked, read astutely and used with discretion. The technology is better, or at least safer, when it is used to create efficiency by those already familiar with the subject matter being handled than when it is relied upon to produce output on topics that the user does not understand well. There is also the potential of bias, political and otherwise, in what is presented. If we use it (and, again, there can be very powerful reasons to do so), then we need to be informed and, to some degree, on our guard.

There may be some uses within the work of the Truth, but what about the application to Bible study and talk preparation? The technology certainly could be used (“Prepare me a document in the style of abc which summarises the message of xyz chapter and encourages people to pqr”); and while this can certainly be a time-saver in effectively analysing and summarising text or ideas that we might want to understand or engage with (potentially saving us a lot of time reading up on a tangential subject), the real question is whether it should be a core component of Bible study and talk preparation.

You get out what you put in

The biggest beneficiary of any talk or study is not the audience but the one who prepares it. It is the actual process of slowly and deliberately reflecting on the Word of life – turning over its phrases in our minds, meditating on its counsel, thinking about the ‘why’ – that yields the real value and has the potential to transform the heart. Technology has already made the chasing down of Bible echoes and allusions, cross-references and the study of words and grammatical nuance so much easier, and this process of automating the ‘techniques’ of Bible study may well continue as technology progresses. But it is not in the techniques as techniques where the value lies – it is in the meditation and the reflection upon what those techniques yield. Hard graft or technology may tell us that a certain word is used here and also there, that there is a possible allusion, cross-reference or typology going on; but it is only by reflection on what those links may mean, on what God may be telling us, on what He wants us to think and do as the great ‘therefore’ of our efforts, that our minds will be transformed and we will develop a character more like His.

The more we understand about how the brain works, about neural pathways and the way connections are made, developed and cemented, the more we see God’s wisdom in giving us a Word to reflect on. It is by the engaging of our brains and hearts on His Word (as well, of course, as in endeavouring to live the spiritual life) that our conscience is developed and our mind is expanded. Good spiritual thinking develops by meditating on God’s Word – He designed it to be so – and we ‘subcontract’ this thinking, connecting and synthesising process to a machine to our significant detriment.

Denying ourselves the benefit

It is because meditating on God’s Word works, because it is powerful in renewing and transforming our minds, that the Law of Moses and Psalm 1 – to take just two examples – urge us to take the personal time to reflect on the Scriptures (“and in His law he meditates day and night”) and to talk about them at all times. A machine may well be able to produce a coherent piece of text that says broadly the right things about what a passage is saying, and that can even construct a righteous-sounding piece of moral instruction for us. But if we use this instead of taking the time personally to search, reflect and be impacted by the Word of God, then we shall have short-changed ourselves, denying our God the opportunity to work that internal change within us that He so desires. He has designed His Word for that very purpose.

If we are not good with words or with organising ideas coherently (for example), then ChatGPT may be able to help us by tiding up our phrasing or improving our expression, possibly even helping us communicate with our brothers and sisters more effectively as a result. But the ‘hard yards’ of studying the Bible, meditating on it for ourselves, and martialling our thoughts into something that makes sense as practical and relevant exhortation for ourselves and our brothers and sisters, are something that we should not outsource. That would be to deny ourselves a crucial benefit of the Word of God. It falls to each of us – whether we happen to be preparing talks or not – to let God’s Word change us by putting ourselves out to spend time with it, meditating on His will and striving to discern its significance for our daily discipleship.

title.rendered: Jesus – Son of God, Saviour of Man

excerpt.rendered: David, Solomon, Hezekiah, and Josiah were great kings of Israel and Judah. But they had their faults – serious faults

content.rendered:
David, Solomon, Hezekiah, and Josiah were great kings of Israel and Judah. But they had their faults – serious faults that had consequences for the whole nation. This should have shown God’s people the need for someone greater who could be ruler of God’s kingdom forever.

It was evident from his birth that Jesus was different. There was an emperor in Rome, and Herod reigned on his behalf in Jerusalem, but the true king was born in humble surroundings in Bethlehem. Rather than being welcomed as the long-promised deliverer, Jesus’ life was threatened from the beginning. It was clear that there would be animosity between the kingdom of men and the kingdom of God.

When the king was revealed, he came not with an army or a government, or with territorial ambitions or grand plans, but with a message – the Gospel of the kingdom (Matthew 4:23). Much of Jesus’ teaching in Matthew, Mark and Luke is about this kingdom message. His first priority as the one born to be king of Jews was to show people what sort of kingdom he was going to reign over – the kingdom of heaven. Then he demonstrated to them the sort of king he would be – one who used his power to conquer sin and defeat evil, to bring justice to the oppressed, and healing to the sick.

The nature of his kingship came to the fore in the last week of his ministry. It began with him entering Jerusalem on a donkey, in fulfilment of Zechariah’s prophecy, “Behold, your king is coming to you, humble and mounted on a donkey” (Matthew 21:5). It ended with him being crowned – not with gold, but with thorns (Matthew 27:29).

Now he sits enthroned (Revelation 3:21), the ruler over the kings of the earth (Revelation 1:5), until the “kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15).

  • Parents: God and Mary
  • Length of reign: “He shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15)
  • Dates of reign: Yet to begin
  • God’s assessment: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

excerpt.rendered: Uzziah was Judah’s second longest-reigning king and is presented to us in scripture as being strong, powerful and successful. His

content.rendered:
Uzziah was Judah’s second longest-reigning king and is presented to us in scripture as being strong, powerful and successful. His name means ‘strength of God’ and he is also known as Azariah which means ‘God has helped’. There appears to be a play on words in 2 Chronicles 26:15, where we are told, “he was marvellously helped, till he was strong”.

Much of Uzziah’s fifty-two year reign was positive. It is recorded that “he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah had done” (26:4). His list of achievements are very impressive (see verses 5-15): he built, he conquered, he fortified, and his name spread far, for “as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper” (verse 5).

Having inherited the throne aged just sixteen, Uzziah was under the spiritual influence of a man called Zechariah. We are told that Uzziah “set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God” (verse 5). It seems however that once Zechariah departed from the scene, Uzziah’s spiritual discernment faded. We are not given much indication that Uzziah had a true love for God, but we are told that “he loved the soil” (verse 10) – he loved the things of the earth. The spiritual health of the nation was also lacking, for Isaiah, Hosea and Amos all issued divine warning against Judah in the days of Uzziah.

Following all his success, Uzziah “grew proud, to his destruction” (verse 16). Despite having no right to the priesthood, he sought the role of Azariah, the high priest whose name he shared, and entered the temple to offer incense. Consequently, he was smitten by God with leprosy.

Uzziah’s pride provides us with a warning to be humble and to rely on God in our lives, for “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

• Also known as: Azariah
• Parents: Amaziah and Jecoliah
• Length of reign: 52 years
• Dates of reign: 791-740 BC
• God’s assessment: “He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD” (2 Chronicles 26:4).

excerpt.rendered: Humans are put in a position of relative authority on the very first page of our Bible. In Genesis 1:26

content.rendered:
Humans are put in a position of relative authority on the very first page of our Bible. In Genesis 1:26 God says that humans would have “dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth”. This is given as a direct command (verse 28). Man and woman are commanded to rule over them. But man is also immediately given responsibility. When God put the man in the garden it was with the instruction to till and keep it (2:15). We can see then that humans are in an elevated position in creation but have a responsibility to look after it on God’s behalf.

When given these positions humans often will seek more power and more authority. When Eve took the fruit and gave it to her husband it was partly because she believed it would make them more like God (3:4-6).

This was false. When we seek to do things on our own terms and reject the responsibilities God has given us, we move further away from God and not closer to Him. God has made us to rule creation with Him, but on His terms, not ours.

 

It is with this in mind that we come to the first responsibility of a king recorded in Deuteronomy 17. He was to write out a copy of the Law and to study it throughout his reign (verses 18,19). There were also limits placed on his power. These would have been very unusual for a king in the ancient world.

The purpose of having a copy of the Law was so that he could learn to fear the Lord his God. It was only with this mindset that he could effectively lead God’s people. God wanted the king to manifest Him to the nation, so that the nation could in turn show God to the other nations. This position of privilege was a position of responsibility too.

When we are baptized into Christ, we become a part of God’s special people. We are being made into royal priests (1 Peter 2:9). God wants a group of people who will show to the world what He is like. Do we want to be a part of that family of God? If so, we need to accept the responsibilities we have to Him.

excerpt.rendered: Having a good death, as we have seen from the experience of the faithful in Scripture, involves a conscious desire

content.rendered:
Having a good death, as we have seen from the experience of the faithful in Scripture, involves a conscious desire to serve God in our last days, to work for Him and for those whom we interact with or are related to, in spite of our frailty. We know that we serve as defective instruments that God, in His mercy, chooses to use for His purpose. That service entails a desire to help and to save, if possible; to engage with others compassionately and with humility. Can there be anyone who demonstrated these things more powerfully than the Lord Jesus Christ?

Our Lord’s good death

The Lord Jesus Christ, in John 17, prayed openly for God to protect his disciples in this world after his departure. He prayed for them to be sanctified through the Word, and appealed to the Father to keep them unified, that their unity might attest to his God-directed work among them. He asked that they be united with him for ever.

The shadow of the cross, his good death, lay across the Lord’s entire life. There is a sense in which his good death began in earnest on the day he was baptised, and that all his words and works ultimately pointed to his suffering service on the cross and the resurrection that would follow. At Golgotha, he asked that his tormentors might be forgiven. During his unimaginable agony, he urged Mary to behold and reflect upon her ‘son’ (Jesus, and then John), and entreated John to ‘adopt’ Mary as his own (John 19:26). In his good death the Lord glorified his Father, showed loving concern for the future and for the needs of his beloved brothers and sisters, and looked forward with anticipation to being united with them for ever. He prayed out loud for them, to strengthen them, to comfort them, and to help them look forward to future glory. A good death involves forgiveness, prayer for and with those whom we are leaving, and sincere desire for peace and unity after we are gone.

More could be written of many of the faithful in their last days. We could speak of Brother Paul, motivating Timothy to follow his example; to take on the labour of service in spite of the hard aspects of that work; to stand out as an example of commitment, faith and love, vigilant and bold (2 Timothy). We might include Peter sharing with his readers what they needed in order to become fully matured and activated believers (2 Peter 1:12-15). We see him inspiring them with what he saw on the mountain, and directing them to the sure Word of prophecy as a source of light and strength in a time of darkness. And John, “the elder”, moves us with his words on love and his rejoicing at seeing the ecclesia “walking in truth” (2 John 1:1,4). 1 All these had a good death, a fruitful walk toward their final sleep.

1 Bible quotations are from the KJV unless otherwise stated.

Your good death

Whatever we may have to struggle with, physically and emotionally, in our last days, we can aim to make ours a good death – to follow biblical examples. Declining mental powers may greatly limit what we feel able to do, and the Lord knows that. Acknowledging the reality of this challenge, a list of things that we might be able do in that time could still include the following:

Put God and His Son first, not your pains and your ailments. This is hard to do, as you may hurt so much, but try to seek God’s help that, in spite of your soreness and your many troubles, He might be elevated through your last days.

Make your last days a preaching campaign. Talk about the signs of the times, the things that God is doing and will do, and your rejoicing at the fulfilment of prophecy today.

Engage in a peace process, a diplomatic mission, a work of reconciliation. All families and ecclesias need peacemakers. The appeals and the counsel of a dying brother or sister carry a weight that you cannot measure. Understanding your family and your brothers and sisters as you do, encourage them to put away their quarrels and their disputes. Your broader perspective, unlike theirs, reduces their differences to their true proportions, and with compassion you might trigger healing that is overdue.

Use your last days as a time of personal testimony. Did God work in your life? Do you now see the many ways in which He was active all the way through? Were there events and experiences that can be explained only as the direct hand of God? Share these things and testify to His greatness and His abiding love.

Acknowledge what you broke and seek forgiveness for past wrongs. Don’t leave without addressing the blunders you made and their impact upon the people you love. All parents make mistakes. Some of them have lasting consequences. Children of parents who experience their death without the resolution of hurts and conflicts carry a burden of pain after we leave them. They have no place to lay it down, and it can poison their lives and their relationships. Don’t let that be the experience of those you leave behind. Talk through what happened and acknowledge the harm that was done. Ask for forgiveness and for their guidance on anything you can do to help heal or fix what you broke. Don’t make your apology ‘you-centric’ (“I feel so bad, I feel terrible”), but make it about and for them (“I realise that what I did affected you this way, I see how I hurt you”).

Admit the effects of sin and mortality and the brevity of life. This is an hour of humility and openness, not a time for denying that you were bruised by sin. Those who hear you will benefit by the admission of those things that hurt your walk, things that God had to cauterise so that you could be spiritually healed. In your last days, you are a living depiction of the final stages of mortality. Talk about that. Let those who hear you know how brief this little life is, and encourage them with those wonderful words:

“Life is the time to serve the Lord,

To do His will, to learn His word;

In death there is no power to know,

Far less in wisdom’s way to go.” 2

2 Hymn 396, Christadelphian Hymn Book, 2002.

excerpt.rendered: When do you go to Sunday School? In the morning or afternoon? I always go in the morning, because our

content.rendered:
When do you go to Sunday School? In the morning or afternoon? I always go in the morning, because our Sunday School is at 10.30am. On many occasions I have been seen running furiously at 10.29am in order to dash into the room just before our Superintendent stood up to announce the hymn; and, although this has happened a few times, I am glad that I got there in the end and did not stay at home.

If your Sunday School is in the morning, how often have you said: “Oh! Mother. I’m tired, please let me stay in bed a little longer”?

But wise Mother always made you get up, and go to Sunday School instead.

Or, if your Sunday School is in the afternoon, how many times have you said: “Oh! Mother, please let me have some more pudding”?

But mother has said “No!” because if you had waited a minute longer you would have been too late for Sunday School.

Perhaps you wonder why I am writing all this. There is a reason for it. Just imagine that the King of England had written to you saying that he would be at your Sunday School next Sunday. What would happen? Would you be saying: “Oh! Mother. I’m tired …”; or “Please let me have some more pudding”?

Of course not! It would probably be like this: “Come along, get up, Mother, please, the King is coming today. I must go to Sunday School, and arrive early”; or “I’m too excited to eat my dinner; please let me go to Sunday School now, because the King will be there.”

Well, now here is the surprise: next Sunday the King will be at your Sunday School! No, I don’t mean the King of England, but our King – Jesus. Yes, Jesus promised to go every Sunday, when he said, “Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

So, don’t forget, be sure to go to Sunday School next Sunday, because our King is even more important than King George VI. Get there early if you can, and if not, hurry to meet Jesus as soon as possible. Our King will be glad to see you, and you, too, will be glad you got there in the end, and did not stay at home. – Harry

From The Christadelphian Children’s Magazine, vol. 1, no. 7, Jul. 1938, p. 138.

title.rendered: Understanding what Christ is doing now

excerpt.rendered: The work of the Lord Jesus is essential to the faith of every believer, and without it our lives would

content.rendered:
The work of the Lord Jesus is essential to the faith of every believer, and without it our lives would be rudderless. Yet how well do we understand what Christ is doing right now? This new book by Brother Roger Lewis provides an in-depth study that sheds light on this often unclear and sometimes misunderstood topic. After a consideration of Christ’s ascension, the book examines Jesus’ roles as commander of the angelic host and as our Intercessor. It considers Jesus as the Bridegroom and the Lord of the household; and it looks at him as King-designate and as our Judge.

Although this is a fairly slim book (just over 100 pages), it deals with the subject in detail. All its arguments are carefully supported by scriptural quotations, and are frequently supplemented by an examination of Old Testament prophecies, parallels and allusions. Readers are shown how these point forward to the role that Jesus currently performs, seated at his Father’s right hand in what the author describes as “the throne room of heaven”.

Each chapter stands in isolation, dealing with a different aspect of Christ’s work. As the sections are not lengthy, it is easy to dip into the book at any particular chapter to get to grips with one topic over a cup of tea.

Old Testament illustrations

One strength of this book is how it draws upon Old Testament passages to help illustrate aspects of Christ’s work now. For example, rather than looking only at New Testament quotations, the section that deals with Christ’s ascension also considers a psalm, the writings of three Old Testament prophets, examples from the life of Joseph, Moses and Elijah, and details from the Law of Moses. Similarly, the chapter on Christ’s role as Mediator explains the distinction between an intercessor and a mediator by taking examples from the lives of Job, Moses and Joshua, as well as examining Paul’s words on the subject.

The Old Testament is also shown to contain a useful parallel when we think about Jesus as King-designate. Our attention is drawn to the amount of time that David committed to preparing Solomon for his role as temple-builder. Using that example as a starting point, the author illustrates how God is currently working with Jesus to prepare him for the work of constructing a new temple. This time of preparation is an important theme of the book. We might consider Jesus’ Kingship as a purely future position, but Brother Roger demonstrates that Jesus’ preparation for the day of his return is currently taking place in heaven. The author writes:

“In the present time, Christ is … watching the Father’s work; he is listening to his Father’s words; he is observing the Father’s way. And in this time of intense preparation, everything that he sees and hears forms part of the training that he is willing to undergo” (page 103).

Jesus’ experiences on earth taught him much; his time in heaven now teaches him more. Brother Roger suggests that this is the reason for the gap between the Lord’s ascension and his second coming – a period that we might feel is lengthy, but which provides the necessary time for Jesus to be fully instructed for his role as King of the world.

Exhortational content

The author does not treat the different topics merely as an academic study, but shows how each aspect of Christ’s work has relevance to our lives. In several places, the material therefore becomes exhortational too. For instance, the author explains that judgment is not solely a future event, and shows how our thoughts and actions are being examined now. He writes:

“The saints of past and present times are all under scrutiny for how they might be employed in the service of the King-designate of the world” (page 27).

Our actions now will affect our roles in the Kingdom.

Loyal servants?

Another example of the exhortational character of the study comes in the chapter that examines Christ’s role as Lord of the household. The reader is asked to consider the total loyalty that a master expects from his servants even when he is absent. The example used is Eliezer, the servant who was faithful to Abraham even when he was many miles away from his master. Readers are exhorted that those who follow Christ are similarly expected to be trustworthy stewards of what is committed to their safekeeping, even while our Lord is not physically present.

Further exhortation arises when the subject of Christ as a Bridegroom is addressed, and from the question of how we should remember his sacrifice. At this point, the book takes a lengthy digression into hymns used for the breaking-of-bread service, and considers whether some of them constitute prayers to Jesus. While this is interesting, it is not directly relevant to the subject of the book. Everywhere else, though, the writing remains focused on the individual topic of each chapter.

Increasing our understanding

It needs to be noted that the frequent use of long and often complex sentences can make the arguments difficult to follow. This means that this may not be a suitable book if English is not your native tongue. However, perseverance is well worth it, because other authors rarely address these topics with such scriptural insight.

There is a handy index of Bible references that speaking brethren may find useful, and copious footnotes provide supporting information for those who wish to check the author’s conclusions in more detail.

This is a book for those who love God’s Word and want to gain a better understanding of Jesus’ current role. Brother Roger deftly uses both Testaments to give readers a glimpse into “the heavenly throne room” where our Lord Jesus is sitting at God’s right hand, attentive to his Father’s words as he prepares for his return.

The Current Work and Role of Christ by Brother Roger Lewis. Price: paperback £10.00 plus postage; e-book £8.00.

excerpt.rendered: The death of Charlie Kirk – Some reflections, written at the time and published in the November 2025 issue of

content.rendered:
The death of Charlie Kirk – Some reflections, written at the time and published in the November 2025 issue of The Christadelphian Magazine:

The shooting of Charlie Kirk during a public speech on 10 September was shocking. For any who are not aware: Kirk was a pro-Trump Christian and an active campaigner for free speech and the values of the US religious right; his wife and children were watching as he was murdered. Whilst not an event of the historical magnitude of the assassination of JFK or Martin Luther King, it still felt like a watershed moment, with outpourings of grief – and, sadly, smirks of satisfaction from some, fuelled by the Internet and the polarising world of social media.

Some of us (particularly our young people) may have already been aware of Kirk; others may have discovered him only after his demise. What, if anything, should our reaction be?

Let us first state the obvious: murder is tragic, whether the victim is politically ‘right’, ‘left’ or neither, and whether they are famous or obscure (more than forty people are murdered every day in the USA). This murder was gruesome, and public, reminding us of the stench of sin. The frequency of murders may go up and down under different political regimes, but until our Lord returns they will always be with us.

Was this murder of particular significance in God’s purpose? Possibly it may galvanise US politics in a particular direction as part of God’s plan, but it is hard for us to say. What it does seem to do is to reinforce the polarisation and tribalism that social media has exacerbated, particularly in Western society. That is something that we should have no part in, human though it is to feel frustration, and even anger, towards those we disagree with. But we are followers of Christ, not human politicians or influencers.

We are grateful to the worldly authorities that allow freedom of speech, something that Kirk argued powerfully for. Some may admire his manner in debate, and some may have found his arguments on particular social issues on which the Bible speaks clearly to be useful. We may perhaps admire Kirk’s commitment to the Christian faith; this was, he said, the most important thing in his life, as it should be for all of us. But we should remember that the Christ that he believed in and the gospel that he proclaimed were probably very different from our understanding in critical respects.

Although we might have agreed with some of Charlie Kirk’s positions (albeit perhaps for different reasons, and with different consequential outcomes), there are many areas in which we would have completely disagreed. Just as his Christianity was not our Christianity, so his politics were not our ‘politics’ – he was a leading supporter of Trump and the Christian right; we, as ‘citizens of heaven’ (Philippians 3:20), stand apart from all this world’s politics and protests. His support of gun law, and no doubt other positions, was not something with which we would be likeminded. As our list of points of potential agreement and disagreement illustrates, we must be careful not to be drawn into this world’s polarities. We stand, not with individual teachers, influencers and leaders, but with the Scriptures and with our Lord Jesus Christ. He it was who turned the other cheek, and who healed the severed ear of his murderers.

Our biblically founded views on some topics will surely line up with views expressed, sometimes eloquently, in society from time to time; but that does not make us part of their tribe. Some Bible teachings may seem to have something in common with ‘the right’ or ‘the left’ on particular matters. For example, our views about family and relationships could sound more like the socially conservative ‘right’, while our views about caring for those in need and being good stewards of the planet could sound more like ‘the left’ – but that does not make us followers or supporters of either; we are followers only of the Lord Jesus. We have no common cause with the politics of this world. The attempt has been made to ‘claim’ Christ for both left and right, and it still goes on – Christ as the true communist or the true capitalist (ironically, both have been argued) – but Christ will not belong to human formulations and categories, and he has made it abundantly clear that his Kingship is not of this world (John 18:36). Our Lord’s teaching is bigger and more fundamental than any human system; at their very best, they can only hope to mimic, flickeringly, the great truths he has revealed.

Even if we find resonances, then, between divine truths and today’s thought-leaders, left or right, the reasons why we have those views, and how we act as a consequence, will usually be very different. We do not stand in common with the world’s causes. Ours is not to strive or protest, nor to march, nor to vilify the views of others, but simply to follow our Lord in meekness. The death of Charlie Kirk was indeed a tragedy in a world full of tragedy and evil; it wakes us up again to the horrors of human nature, and to the brokenness of a world in which such a thing could happen. But it is through Christ, and him alone, that all will be put right, and in whom our true identity is to be forged.

excerpt.rendered: The actions of every king of Israel or Judah were on display for all to see. They were to lead

content.rendered:
The actions of every king of Israel or Judah were on display for all to see. They were to lead the people by example. They also needed to guide their children so that they, in turn, could inherit the throne and continue to lead the people in God’s ways.

We cannot consider this topic without mentioning Jeroboam the son of Nebat who caused the people to sin (2 Kings 3:3). His actions left a legacy that his descendants and other kings would be associated with if they did not follow God. He set up false priests, including himself, in the high places (1 Kings 13:33). Not only did he personally disobey God, but he was a stumbling block for the nation and caused the people to sin (1 Kings 14:16). Do we ever make it harder for people to do good?

Another king, Ahab, was a bad example for the people of Israel. He was influenced by his wife Jezebel to do terrible things, from idol worship to murder. Let us consider our own actions and the example we set. Are we being negatively influenced by our peers or people in the world to do things that we know are not right?

Let us now consider Asa king of Judah. It is said of him that “the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days” (1 Kings 15:14). In the previous verse, we see that his mother erected an image of the pagan goddess of motherhood and fertility, Asherah. This is often associated with sexual immorality. Asa removed the image and burned it while also removing his mother as queen. He understood what it meant to be an example to the people while in a position of authority. What idol do we need to destroy in our lives so that we can be a better example?

Our Lord Jesus Christ is the perfect role model. As aspiring kings and priests (Revelation 5:9,10) we need to consider our actions and their consequences. What example are we setting for our friends, family, and brothers and sisters? Let us strive to follow in the footsteps of our Lord Jesus Christ.

excerpt.rendered: The report that Nehemiah received from Hanani – that the walls of Jerusalem were broken down – made him weep.

content.rendered:
The report that Nehemiah received from Hanani – that the walls of Jerusalem were broken down – made him weep. The walls of protection for God’s chosen city were in ruins, and the city and its inhabitants were defenceless against their enemies. From that point forward, Nehemiah made it his mission to rebuild the walls of the city.

The first thing that Nehemiah did was to pray to God, asking for His blessing. Next, he requested leave from the palace of King Artaxerxes to rebuild the wall of Jerusalem. Then, once he arrived at Jerusalem, he appealed to those who had returned from exile to rise up and rebuild the wall together.

But there were two reasons why Nehemiah wanted to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem: one a physical reason, and the other a spiritual reason.

First, the wall needed to be rebuilt to provide protection to the city and its inhabitants – especially for protection of the Temple which had been rebuilt. The rebuilding of the wall presented an opportunity for those who had returned from exile to work together with one mind and build the protection of God’s chosen city.

Secondly, from a spiritual perspective, the wall acted as a reminder to the Jews that they needed to separate themselves from the surrounding Gentiles who would lead them spiritually astray. Creating a physical wall made this spiritual
separation easier to practise.

We today bear the same responsibility as Nehemiah, and the builders, in building the ‘walls’ in our lives and in our ecclesia. We need to ensure that our own personal walls are built strongly to protect us from the things of the world. We
need walls without weakness to ensure that we are able to resist the temptations which we come across daily.

But we also need to ensure that the ‘walls’ of our ecclesias are built up likewise. The walls of our ecclesia need to provide the brothers and sisters inside a place of safety from the evils of the world which we live in. It is our responsibility to ensure that we maintain the true doctrines taught by the Bible, and don’t allow the thoughts of the world to come in and corrupt it.

Though this may be a daunting responsibility, we don’t have to do this alone – because, just as Nehemiah had the support of those willing to build with him, we likewise have our brothers and sisters with us, with one mind, striving too to build those walls.

excerpt.rendered: “My son, do not forget my teaching, but keep my commands in your heart, for they wil prolong your life

content.rendered:
“My son, do not forget my teaching, but keep my commands in your heart, for they wil prolong your life many years and bring you peace and prosperity. Let love and faithfulness never leave you; bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart. Then you will win favour and a good name in the sight of God and man”. Proverbs 3:1-4 (NIV)

In Proverbs 3:1, King Solomon entreats his son (either a literal son, a student, or directly addressing the reader) to “keep my commands in your heart” (NIV) – in other words, to pay careful attention to his teaching. In the same way that Solomon penned the Book of Proverbs for his son, our heavenly Father wrote the Bible for His sons and daughters to live by.

We might associate the word ‘commandment’ with a list of moral rules and laws like the Ten Commandments. However, God’s commandments can be looked at more generally as encompassing all His words of instruction to His children, recorded in Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16-17_. We are called to write these not on tables of stone, but on the tablet of our hearts (Proverbs 3:3; 7:3; 2 Corinthians 3:3).

How can we keep God’s Commands in our Hearts?

To ‘keep’ something can man to store a prossession in a safe or secret place. We are called to possess God’s commands – not to stow them away in a forgotten corner, but rather to treasure them within our hearts, the centre of our physical, emotional and spiritual being (Proverbs 7:1).

Solomon’s father, King David, expressed in Psalm 119:97: “Oh how I love Your law! It is my meditation all the day.”

David teaches thta love is the first and most essential ingredient in keeping God’s commands (see 1 John 5:2). He loved God’s teachings, following them not out of obligation or pure habit, but with his whole heart (see Matthew 22:37). The second essential ingredient is to meditate on God, which means to make time in our day and space in our hearts for wisdom. There are many ways in which we can do this daily: we can study Scripture, reflect on what He has done in our lives, momorise verses, and spend time with Him in prayer. Meditation can even mean to sing, dance and make music for Him.

Choosing Life

As Solomon desired his son to have a long and prosperous life, so God desires taht none of His children should perish but that all should have eternal life in His kingdom (2 Peter 3:9). God articulates this in Deuteronomy 5:29: “Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear Me and to keep all My commandments, that it might go well with them and with their decendants for ever!”

Despite this, God cannot force us to love Him or to keep His commands. He has given us free will to choose a loveing relationship with Him, resulting in eternal life, or to go our own way, ultimately leading to death (Deuteronomy 30:19,20).

It is a simple thing that our Father asks of us, which reaps wonderful rewards: peace, prosperity, favour, a good reputation and immortality. We do not deserve any of these things, but God will readily bless us if we simply keep His commands in our hearts.
