content.rendered:
1 | Concordance

A concordance can help you get closer to the original meanings of the words used, find verses, trace words throughout the Bible, and help to establish cross-references.

2 | Common sense

Simply put, we should ask the question, ‘Does our interpretation of this verse / passage / section of Scripture make sense and align with the rest of Scripture?’ Careful thinking is required, but is far more satisfying than looking the answer up in a book.

3 | Consistency

The Bible has a consistent message and consistent doctrines. If it is not consistent, it is not of God (Malachi 3:6) Inconsistencies are usually resolved by application of “Context”, “Common sense” or by consulting a “Concordance”.

4 | Context

The words, verses and chapters that surround the section of Scripture we are studying; and the historical environment of the section (this could include customs, culture, personalities and politics of the time).

5 | Clues

This step is about carefully reading the passage and seeing if we can detect the clues. The objective is to ask questions to unlock as much information as we can about the Word of God (What, Why, When, How, Where and Who?).

6 | Citation

Scripture is full of phrases like “As it is written” and “You have heard it said” and “Have ye not read?” and so on. The Old Testament is full of information that finds its fulfilment in the New Testament. Citations provide examples of fulfilled Bible prophecies, direct us to our Lord Jesus, add power to the verses using the citation, show us ‘types’ and affirm the consistency of Scripture.

excerpt.rendered: The future of our preaching in the last days In the summer of 2021, an article was published in The

content.rendered:
The future of our preaching in the last days

In the summer of 2021, an article was published in The Christadelphian under the above title. 1 It was prompted by concerns that, after the COVID pandemic, too few ecclesias had reopened their doors to resume the preaching of the gospel. Nearly three years on, it is appropriate to revisit the question of how well we are obeying the command, “Go into all the world and preach the gospel” (Mark 16:15, NKJV) in the United Kingdom.

1 June 2021, page 261.

An assessment

Christianity has been having a bad time over the last two decades, and the pandemic accelerated a reduction in the public preaching of the gospel. Fewer and fewer of the churches around us advertise regular services devoted to bringing new converts to repentance and baptism – and, perhaps not surprisingly, the number of people professing Christianity has been dwindling at an alarming rate. Many churches now hold only one service on a Sunday as congregations dwindle. To outward appearances, the preaching of the gospel appears to be in headlong retreat.

In contrast, we might have expected to have seen a steady return to the provision of a regular preaching service in each and every ecclesia in the UK. Unfortunately, this has not happened. A review of the ecclesial entries in the CALS Diaries for 2023 and 2024 reveals a rather depressing picture.

In 2023, there were 231 ecclesias listed as holding a breaking of bread service weekly or at least regularly; in 2024, there are only 215, and some of those remaining are very small, meeting in homes or sometimes almost always on Zoom.

In 2023, 145 ecclesias were listed as having Bible Hour services, so it appears that the effects of the pandemic on anxiety about meeting together had not altogether disappeared; in 2024, far from recovering, as might have been hoped, the number has dropped to only 115 – meaning that the offering of the gospel to the general public by means of regular preaching meetings happens in only fifty-three percent of our ecclesias.

What about the Iranians?

At the same time, the number of baptisms in our community in the UK over the last two years has been at its highest level for a very long time. Most of these baptisms have been of refugees from Iran and other countries where there is persecution, although more recently there have been signs of an increase in the number of UK-born young people asking for baptism. From a quick review of “News from ecclesias” in the December 2023 and January 2024 issues of The Christadelphian, there is clear evidence, in baptisms and transfers, of Iranian-related activity in at least forty-five ecclesias – and this work has involved intensive and detailed preaching, often in Farsi. Many of our new Iranian brothers and sisters have also shown an enthusiasm to take up the command to preach to those around them, although their role is likely to be limited until they have learned English.

Some ecclesias have felt unable to discharge the responsibility to preach through holding Bible Hours for the general population as well as preaching to Iranians, who are generally more eager to hear the gospel.

What about preaching methods?

The lockdowns of the pandemic also forced our community to consider whether there were other ways of preaching the gospel, even when we could not meet together in person. As a result there has been a proliferation of preaching using social media, YouTube, 2 ecclesial websites and other innovations. These can have the virtue of reaching out to audiences across the world, but do not often bring us into direct contact with those who are viewing these resources. Nor do they provide the opportunity for brothers and sisters to hear the essential teachings of the gospel repeated on a regular basis – something that is very important to ensure that all of us retain a good grasp of the Truth we share.

2 For example, the excellent range of video presentations at www.gospelonline.co.uk/online-gospel-talks

One of the reasons for Israel being commanded to come together in person for the great festivals of the Jewish calendar was that they should be reminded of their faith and its practical implications for their everyday lives. The command in the New Testament to the disciples in the early church was, likewise, intended to ensure that their faith and commitment was constantly reinforced by meeting together to consider the truth of the gospel. When they failed to do this, those who should have been faithful to their God and to the Lord Jesus Christ quickly fell away from that one true gospel – as is sadly evidenced in so many of the letters of the apostles in the second half of the New Testament.

Of course, there will be many other ways of making sure the gospel reaches the public. Billing still has the advantage of reaching every household in a given area; 3 Bible Learning Centres provide an active presence on our high streets where most people will be found; 4 campaigns, market stalls and other special efforts need to continue to take the gospel to the public – and individual witness is still critical.

3 The large amount of direct mail that we receive continues to show that retailers and others believe that the delivery of information to every house works! More widespread billing on a regular basis of materials designed for the CALS might enable this, and could also help to engage our Iranian brothers and sisters in an important ecclesial activity.

4 Solihull Bible Learning Centre has had over 45,000 visits by non-Christadelphian adults since its opening and is currently averaging over fifty such visits a week. Of these fifty visitors, perhaps as many as ten will take free literature from our displays – which means that the gospel is being spread to all sorts of places and people.

Where ecclesias are very small or lack the resources to sustain preaching both to the Iranian community and to the UK-born population, we may need to experiment, perhaps by ecclesias working together locally to hold regular preaching meetings, perhaps using the extensive library of preaching presentations now available on YouTube and other platforms in Bible Hours, collaborating in offering online courses, and so on.

Regular preaching open to all

It is sometimes argued that there is no point in holding regular Bible Hours when we get so few visitors from outside our community attending them. A long time ago, in my working life I was heavily involved in quality-assurance programmes related to school and education business-partnership activities such as the provision of work experience, the quality of careers advice and the development of an understanding of business. My mentor at the beginning of this work had a very clear and powerful message: if there was no quantity of activity, then there could most certainly be no quality in its delivery. The same is true in relation to the public preaching of the gospel: we can only have visitors attend if there is a Bible Hour for them to attend!

Many of us have friends and neighbours to whom we try to talk about the gospel message to encourage them to read the Bible for themselves. At a certain point in these discussions, we need to have a public meeting to which we can invite them. Sometimes these can be special events, some of which we used to call Special Efforts, which were sometimes arranged, perhaps at short notice, to capitalise on public anxieties related to events such as the war in Ukraine, the current crisis over Gaza in the Middle East, and even alarm about the climate and the future of the world. It might be a good time to revive some of these efforts, 5 as they provide events to which interested friends can be brought. Sometimes there may be other events such as Carol Services, celebrations of the harvest and even the anniversary of the Resurrection, all of which can provide an opportunity for powerful witness to the Truth and the need for repentance and baptism. Baptismal services can also be good opportunities to show friends the joy of the gospel.

5 The provision of monthly or bi-monthly subjects supported by print-ready materials informing and inviting the public could go a long way to reviving the idea of Special Efforts.

The previous article summarised the need for Bible Hours as follows:

  • Bible Hours should provide regular, systematic coverage of the teaching of the gospel. They cover some subjects, such as the essential need for repentance and baptism or the wrong doctrine of the Trinity, which are not always covered in exhortations or Bible Class addresses.
  • Bible Hours are open to everyone who wishes to come in to hear; and, if the subjects are chosen with care, they proclaim the key beliefs on which salvation depends, on noticeboards outside our halls as well as inside.
  • Bible Hours are an open declaration that we believe that the Bible is God’s Word.
  • Bible Hours provide an essential opportunity for us to be reminded of what we believe and why we believe it.
  • Bible Hours are one way of ensuring that we have meetings to which we can invite our friends and neighbours and so discharge our responsibility to preach to those around us, whether they are prepared to listen or not.
  • Bible Hours provide regular events where our young people can hear the gospel, meet with others and be encouraged to take up their cross and follow Jesus; but for this to happen we ourselves need to show that we value the preaching of God’s Word by being there in the audience.

“Necessity is laid upon me”

In all these ways we need to preach the Word with boldness whatever the circumstances, not being afraid to take the message of the need for repentance out to this wicked world. We must not be frightened to preach the unpopular message which this will be to some of those who do not wish to change their lives and would prefer not to have their consciences stirred. We need to remember that the work of bringing salvation to others has never been popular, especially when compared with more socially acceptable charitable and welfare activities. But the necessity to preach is laid upon each one of us because of what the Lord Jesus Christ has done for us. For, as Paul says, “we are ambassadors for Christ, God making His appeal through us” (2 Corinthians 5:20, ESV), and our Lord Jesus Christ gave his life to bring life to all who will hear his words and act upon them. Our job is to cry aloud on his behalf; and we need to do it now!

excerpt.rendered: Principles, Preaching and Problems We are so familiar with using chapter and verse numbers to reference passages in the Bible

content.rendered:
Principles, Preaching and Problems

We are so familiar with using chapter and verse numbers to reference passages in the Bible that we can forget that in the original manuscripts there were no chapters and verses. When Moses wrote down the Law, or Luke wrote his Gospel, or Paul wrote his letters, they didn’t split their writings into chapters and verses; they each wrote a continuous piece of writing.

We don’t have the original manuscripts, but in the most ancient copies that we do have the text is split into unnumbered sections and paragraphs. Because writing materials were expensive, the writers didn’t waste space by showing these divisions. They began a new line to indicate a new section, and they left a short gap on a line to indicate a new paragraph.

Through the ages, people have found it convenient to split up the Bible text in various ways. In ancient Israel, for example, the Torah (the five books of Moses) was divided into 154 sections, so you could read one section each week and go through the whole Torah in three years. The New Testament was divided into sections by early Christians to help with planning the readings for their services. But neither of these systems is the same as our chapters and verses.

Chapters and verses

The chapter divisions that we know were added by Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, around 1227; he would have added them to his Latin Vulgate version of the Bible. They were incorporated into Wycliffe’s English translation (from the Latin) in 1382, and into Tyndale’s translation (from the original languages) in 1525–35. These translations had no verse numbers.

Around this time, Jewish scholars called the Masoretes were working to preserve the text of the Hebrew Bible, which was divided into sections and paragraphs. They incorporated chapter numbers into their text. In most cases, the chapter divisions coincided with one of their existing divisions – but not always, and that’s why sometimes their chapters don’t coincide with ours, as you may have noticed from footnotes in your Bible.

In 1448, a Jewish rabbi called Isaac Nathan ben Kalonymus, who lived in France, divided the Hebrew Bible (our Old Testament) into verses. This was because he was working on a Bible concordance, and verse numbers made it easier to reference the text. Then in 1551, Robert Estienne (also known as Robert Stephens), a printer in Paris, divided the chapters into verses when he printed the Greek New Testament. The first English translation to make use of these verse divisions was the 1560 Geneva Bible, the most popular translation of the Elizabethan age. The King James Version of 1611 followed this practice.

One strange feature in both the Geneva Bible and the King James Version is that each verse starts on a new line. There are also paragraph marks (¶) called pilcrows. This layout can make the text very disjointed and you can lose the flow of the narrative. Modern translations usually have a better layout. There are sections (each dealing with one topic) with section headings, and the text is laid out in paragraphs. These things help us to understand the structure of the text.

Chapters and sections

Chapters and verses are very useful for referring quickly to a specific piece of text, and indispensable for Bible study. But if we read the Bible one chapter at a time, instead of by sections, then we can easily lose the context, or the flow of the argument, because chapter divisions don’t always occur at sensible places. Breaking up a book according to chapters for study or for our daily reading is usually not the best approach, therefore. For example, 1 Corinthians talks about twelve main topics. We could break down the letter into the following sections:

  1. Chapters 1–4: divisions in the church
  2. Chapter 5: a case of incest
  3. 6:1-11: lawsuits
  4. 6:12-20: sexual immorality
  5. Chapter 7: marriage
  6. Chapters 8–10: meat sacrificed to idols
  7. 11:1-16: women’s hair
  8. 11:17-34: the Lord’s supper
  9. Chapters 12–14: Spirit gifts
  10. Chapter 15: resurrection
  11. 16:1-12: Paul’s plans
  12. 16:13-24: Paul’s greetings.

Three chapters (5, 7 and 15) are about one topic each; the other topics are only part of a chapter, or take more than one chapter. The chapter divisions confuse the structure of the book. The New Testament scholar A. T. Robertson wrote, “The first step in interpretation is to ignore the modern chapters and verses.” 1 It is a useful exercise to read the Bible in a way that doesn’t distract us with man-made chapter and verse divisions. There are editions of the ESV and the NIV, for instance, which allow this.

1 A. T. Robertson (1925), An Introduction to the Textual Criticism of the New Testament, Broadman Press, Nashville, p. 101.

Differences between languages

There are quite a few places where the chapter divisions don’t match in the Hebrew and English Bibles. Most English translations show these differences in a footnote. For example: in English Bibles, the last verse of Genesis 31 is verse 55, but in Hebrew Bibles that’s chapter 32, verse 1. That means that in the rest of chapter 32 the verse numbers are one higher in Hebrew than in English. The Hebrew division seems to make more sense: 31:55 really belongs with chapter 32.

The Book of Psalms shows another problem. The headings of the psalms are part of the Hebrew text, and in Hebrew they have verse numbers. In English Bibles, these headings have no verse numbers. Again, the verse numbers in the Hebrew psalms are often one higher than in the English Bible. Take Psalm 3, for example:

Verse number Text
Hebrew English
1 “A psalm of David. When he fled from his son Absalom.” 2
2 1 “Lord, how many are my foes! How many rise up against me!”
3 2 “Many are saying of me, ‘God will not deliver him.’”

2 Bible quotations are from the NIV.

These differences cause us no problems if we read the Bible only in English; but they can cause problems if we read the Bible in other languages, because some translations follow the English chapter and verse numbers (Persian, Chinese, Indian languages and other translations done by British missionaries), and some translations (Czech, Dutch, Russian and so on) follow the Hebrew ones. One of the first things you learn when you go abroad for the Christadelphian Bible Mission is to check your Bible references to make sure that they’re correct in the audience’s language. Otherwise, your audience and your translators could be very confused!

Some examples

Now for some examples of unfortunate chapter divisions; you may be able to think of others.

Genesis 1–2. The creation record is not complete in chapter 1; it goes only to the sixth day. We have to read to 2:3 to read about the seventh day and the end of the account. There’s a natural break after 2:3. Verse 4 then starts with something like, “This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created”, marking a new section. If we’re reading the creation account, therefore, let’s not stop at the end of chapter 1; let’s keep going to 2:3.

Isaiah 52–53. We may know that Isaiah has four sections called “the Servant Songs”, which are about God’s servant who is to come. The fourth Servant Song starts in Isaiah 52:13 and carries on to the end of chapter 53 – there’s a chapter break in the middle of the song. In The Bible Companion reading plan, we read chapter 52 one day and chapter 53 the next day, so we may forget that chapter 53 is not the start of the song. Modern translations help because there’s typically a section heading before 52:13. The song has a structure – it splits into five stanzas of three verses each, and those stanzas form a ‘chiasmus’ pattern:

Verses Section Theme
52:13-16 A Exaltation
53:1-3 B Rejection
53:4-6 C Forgiveness through him
53:7-9 B’ Rejection
53:10-12 A’ Exaltation

Having a chapter division part-way through the song ruins this structure.

Daniel 10–11. Daniel 10 contains a message from an angel, beginning in verse 11. The second half of the last verse of chapter 10 and the first verse of chapter 11 seem to be a single thought, a kind of ‘aside’, and in several translations it’s in brackets:

“(No one supports me against them except Michael, your prince. And in the first year of Darius the Mede, I took my stand to support and protect him.)”

The angel continues with the actual prophecy in 11:2. There’s a chapter break in the middle of a parenthesis. In The Bible Companion, we read Daniel 10 on one day and Daniel 11 on the next day, so we stop in the middle of a prophecy – and even in the middle of a bracketed comment.

John 7–8. In some translations, the chapter break comes in the middle of a sentence:

“Then they all went home, but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. At dawn he appeared again in the temple courts …”

The narrative is continuous: chapter 7 ends with the Jewish leaders condemning Jesus, and chapter 8 starts with the Jewish leaders setting a trap for Jesus. You could have a break at verse 2, but perhaps it would be better to have no break at all.

Acts 7–8. The first part of 8:1 – “And Saul approved of their killing him” – belongs with chapter 7. Saul is introduced in 7:58, so it makes sense to include this sentence with that.

Colossians 3–4. Starting in 3:18, Paul addresses different sections of the church: wives, husbands, children, parents, slaves. But there’s a chapter break before we get to masters in 4:1. It’s a mystery why this verse was separated from the end of chapter 3; the break should be after 4:1.

1 John 1–2. 1:6–2:2 is a section about sin and forgiveness. Verses 8-10 say that we must acknowledge our sins if we wish to be forgiven. Then 2:1,2 continue the same theme: if we do sin, we have someone to help us. These verses belong to the previous chapter. Most translations have a new section heading for 2:3.

Verses

Verses are not such a problem when it comes to unfortunate divisions. Modern Bibles are more paragraph-oriented, so even when a verse number comes in the middle of a sentence we don’t worry about it too much. Ephesians 1:3-14 forms one sentence in Greek, which English translations usually break down into smaller sentences. But even this approach divides the passage into 12 verses, and these divisions can be problematic. Look at the ‘join’ between verses 4 and 5:

“For He chose us in him before the creation of the world to be holy and blameless in his sight. In love He predestined us for adoption to sonship through Jesus Christ, in accordance with His pleasure and will …”

A new sentence begins just before the end of verse 4 and continues into verse 5. In some translations, the phrase “in love” is tacked on to the previous sentence, giving the reading, “God chose us … in love”; but several translations, including the ESV, the NASB and the NIV, agree that it belongs to what comes immediately after it: “In love He predestined us …”

Sometimes there’s a gap in the verse numbers. For example, in Acts 8, verse 37 is missing or relegated to a footnote in most English translations. The reason for this is that the verse numbers were devised in the fifteenth century but since then more reliable manuscripts have been found and they don’t include verse 37; it has been identified as a later addition to the original text. Perhaps someone thought that it would be a good idea to include the eunuch’s confession to make it a more useful story.

Suggestions

I suggest that when we read the Bible we should look not at the chapter divisions but at the section headings. The chapter and verse numbers are a man-made system of numbers, which certainly make it easy to find and even remember things; but otherwise they don’t mean anything. Perhaps we should try to forget them! This is easier to do in modern translations in which section headings are emphasised as much as, or even more than, the chapter and verse numbers.

Whenever you read a chapter, have a look at the text on either side and see if the chapter divisions make sense. Look too at the section headings to see where the ‘natural’ breaks come. Of course, section headings are also man-made and can sometimes be wrong. So look at other translations, or commentaries, to see if they agree where the sections are; sometimes there are different ways in which we can split up the text.

If you are the Sunday president, feel free to adapt the Bible readings to include a complete thought, rather limiting it to a chapter. For example, if the reading is Genesis 1, carry on to 2:3; if the reading is Isaiah 53, start in 52:13. This will help to give everyone a better understanding of the subject matter – which is why we read the Bible.

Finally, consider other systems for daily Bible reading. Brother Robert Roberts’ Bible Companion is deeply engrained in Christadelphian tradition and practice, and much appreciated by many, so it would be difficult to replace it entirely. But perhaps a section-based plan, which didn’t deviate too much from it, could be used alongside it. It would take a bit of work, but it could be worth it.

title.rendered: Is it time for you? – Haggai 1

excerpt.rendered: Do you ever find yourself stuck in a rut? Maybe it’s a book you’ve been meaning to read, a word

content.rendered:
Do you ever find yourself stuck in a rut? Maybe it’s a book you’ve been meaning to read, a word in the Bible you think would be an interesting study, or a talk looming on the horizon but, for whatever reason, you just can’t seem to get started.

There are so many excuses we can give ourselves:  “Work is so busy right now”, “I’m swamped with homework” or “But I need to go to the gym to stay fit” to name a few. Or maybe we just feel that now’s not the time – we need to have everything else sorted out before we start doing that.

This was how the children of Israel felt at the time of Haggai the prophet. They had looked at the seventy-year prophecy of the destruction of the Temple (2 Chronicles 36:17-21) and worked out that they still had four years left until the Temple needed to be rebuilt (Ezra 4:24; 6:15). There was a lot of work to do, but they just needed that first push to get started. Sometimes a big task like Bible study can be pretty overwhelming too.

God gave them the push they needed in the words of the prophet Haggai – have a read of the first chapter (only fifteen verses). Notice the contrast between verses 2 and 4: the people say that it’s not yet time to build God’s house, and God responds with the question: “Is it time for you to dwell in houses while My house lies waste?”

Naturally, we will spend much of our lives doing things other than direct service for God – there are exams to pass, jobs to do and bills to be paid after all. But God asks a simple question: With all that time we spend on ourselves, should we not give some back to Him?

Verses 6-11 show that, although we may work for things like money, food and clothes, these alone are not enough to satisfy us anyway (Matthew 4:4). The only treasures worth laying up are those in heaven (Matthew 6:19- 21).

So what’s the key message of Haggai 1? It’s repeated for us in Haggai 1:5 and 7. “Consider your ways” – or, more literally translated, “Set your heart on your ways.”What do we prioritise in our lives: ourselves or our heavenly Father? This is something to really think about – to set our hearts on.

So that’s what the people did, and in verse 12, the huge task began. What’s God’s response in verse 13? “I am with you, saith the Lord.”

If God is for us, who can be against us (Romans 8:31)? So the final message of Haggai 1 is that, once we start our service to God, He is with us and He will bless it and be glorified in it (Haggai 2:4-9).

“Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares the Lord, Be strong, O Joshua, son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land, declared the Lord. Work, for I am with you, declared the Lord of hosts…” (Haggai 2:4)

title.rendered: Rebuilding the Temple: be strong and work

content.rendered:
It is said that the hardest part is starting.

Under the leadership of Zerubbabel and Jeshua, the children of Israel could have felt discouraged by the scale of the mission before them in rebuilding the ruined house of God, but they gathered together as one man in Jerusalem to begin the work (Ezra 3:1). In order for the people to obey God’s commandments in the Law of Moses, the Lord’s house needed to be built to allow the necessary sacrifices, feasts and laws to recommence.

“And all the people shouted with a great shout when they praised the Lord, because the foundation of the house of the Lord was laid.” (Ezra 3:11)

The rebuilding of the Temple was done in stages, and would take around twenty years in all, because of adversity that arose. First, the altar was rebuilt in order to re-establish the daily burnt offerings and the appointed feasts, for all those who would “willingly offer a freewill offering to the LORD” (Ezra 3:2-7). How imperative it is that we offer our praise and sacrifices to God with a willing heart!

Certain Levites were appointed to oversee the work of the house of the Lord (Ezra 3:8,9). Again, we are being shown a principle of careful selection of those who are spiritually mature to be the overseers of our work in the ecclesia.

In the second year of their return, the builders laid the foundation of the Temple of the Lord. It should have been a triumphal moment, and the people did indeed shout aloud for joy, but their cry was mingled with the weeping of many of the elders who remembered the former glory of Solomon’s Temple when the glory of the LORD had filled it (1 Kings 8:10-13) – an event which is not recorded as happening in the rebuilt Temple (Ezra 3:10-13; Haggai 2:3-4). Nor could this rebuilt Temple compare with Ezekiel’s vision of the grand temple to come in the Kingdom age (Ezekiel 40–48).

So often in life we face setbacks, fears, disappointments and despair, even within our ecclesias. The Lord understood His people’s sadness and yet He commands them to “be strong” and “work; for I am with you” (Haggai 2:4).

If we are building upon the firm foundation of the God of truth and His commandments, then we too should keep working in ‘the house of the Lord’, waiting patiently on Him and trusting in Him, remembering that all we do in this present age is preparation for future glory. So let us fix our eyes upon Jesus and the glory of the Kingdom of God to come (Ephesians 2:21,22; 1 Corinthians 2:9).

content.rendered:
Previously we looked at Acts 1:21-26, the only New Testament passage that mentions the drawing of lots in the context of ecclesial decision-making. We saw that this passage could not be used to justify a random process of selecting brothers and sisters to undertake roles within the ecclesia. Specific qualifications were required for the task of replacing Judas Iscariot; and the apostles – seemingly unable to decide between two equally qualified candidates, Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias – then called upon the Lord Jesus to indicate his choice. The process can be summarised as follows:

Acts 1: selecting a replacement apostle
  • Verse 15 – The selection process is instigated by Peter, an existing apostle, who explains the issue before the whole company of believers.
  • Verses 16-20 – The decision is based upon sound exposition of the Scriptures.
  • Verse 21 – A solution is suggested by Peter, who identifies potential candidates.
  • Verse 22 – These candidates have to meet certain stated criteria.
  • Verse 23 – A ‘shortlist’ of candidates is agreed jointly.
  • Verse 24 – A prayer is made for the Lord to indicate his choice.
  • Verse 26 – Lots are used to determine the final outcome (there is no indication what form these lots took).

Other decisions

Whilst no other passages mention the use of lots in this way, Scripture does record other occasions on which the first-century ecclesias had to make decisions, including choices about who would serve in those ecclesias. Generally speaking, each of these follows the pattern that we saw in Acts 1. We will review them briefly, one by one. The passages are, of course, worth reading in full.

Acts 6: dealing with murmuring in the ecclesia
  • Verse 2 – The process begins by the apostles calling together the whole ecclesia to explain the issue. The ministering of God’s Word is to remain their priority.
  • Verse 3 – A suggested solution is put forward: the ecclesia is to identify specific candidates who meet certain qualifications.
  • Verse 5 – The ecclesia sanctions this suggestion, and finds suitable brothers for the work.
  • Verse 6 – Those chosen to serve are referred to the apostles for their approval.
  • Verse 7 – The decision results in the increased spread of the gospel and more converts to the faith.
Acts 15: addressing the problem of the Judaisers
  • Verse 6 – The apostles and elders instigate the proceedings.
  • Verses 7-11 – The problem is discussed in the light of Scripture teaching and existing apostolic practice.
  • Verse 12 – The whole ecclesia is gathered together to listen.
  • Verses 13-18 – Further exposition of relevant Scripture passages takes place.
  • Verses 19-21 – The Apostle James suggests a solution based on this teaching.
  • Verses 22-27 – The recommendation is agreed to by the whole ecclesia, who appoint chosen individuals who have a proven track record of faithful service.
  • Verses 31,32 – Implementing the recommendation leads to great encouragement in the ecclesias.
1 Timothy 3: qualifications for ecclesial servants (“bishops” and “deacons”, KJV)
  • Verse 1 – The apostle commends those who aspire to service in the ecclesia.
  • Verses 2-7 – To serve properly, candidates are required to meet a detailed list of qualifications. These include spiritual considerations (not merely ‘practical’ ones). Candidates should not be recent converts to the faith.
  • Verses 8-13 – The apostle gives a further list of qualifications required.
  • Verse 11 – Good characters are also required in the wives of those who wish to serve. (Some understand Paul to be referring to female ecclesial servants; the RSV has “a deaconess” in Romans 16:1.)
  • Verse 15 – These instructions are for the disciples to know how to behave properly in the ecclesia.
Titus 1: appointing ecclesial servants (“elders” and “bishops”, KJV)
  • Verse 5 – The selection of ecclesial servants is delegated by the apostle to local decisions in each city (presumably meaning each ecclesia). The method of selection is by specific appointment, not by the drawing of lots.
  • Verses 6-8 – The list of criteria for these servants is again based upon specific spiritual criteria.
  • Verse 9 – There is special emphasis on the ability to uphold and teach the gospel faithfully.

Drawing conclusions for today

This two-part article is not intended to be exhaustive, and we may feel that there are other passages which have a bearing on this topic. Circumstances in twenty-first-century ecclesias do not exactly match those in the first century, as we no longer have Spirit-guided apostles to take a lead when it comes to making decisions in our ecclesias. However, some clear lessons can be learned from the passages summarised above, from which something of a pattern emerges:

  • The whole ecclesia was involved in the decision-making process.
  • The decision is expected to be based upon, and to uphold, sound biblical teaching.
  • Often, a solution was suggested by a brother particularly well versed in the Scriptures.
  • Specific qualifications had to be met by the candidates.
  • The decision-making process was always intended (1) to build up the ecclesia and (2) to facilitate the effective spread of the gospel.

Were we to select our ecclesial servants by drawing lots, therefore, we might well be disregarding clear biblical criteria for the roles in question. It might even lead to our appointing inappropriately qualified brothers and sisters.

Whatever the strengths and weaknesses of a secret ballot to select those whom we wish to serve us in our ecclesias – and there may well be better alternatives – at least this process allows each brother and sister to participate conscientiously in the process, encouraging us to ponder what Scripture has to say about roles in ecclesial life and those available to fill them. We can only benefit if the spirit of the first-century decision-making process is followed faithfully.

(Part 2 of 2)

excerpt.rendered: “We beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth” (John

content.rendered:
“We beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). 1

1 Bible quotations are from the NKJV.

John applies these beautiful words to Jesus, who personified grace and truth, bringing them to life. As we break bread together, it is helpful to come to an understanding of why they are so important.

We can see from John’s words that grace and truth are a practical expression of God’s glory, the means by which mortal men and women are saved. Later in his Gospel John develops this theme, showing what grace and truth mean in our daily lives. Before looking at what he has to say, however, we need to review the background to his words, and this is found in Ezekiel’s visions of God’s glory.

Ezekiel sets the scene

Because of their rebellion against God, the Jews had been overrun by Babylon and taken into exile. This separation of God from His people is symbolised by His glory departing from the Temple (see Ezekiel 10 and 11). Note how it happens: it is a gradual process. God’s glory leaves the Holy Place, first hovering over the threshold, then moving to the cherubim, then to the east gate, and finally coming to rest on the Mount of Olives. God appears to be reluctant to leave His people; they are His children, and He loves them greatly, so His presence leaves them slowly. This gradual removal is an illustration of His grace, but this separation has to happen to fulfil the truth of His Word. Immediately, we see that God’s glory is inextricably linked to grace and truth.

Because of this love for His people, God can never abandon them; so the glory does not disappear, but remains on the Mount of Olives, awaiting the time for it to return. That time was the coming of the Lord Jesus. As John has told us, our Lord radiated God’s glory. Yet, at his first coming, the glory was acknowledged only by a faithful few. A later vision of Ezekiel reveals the glory returning at Jesus’ second coming, when it will be recognised by all Jewish people, and ultimately by the whole world (Ezekiel 43:1-5). In this vision, the return is a reversal of the removing process: it begins on the Mount of Olives and comes to the Temple, filling it with glory.

Jesus illustrates Ezekiel’s vision

An illustration of this second vision is found in John 8:1-11, where Jesus ‘acts out’ Ezekiel’s prophecy of his second coming. John records Jesus bringing God’s glory into the Temple, and the dramatic events that ensue provide an insight into the meaning of grace and truth. Let’s follow what happens, step by step.

To fulfil the type, Jesus begins on the Mount of Olives and makes his way to the Temple (verses 1,2). If our understanding is correct, then the Temple should next be filled with God’s glory, in keeping with Ezekiel’s vision. But what do we find? The Pharisees, with their false religion and hostile attitude, confront Jesus with a woman taken in the act of adultery (verses 3-6). Surely nothing could be more different from the glory of God! But watch grace and truth get to work.

Jesus said: “He who is without sin among you, let him throw a stone at her first” (verse 7). It was a statement of truth, and it caused the Pharisees to leave (verse 9). God’s glory in the form of truth had dispelled false religion. This incident illustrates what our Lord will do at his return, when all religions except the one which is true will be removed.

So, Jesus was left alone with the woman (verse 10). A key point now is the fact that she had been caught in the act of adultery. For a second time we see truth in action, for the truth of God’s Word revealed her failing and she could not deny it – her sinful state was laid bare before the judge of all the earth. In this type of Jesus’ return, she represents all disciples who will meet with Jesus. Our lives will be completely exposed, and there will be no secrets. The Pharisees should also have brought the man who was guilty of adultery, but their failure to follow the Law of Moses enabled the type to be fulfilled. It meant that the woman was standing alone before Jesus, representative of the Bride when he returns.

And so came the grace. Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you” (verse 11) – words to be echoed when our Lord welcomes faithful disciples: “Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom …” (Matthew 25:34). His direction that followed – “go and sin no more” – will certainly apply to the saints as they are given divine nature.

God’s glory had indeed filled the Temple, in the form of grace and truth.

The disciples’ role

If we are to glorify God, therefore, we must be wholly committed to truth, both in our beliefs and in our way of life. The woman is a type of all saints. We too are ‘caught in the act of adultery’ – not literally, but spiritually. Paul tells us that, as a bride, we are “betrothed” to the Lord Jesus and so need to remain faithful to him (2 Corinthians 11:2). Yet, on occasion we all flirt with the world; it is in our nature, and we need to recognise this. The woman had to admit her failings, and so do we. The light of truth must shine on our hearts so that we see ourselves as we really are, removing the deceit which comes so easily. Like her, we must be spiritually laid bare before our Lord.

Then we can receive the grace. Our God is a God of love, expressed in His name:

“The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abounding in goodness and truth …” (Exodus 34:6).

Jesus perfectly reflected his Father, and his disciples are “those who receive abundance of grace” (Romans 5:17), and who know they can “come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16).

Grace and truth in the emblems

John brings together these thoughts about grace and truth in his First Letter:

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1:8,9).

We have indeed received grace through our Lord Jesus, and nowhere is this clearer than in the sacrifice that lies behind the emblems that we share. If, then, God is to be glorified in us, we need in turn to speak the truth in our hearts:

“But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28).

Let us do just that, and, in recognising ourselves as we really are, humble ourselves to receive the grace enshrined in these emblems.

excerpt.rendered: “Gentle words are a tree of life; a deceitful tongue crushes the spirit” (Proverbs 15:4, NLT). In 1940, during one

content.rendered:
“Gentle words are a tree of life; a deceitful tongue crushes the spirit” (Proverbs 15:4, NLT).

In 1940, during one of the darkest times of World War II, British prime minister Winston Churchill delivered his famous “Finest Hour” speech. Facing the imminent threat of a large-scale Nazi invasion, Churchill’s powerful and carefully chosen words needed to rally a nation. It would have been easy for him to surrender, give up, and fill his speech with negativity; instead, he decided to call on the country to fight and defend itself.

The power of our words is a recurring theme throughout God’s teachings. These teachings emphasise how we must use our words for good and promote wisdom, kindness, and integrity in our speech.

This is something I often struggle with. My go-to response in many situations is to be negative. Someone once described me as ‘a prophet of doom’ due to my ability to build many situations into the end of the world! I often find it difficult to stop and switch to a positive mindset.

As I have grown older, I have begun to realise how powerful it is to hear and give positivity and encouragement to myself and others. This was further emphasised when exploring speech in the Scriptures.

Proverbs 12:18 highlights this contrast between negative speech, which can turn into hurtful speech, and the healing effect of wise and positive words. The verse states: “There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.” Though I’ve never experienced being thrust by a sword, I can imagine that it is painful! The verse provides a graphic depiction of the power and pain that our words
can bring. We should use them to bring people up, not down.

How do we know if we are speaking wisely? James 3:17,18 describes wisdom from above as “first pure, then peaceable, gently open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.” All these attributes directly relate to positive words that foster a sense of peace and healing, not only for others but also for ourselves.

Young people, as much as everybody else, have the responsibility and opportunity to make a difference with our words: to promote positivity; to build up and not to tear down. Here are some practical ways which I and others have found helpful when practising positive speech:

  1. Speak encouraging words daily: Make it a habit to compliment and encourage those around you. A simple “You’re doing a great job” or “I appreciate you” can uplift someone.
  2. Practice gratitude: Start a gratitude journal, where you write down daily things that you’re thankful for. Sharing these thoughts with others and God can spread positivity!
  3. Mind your language: Before speaking, consider the impact of your words. Ask yourself, “Is this kind? Is it necessary? Is it true?”
  4. Reflect on Scripture: Regularly read and meditate on verses like Proverbs 15:4 and James 3:17,18. Let these teachings guide your speech and actions.

Let’s commit to using our words to build up, not to tear down, creating a ripple effect of positivity within our community.

excerpt.rendered: “When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom” (Proverbs 11:2). Pride is a key theme throughout

content.rendered:
“When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom” (Proverbs 11:2). Pride is a key theme throughout Proverbs, showing how important it is to be aware of it. Pride can be easy to identify in others and difficult to notice in ourselves. This may be why it is mentioned so frequently. Almost every time pride is mentioned, it is contrasted with humility or wisdom, providing us with a way to avoid it.

“Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). These are words that we know well, and they paint us a picture: whenever we are proud, we are setting ourselves up for failure. The reason for this is that, when we are proud, we are shifting from having faith in God to having faith in ourselves. For this reason the author writes, “Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 16:5, KJV).

We must not take pride in our livelihood, our possessions, or our status. These are all things that can be taken away from us in a moment. Instead, we must place our trust in God who will always be with us. Consider King Nebuchadnezzar who had an entire kingdom – but it was all stripped from him so that he might learn humility and that God is in control (Daniel 4:31-33).

Let us instead be more like Jesus, the perfect example of humility, who had good reason to be proud and yet resisted so that he could give glory to God. “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring” (Proverbs 27:1).

excerpt.rendered: “Never get old.” Advice given to me in my youth by an elderly sister. At the time, I thought that

content.rendered:
“Never get old.” Advice given to me in my youth by an elderly sister. At the time, I thought that old age seemed better than the alternative. I still do! Now I find myself the same age as ‘old people’. I find the words of Ecclesiastes 12 an apt description of life. I think Solomon is suggesting that old people are a visual aid, to remind us to “Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth” (verse 1).

A further reminder of this principle is given in Proverbs 20:29: “The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendour of old men is their grey hair.” Proverbs 16:31 adds: “Grey hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life”

Grey hair is a symbol of old age. So, what is glorious about being old? Well, Solomon adds a further criterion: “in the Lord”. A long time in God’s service brings with it a wealth of wisdom, knowledge and experience.  That is the glory of grey hair that Solomon talks about. God has provided for us a resource to be used when we seek advice and guidance in our life as Christians.

Solomon adds a note of caution, however. As we get older, we may become resistant to change and take comfort and security from routine. In Ecclesiastes 7:10 Solomon advises: “Say not, “Why ere the former days better than these?’ For it is not from wisdom that you ask this.”

The truth found in the Bible does not change. There is wisdom in being able to differentiate this truth from human traditions. For example, when change is suggested, older brothers and sisters must decide if this is a change to the Truth that they hold dear, or a change in procedure that will help young people in their life as Christians. For instance: will it help to spread the gospel message more widely than traditional ways of preaching?

Grandparents are notorious for spoiling their grandchildren. Solomon comments on family life in the Lord. “Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of children is their fathers” (Proverbs 17:6). What a wonderful blessing it is to see your family grow up in the Lord, to watch grandchildren learn from their fathers as your children learned from you!

We are all aware from the media that increasing numbers of older people is putting a strain on health services and the care sector. We are lasting longer. But Solomon warns us not to see older Christians as a burden because they live too long: “Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old” (23:22). Rather, we are told to honour father and mother. Their old age is an opportunity to show our love for God by showing our love for them.

Each age group has much to offer, and each group is dependent on the other to create a complete community built up together in love.

title.rendered: Should we sing hymns to Jesus?

excerpt.rendered: Question of the month The Apostle Paul teaches believers to “[speak] to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual

content.rendered:
Question of the month

The Apostle Paul teaches believers to “[speak] to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody with your heart to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19; see also Colossians 3:16). 1 In seeking to follow this teaching, ecclesias – and individual consciences – are sometimes exercised by the question of whether the words that we sing may be addressed to the Lord Jesus Christ.

1 Bible quotations are from the NASB 1995 except where otherwise stated.

Differences of opinion

There is a wide range of opinions on this topic. At one extreme, some may make no distinction between the Father and the Son, praises and petitions being offered to them both without discrimination. At the other extreme, an ecclesia may find itself in a situation where some brothers and sisters are singing sincerely to Jesus while others are refusing to do so – indicating that the ecclesia is not of one mind in this matter, as we ought to be when we meet to remember him.

It is sometimes suggested that, since there are no New Testament instances of hymns being sung to Jesus, it simply ought not to be done. Before we consider whether this is true, we might just ask how many hymns are recorded in the New Testament at all. It is not as if we have a large number of Christian hymns, all of which are addressed to God, from which to reach a conclusion. The question of whether it is right to sing to Jesus is more nuanced than this, therefore.

Honouring the Son

Of the scriptural principles that we can use to determine our approach to this matter, the first is surely that we should never lose our appreciation of the supremacy of God and the importance of honouring Him first and foremost – as Paul succinctly puts it: “from Him and through Him and to Him are all things” (Romans 11:36). This is a principle that the Lord Jesus endorsed in his teaching. Any approach to our hymn singing which failed to give primacy to God would be deeply flawed, therefore.

Yet we should not overlook the fact that honouring God entails honouring Christ, the one who is “the radiance of His glory” (Hebrews 1:3) – God manifested in the flesh, as we have always understood him to be. It is possible that, while seeking to honour God as we ought, we neglect to give Christ the honour that God says he is due. The danger of this is spelt out by the Lord Jesus himself:

“[God] has given all judgment to the Son, so that all will honour the Son even as they honour the Father. He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him” (John 5:22,23).

Jesus’ guidance

We have further guidance from the Lord. The Book of Revelation is his last message to his bondservants. Here, in a vision of the ‘heavenly throne room’, the resurrected Lamb – “looking as if it had been slain”, yet “standing” (5:6, NIV) – approaches the One on the throne to receive from Him the seven-sealed scroll. He is the only one in all creation qualified to do so. In response:

“the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb … And they sang a new song, saying, ‘Worthy are you to take the book and to break its seals; for you were slain, and purchased for God with your blood men from every tribe and tongue and people and nation’” (verses 8,9).

Here is a clear New Testament instance of praise being sung to the Lord Jesus Christ.

One common interpretation of this vision is that it depicts the saints praising Christ in the future Kingdom of God (so we will be permitted to sing to him then). However, we should note that this song is sung to the Lamb prior to his breaking the seals on the scroll in chapter 6 – that is, before he begins the series of events which takes readers from the Apostle John’s day to the Kingdom. However we identify the singers in Revelation 5, therefore, this scene shows praise being offered to the Lord Jesus during the period of his absence from us.

No doubt it was such an appreciation of things that has always led the compilers of the Christadelphian Hymn Book to include hymns which praise the Lord Jesus. 2 Number 385 of the current edition, for example, is a musical setting of the very similar words of Revelation 1:5,6, the text of the KJV being altered only very slightly:

2 On this, see: “Giving honour to the Son”, The Christadelphian, vol. 134, no. 1,592, February 1997, p. 47.

“Thou hast loved us, and hast washed us from our sins in thine own blood … To thee be glory and dominion for ever and ever.”

Declaring our faith

Yet these are more than words of praise; they include a statement to the Lord – a declaration by saints of what he has done for them: “Thou hast … washed us from our sins …” Consequently, in addition to the hymns which praise Christ, we have a number of hymns by which we can declare, direct to Christ, our conviction of what his sacrifice has accomplished for us. This is edifying for an ecclesia and faith-strengthening on an individual basis. Take hymn 215, for example:

“We saw thee not when thou didst come

To this poor world of sin and death …

But we believe thy faithful word,

And wait for thy return, O Lord.”

To declare our faith to our Lord in song is one way of expressing to him our deep gratitude that, “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Saying ‘thank you’

There are other biblical reasons for singing to Christ. Paul thanked him for his work (see 1 Timothy 1:12), for example. It would be strange if any of us had never thanked, from our heart, the man who, for the forgiveness of our sins, “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). May we not do that by singing to him? Indeed, we do have hymns which thank the Lord – see, for instance, verse 3 of hymn 380:

“Partakers of the bread, we lift our hearts to thee;

The power of sin is dead; thy love has set us free.

We thank thee thou hast blessed us thus …”

What about petitions?

We have seen that hymns which contain words addressed to the Lord Jesus are not all the same (which suggests that a ‘blanket’ approach to them would be too simplistic). One area for particularly careful consideration is hymns which are petitions to Jesus – asking him to do something for us, or to grant our requests. We would be justified in echoing the words of the Apostle John, “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20) – the Bride of Christ expressing her earnest desire for her absent Bridegroom’s return, as it were.

But then there is Paul’s instruction to the believers at Philippi: “let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Does this mean that no petitions ought ever to be made to Christ? Is that the conclusion that we would come to from considering the example of the apostles, as revealed in their inspired letters, or of the multitudes who came to the Lord even during his earthly ministry? Where should we draw the line? This is a question not easily answered in a single article, but in this area a study of the biblical evidence would lead us to the conclusion that petitions should be offered principally – though not necessarily exclusively – to the Father.

Unexpected guidance?

Hallelujah, sing of Jesus,

His the sceptre, his the throne;

Hallelujah, his the triumph,

His the victory alone:

Hark! The songs of peaceful Zion

Thunder like a mighty flood;

Jesus, out of ev’ry nation,

Hath redeemed us by his blood.

Hallelujah! not as orphans

Are we left in sorrow now;

Hallelujah! he is near us,

Faith believes, nor questions how;

Though the cloud from sight received him

When the forty days were o’er,

Shall our hearts forget his promise

‘I am with you evermore’?” (Hymn 295, verses 1,2)

There is a less obvious part of Scripture which gives us important guidance on singing hymns to the Lord Jesus Christ: the Book of Psalms. The psalms are the ‘hymn book’ of the nation of Israel, the ‘ecclesia’ of the Old Testament period. It is therefore relevant to observe that some of the psalms – although written centuries before his birth – are addressed ‘to’ the Lord Jesus Christ.

Even if we exclude those psalms in which it is God who is addressing His Son (which might not be justification for us to sing to him), we are still left with at least psalms 45, 68, 91, 102 and 118. In each case – we are told by New Testament scriptures – the writer is, in the Spirit, addressing Christ. To take one example: in Psalm 102:24-27 the psalmist says:

“I say … ‘Of old You founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands. Even they will perish, but You endure; and all of them will wear out like a garment; like clothing You will change them and they will be changed. But You are the same, and Your years will not come to an end.’”

Hebrews 1:8 tells us that these words (quoted in verses 10-12 of that chapter) are being spoken to “the Son”. Here is the Spirit’s own testimony, therefore, of another ‘hymn to Jesus’. We may not have thought of looking for such hymns in the Old Testament. Who can say that Psalm 102, understood in the way that it is expounded in Hebrews, was not amongst the “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” sung by the ecclesias in the first century?

The Lord’s approval

Finally, there is further guidance from the Lord. Late in his ministry, as he entered Jerusalem only a few days before his crucifixion, he was met by enthusiastic crowds who welcomed him with words taken from Psalm 118:

“Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest!” (Matthew 21:9; compare Psalm 118:25,26).

On this occasion, those praising the Lord – using scriptural words to do so – were specifically commended by him (interestingly, using the words of another psalm):

“Yes; have you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies You have prepared praise for Yourself’?” (Matthew 21:16, quoting Psalm 8:2).

If some from natural Israel were approved by the Lord for ‘singing’ to him in the days of his flesh, may not spiritual Israel do so now that “All authority has been given to [him] in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18)? The only people with whom the Lord found fault on that occasion were those who objected to the words of a psalm being addressed to him: the chief priests and the scribes.

As Brother Roger Lewis puts it in his new book:

“Hymns which elevate the Son, then, have been sung in our community since the very first Christadelphian hymn book. They were sung by our pioneer brethren, who had a firm understanding of the supremacy of God yet saw no conflict with a clear recognition of the work of the Lord Jesus Christ. Present in every subsequent hymn book, such hymns have been sung by every generation of the household ever since. To ascribe honour to him, to confess his status, to express our thanks before him, to declare our belief in him, to lament his continued absence, to entreat for his return, and to remember his atoning sacrifice are matters which should excite our highest attention. Those hymns which include such references to Christ, and which focus on his place in the purpose of Yahweh, are not God-dishonouring, for ‘Christ is the head of the church [ecclesia]: and he is the saviour of the body’ (Ephesians 5:23). In singing these songs we recognise our Saviour’s work, and especially so at the table of his fellowship feast.

“Mourning the Bridegroom’s absence, remembering the Lord’s great sacrifice, keeping the commandments of Christ, and honouring the Saviour in song are means which help us to nurture and sustain a developing relationship with our absent Lord, until he come.” 3

3 Roger Lewis (2023), The Current Work and Role of Christ, The Christadelphian, Birmingham, p. 60.
