content.rendered:
It is a strange question, yet perhaps not so strange for people of the ancient Middle East. Most worshipped local or regional gods and goddesses: the Canaanites followed Baal, the god of fertility and storms, and Mot, their god of death; the Hittites worshipped Inara, goddess of nature and fertility, and Arinna their sun goddess; and so on. These were their gods, in whom they trusted for benefit and protection. Consequently, they were localised. We get a hint of this in 1 Kings 20:28, where Yahweh says:

“Because the Syrians have said, ‘The Lord is God of the hills, but He is not God of the valleys,’ therefore I will deliver all this great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord.” 1

1 Bible quotations are from the NKJV except where otherwise stated.

They had made the mistake of reducing Yahweh to the level of one of their regional deities.

Limited gods

Not only did they worship gods of their own invention, but most ancient people were animists: they attributed living properties or divinity to inanimate, natural bodies such as the moon, stars and planets. Because of its dominance and life-giving power, the sun was deified in most cultures, from the Mayans in the West to the Druids of England and the Sumerians of the Near East. To the ancients, the universe must have seemed vastly greater than their gods, both terrestrial and celestial, who were local or limited in some way. This is seen in the multicultural rituals performed at the winter solstice to ensure the return of the sun to its summer zenith. Great though they believed their gods to be, these peoples remained constrained within the universe. For example, the Egyptians believed that the goddess Nut, arrayed in stars, was splayed above the earth, while the sun god was pulled across the sky in a boat. For ancient people, the universe was too big for their gods, who were contained within it.

A unique God

In contrast, the God of the Hebrews makes a very clear statement about His unique position:

“Thus says the Lord, the King of Israel … ‘I am the First and I am the Last; besides Me there is no God. And who can proclaim as I do? Then let him declare it and set it in order for Me, since I appointed the ancient people … Is there a God besides Me? Indeed there is no other Rock; I know not one’” (Isaiah 44:6-8).

Yahweh states not only that He is greater than any man-made gods, but also that they are not gods at all, merely constructs of the human mind and of superstitious fear. King David understood this when he declared:

“For the Lord is great and greatly to be praised; He is also to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the peoples are idols, but the Lord made the heavens” (1 Chronicles 16:25,26).

Such insight is unique to the Hebrews: not only is their God unlike any other god; He is the Creator of the universe itself – its very cosmogenesis. This makes Yahweh completely different from the fabricated imaginings of Israel’s neighbours.

The size of the universe

If the universe is too big for the gods-that-are-no-gods, what about Yahweh? How does He stand in relation to the observable universe? To put this into context, we must consider a few things about the universe – starting with its size. It is on a scale beyond human comprehension. We can barely appreciate the size of the earth, let alone imagine that a million earths would fit into our sun; or that the sun is an ordinary-sized star twenty-six times smaller than Arcturus (mentioned in Job 9:9 and 38:32), the brightest star in the constellation Boötes (the Herdsman), once believed to guide the constellations of the Great Bear and her cub (Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, also mentioned in Job).

How difficult it is for us to comprehend that our solar system is part of a local interstellar neighbourhood, which is itself part of the Milky Way galaxy, which in turn is part of a local galactic group (including the neighbouring Andromeda galaxy); or that this group of galaxies is but a constituent of a supercluster of galaxies in the constellation Virgo; and that there are countless clusters of such superclusters that together make up the observable universe!

If we travelled at the speed of light for one year, we would cover 9.5 trillion (million million) kilometres. Yet it is so vast that it would take us 93 billion years travelling at this spectacular speed to cover the span of the presently observable universe. The universe is unimaginably big!

Age, material and perfection

What of the age of the universe? Based upon data from observation missions such as COBE, 2 WMAP 3 and the more recent James Webb 4 space telescope, it appears to be at least 13.8 billion years old, with some studies dating it even older. 5 According to current scientific understanding, the universe appears to be unimaginably old. What’s more, for us living within this universe, the illusion of time appears to ‘flow’ in one direction only – sometimes faster, sometimes slower, but relentlessly forward. Being a component of the universe, we are born prisoners of time.

2 lambda.gsfc.nasa.gov/product/cobe/

3 map.gsfc.nasa.gov/

4 webb.nasa.gov

5 Rajendra P. Gupta, “JWST early Universe observations and ΛCDM cosmology”, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, vol. 524, no. 3, Sep. 2023, pp. 3385–95. Available at doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stad2032

What about the material of the universe – how massive is it? How much of it is out there? On a clear night, when we gaze at the white band of the Milky Way, we’re seeing a side-on view of a galaxy of about 100 billion stars similar to our sun. Yet the universe has around 2 trillion such galaxies, each made up of 100-200 billion stars. To put it another way, there are more stars in the universe than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of the world! Perhaps even more staggering is that the matter we can observe is estimated to be only five per cent of the total mass of the universe. The rest is currently-undetectable ‘dark matter’ and ‘dark energy’. The universe is unimaginably massive!

What about the perfection of the universe? Lord (Martin) Rees, 6 the Cambridge academic and current Astronomer Royal, has shown that the universe can be described by six numbers which define its forces, size, texture, duration, and properties. Set at just the ‘right’ values, they support a universe which not only promotes life but also encourages it to thrive. If these values were set any differently, then there would be huge consequences: stars could not shine to give warmth and light; elements like carbon, essential for life, could not form; the universe itself would either expand too fast or collapse in on itself. Consequently, the universe is described as strongly ‘anthropic’ – supportive of human life – a characteristic known to some as ‘the Goldilocks Effect’. It’s just right! The laws of physics which make this possible appear to be unchanging and universal – they are unimaginably perfect!

6 www.martinrees.uk

In summary, the universe appears big, old, massive and perfect – concepts which we battle to comprehend, given our limited human scale, limited lifespans and limited minds.

Five statements about God

Set against the vastness of the universe, made of God and by God, the Bible contains five statements that place Him above and beyond the universe.

1. Yahweh is bigger than the universe – God is outside space.

Solomon states this truism in 1 Kings 8:26,27:

“I pray, O God of Israel, let Your word come true, which You have spoken to Your servant David my father. But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain You. How much less this temple which I have built!”

Even the expanse in which the heavens are contained is unable to contain Yahweh. What He created is unable to contain Him – He is greater than the universe itself.

2. Yahweh is timeless, unlike the universe – God is outside time.

In the opening work of Book 4 of the Psalms, a book that shows the sovereignty of Yahweh over everything, we read:

“Lord, You have been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever You had formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, You are God. You turn man to destruction, and say, ‘Return, O children of men.’ For a thousand years in Your sight are like yesterday when it is past, and like a watch in the night” (Psalm 90:1-4).

Being outside the march of time, God is not defined by time or constrained by it. It has no direction or flow to the one who ‘looks in’ on His universe. The Christian author C. S. Lewis wrote:

“God, I believe, does not live in a time-series at all. His life is not dribbled out moment by moment like ours: with Him it is still 1920 and already 1960 … God is outside and above the Time-line. In that case, what we call ‘tomorrow’ is visible to Him in just the same way as what we call ‘today.’ All the days are ‘now’ for Him. He does not remember you doing things yesterday; He simply sees you doing them … He does not ‘foresee’ you doing things tomorrow; He simply sees you doing them: because, though tomorrow is not yet there for you, it is for Him.” 7

7 C. S. Lewis (1944), Mere Christianity, pp. 147-8.

Peter makes an helpful analogy with Psalm 90:

“But do not let this one fact escape your notice, beloved, that with the Lord one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day” (2 Peter 3:8, NASB 1995).

For God, who transcends time, they are alike – time does not affect Him.

3. Yahweh originated the universe – God is the ultimate source of all.

Not only is God greater than the universe in space and in time; He is its originator – despite its vastness, the created universe is less than the Being who formed it. In Isaiah, God declared:

“I am He, I am the First, I am also the Last. Indeed My hand has laid the foundation of the earth, and My right hand has stretched out the heavens; when I call to them, they stand up together” (Isaiah 48:12-13).

The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews understood this. It is beautifully summed up in the following translations of the same verse:

“By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible” (Hebrews 11:3, ESV).

“by faith we understand the ages to have been prepared by a saying of God, in regard to the things seen not having come out of things appearing …” (YLT). 8

8 Young’s Literal Translation (public domain).

Another translation suggests the idea that the universe did not come about from anything that was already in existence.

The understanding that comes from this verse is that what exists was brought into being by God’s will alone – God spoke, and it was so, by divine fiat. God is not only the Creator of the universe; He is also its source and substance.

4. Yahweh is the changeless sustainer of the universe – God is the ultimate guarantor of a life-sustaining universe.

In Isaiah, God declares that He is not only the Creator of the universe but also the source of life in it. Yes, the universe is life-supporting (anthropic); but this is so because it was made so by God. In His wisdom, he has shaped a vast universe to support and encourage life, and to be its sustainer and changeless guarantor:

“Thus says God, the Lord, who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread forth the earth and that which comes from it, who gives breath to the people on it, and spirit to those who walk on it … I am the Lord, that is My name” (Isaiah 42:5-9).

The psalmist says of God:

“Of old You laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands. They will perish, but You will endure; yes, they will all grow old like a garment; like a cloak You will change them, and they will be changed. But You are the same, and Your years will have no end” (Psalm 102:25-27).

Unlike the changing, decaying nature of the universe and everything in it, God’s qualities and laws God don’t change. His constancy underpins the fabric of life in the universe, in both the natural and spiritual domains.

5. Yahweh is the life-giver of the universe – God is the only one who can ‘reverse time’ to restore life to the dead.

No one other than God, who transcends time, can save from time and reverse time’s inexorable effects on those who were born its prisoners. Paul wrote to the Romans that only God “gives life to the dead and calls those things which do not exist as though they did” (Romans 4:17).

The nineteenth-century Austrian scientist Ludwig Boltzmann discovered that disorder increases with time – things decay – and, tellingly, had this law engraved on his tombstone. While this law is true in normal circumstances, it doesn’t take into consideration God’s power to reverse the effects of disorder and decay on those who love Him. For God, the dead in Christ only sleep, though their mortal remains return to the elements from which the universe is made.

Conclusions

Is the universe too big for our God? Certainly not! He is greater than the universe, above and beyond it in every way; transcendent and powerful – and yet as close to each of us as our next prayer. Perhaps that prayer will echo the wonder and gratitude of David when he prayed:

“O Lord, our Lord, how excellent is Your name in all the earth, who have set Your glory above the heavens! … When I consider Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars, which You have ordained, what is man that You are mindful of him, and the son of man that You visit him?” (Psalm 8:1-4).

How should we select those whom we wish to serve us in our ecclesias? Many ecclesial roles are taken on voluntarily, amongst the countless acts of service that should characterise life in Christ. Sometimes roles are taken on more or less by default, there being only so many willing servants as there are roles to fill. When there are more volunteers than jobs, however, many ecclesias have a process of choosing the brothers and sisters whom they wish to undertake certain roles, typically via a ballot of members. The same process may be followed even when brothers and sisters are willing to continue in their current roles, as this provides the ecclesia with a regular opportunity to endorse the work that is being done on their behalf.

It might be pointed out that the New Testament Scriptures record no instances of an ecclesia balloting its members in the way that many ecclesias do today. In the light of this observation, it is sometimes suggested that it would be more scriptural for brothers and sisters to be selected for office by the drawing of lots – a process for which there are biblical precedents.

The purpose of this article is to consider whether drawing lots is a suitable process for today’s ecclesias to follow. These thoughts have been compiled from notes made some years ago, when it was suggested to me that this procedure ought to be adopted in place of an annual ballot of ecclesial members. They are not intended to be a comprehensive treatment of this topic; readers may feel that there are other passages of Scripture, not dealt with in this article, which have a bearing on this topic. As ever, constructive comments would be welcome and may be submitted to the Editor for possible publication in the magazine.

New Testament words

Which Greek words are translated “lot” or “lots” in the New Testament? There are just two. 1

1 This analysis has been undertaken from the NASB 1995 (from where the Bible quotations in this article are taken). A study of the KJV would yield very similar results.

First, there is a verb, lagchanō. This is used of the priest Zacharias, who was “chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense” (Luke 1:9; compare 1 Chronicles 24:1-18), and of the Roman soldiers at the foot of the cross, who said of Jesus’ seamless tunic, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to decide whose it shall be” (John 19:24), in fulfilment of the prophecy of Psalm 22:18. 2 This verb is never used in the context of ecclesial decision-making.

2 The word is translated “received” in its two other occurrences (Acts 1:17; 2 Peter 1:1).

Secondly, there is a noun, klēros. This too is used of the casting of “lots” for the Lord’s garment at his crucifixion (Matthew 27:35; Mark 15:24; Luke 23:34; John 19:24). 3 It is also used of the process adopted by the eleven apostles, after the Lord’s ascension, to select a replacement for the traitor Judas Iscariot. Peter says to his fellow apostles:

3 Elsewhere, the word is translated “share” (Acts 1:17), “portion” (8:21), “inheritance” (26:18; Colossians 1:12) and “allotted to [one’s] charge” (1 Peter 5:3).

“‘… it is necessary that of the men who have accompanied us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us – beginning with the baptism of John until the day that he was taken up from us – one of these must become a witness with us of his resurrection.’ So they put forward two men, Joseph called Barsabbas (who was also called Justus), and Matthias. And they prayed and said, ‘You, Lord, who know the hearts of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen to occupy this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.’ And they drew lots for them, and the lot fell to Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles” (Acts 1:21-26).

Here is a clear instance, it is sometimes argued, of lots being used to select someone for an important role in the infant ecclesia. As this is the passage most frequently used to justify the same process today – in fact, the only such New Testament passage – it is appropriate to examine it in full.

The apostolic procedure

What do these verses tell us about the selection of Matthias as Judas’ replacement? There are several aspects to note besides the actual use of lots:

  • verse 15: the procedure is instigated by Peter before a full gathering of the believers
  • verses 16-20: Peter recognises that Judas’s fall was predicted in two psalms of David (69:25; 109:8)
  • verse 21: Peter identifies the need for a twelfth apostle 4

    4 The need for twelve apostles may have been deduced from the Lord’s earlier promise: “in the regeneration when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28; see too Luke 22:30).

  • verses 21,22: specific requirements for the role are identified: candidates must be male, must have followed the Lord Jesus from the time of John the Baptist’s ministry until Jesus’ resurrection, and must have seen the risen Lord
  • verse 23: candidates meeting these requirements are proposed from within the ecclesia.

From this we see clearly that there was much more involved than a replacement for Judas being chosen, at random, from an unlimited pool of willing but unqualified volunteers. One (and only one) man was required, and he needed certain qualifications to be considered for the role.

Two qualified candidates

When, therefore, the gathering “put forward two men”, Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias (verse 23), it appears that the final choice had to be made from two equally qualified candidates. Had there been only one suitably qualified individual, then presumably he would have been endorsed for the task automatically, with no further input required of the ecclesia. As it was, with the apostles unable to distinguish between the two men, the final choice from the ‘shortlist’ was committed to Christ himself: “And they prayed and said, ‘You, Lord, who know the hearts of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen to occupy this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place’” (verses 24,25). 5

5 I believe that “the Lord” in this verse is the Lord Jesus; the request for him to indicate which of the two candidates he had “chosen” corresponds exactly to the record of his selection of the original apostles, when “he called his disciples to him and chose twelve of them, whom he also named as apostles” (Luke 6:13) – the verb is the same in each passage. Incidentally, therefore, here is an instance of a prayer being addressed to Christ – a topic for consideration on another occasion.

Only after all this has been done is the drawing of lots mentioned: “And they drew lots for them, and the lot fell to Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles” (verse 26). And even at this stage, there is no indication at all of what form the lots took. We may have ideas on this, based upon Old Testament passages which mention the drawing of lots, but we do not know.

Informed decision-making

From the one New Testament passage that records the use of lots in an ecclesial decision-making situation, therefore, we might struggle to justify the use of this process in our ecclesias today. At the very least, before doing so we ought to satisfy ourselves that the circumstances truly match those when the apostles asked the Lord Jesus to make the final choice of a replacement for Judas. On the evidence of the details given to us, Acts 1 could not be used to allow all willing candidates for an ecclesial role to submit themselves to the drawing of lots regardless of their suitability – like names being put into a hat for the selection of one at random. That is not what is being described.

In the second part of this study, we will consider other New Testament passages which have a bearing on the ways in which we select members for ecclesial roles. Although none of these mentions the drawing of lots, there are parallels with the decision-making process that we see in Acts 1.

(Part 2 coming soon)

What’s the most valuable thing that you own? Whether the answer is a fifteen-bedroomed, beach-front holiday home in the Caribbean, or a broken-down old van which probably won’t make it through its next safety check, is irrelevant. It’s how we use such things that’s important – and whether they matter to us more than they should. However, we all possess things that are valuable.

What’s the most precious thing you own? It could be argued that this question has already been answered. To some, there is nothing more precious than the house or the car. These are the things that they would miss most if they were ever taken away. For members of the body of Jesus Christ, however, this should never be. We have something that is truly precious – beyond price. And, although certain items in the world are regarded as priceless, what we have is worth more than all the money in the world:

“ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold … but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot …” (1 Peter 1:18,19). 1

1 Bible quotations are from the KJV.

So the blood of Jesus – meaning the death of our beloved Master and Lord – is “precious”. But it is very different from things which may be counted as precious in this world – paintings or gems, for example. For a start, we’re thinking of something that can’t be seen or touched. We require faith in its existence. And, unlike other things which may be regarded as precious, the benefit of an association with the blood of Jesus never diminishes. The privileges of Christ’s death for believers are both present – we are forgiven, by grace, and are the children of God now – and future – we look forward to the Kingdom which will certainly be established on earth one day, hoping and praying that we will be permitted to share that time of glory.

How is Jesus’ blood special?

Let’s be clear: the blood of our Master was not, of itself, different. He was “made like unto his brethren” (Hebrews 2:17). The blood that was shed almost 2,000 years ago was no different, physically or biologically, from that of the two thieves who died alongside him. But because of the life that Jesus had lived, his death was definitely different – special, unlike that of any other man or woman:

  • Jesus never did anything wrong (1 Peter 2:22); sin was conquered and condemned in his flesh (Romans 8:3) – all day, every day.
  • He “offered himself” in faith to God (Hebrews 9:14). Try making sense of this if you believe in a triune Godhead!
  • He knew that he would be raised and glorified (Hebrews 5:7). There was not the slightest doubt in his mind.

This was, therefore, the most far-reaching event in the history of the world. This is why the shedding of the blood of this one man (and his glorious resurrection that followed) mattered then, and matters now – so very much. This is why Christ’s blood is precious.

Corruptible … incorruptible

There is an interesting play on words in 1 Peter 1. We are not redeemed with corruptible things, such as silver and gold. Naturally speaking, this isn’t true. Gold is one of the least corruptible materials on earth. To a lesser extent, this is also true of silver and other metals. I’m currently looking at a twenty-pence piece which was minted in 1993. It’s virtually unchanged from the day when it was new, thirty years ago. But look at a photograph of yourself from thirty years ago and you will see great changes!

This apparent contradiction is made all the more powerful when we note that Peter describes Christ’s blood as being “precious” (and, by implication, incorruptible). Blood, especially in a hot climate and without the methods of keeping items cool that we have in the Western world, corrupts quickly; but apparently not in the case of the blood of Jesus. This is a typical example of Scripture stating something that is naturally contradictory to prove an important point. In the natural world, gold outlasts almost any other material – and definitely any mortal being. But all the gold in the world is worth nothing compared with what we have. The mercy that has been shown to us, and the hope of immortality, made sure through the blood of Jesus, is worth more than all of Elon Musk’s billions. He is a beggar on a street corner compared with you and me.

Rejecting Jesus’ sacrifice

In Hebrews 10 we read of some who, despite having learned and responded to God’s Word, were sinning wilfully. For such a person, writes the apostle, Christ’s sacrifice is ineffectual. It isn’t that it is unpowerful or faulty – indeed, the opposite is true. It’s just that some people in the first century were, by their actions, placing themselves outside its influence. The language used is powerful and graphic. Those who despised the Law of Moses were punished, but:

“of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?” (Hebrews 10:29).

Treading underfoot the blood of Jesus – it’s almost too horrendous to contemplate! The context here is of believers meeting together (see verse 25). So those who choose not to keep fellowship when they could – those who reject fellowship altogether and return to the world – are doing far more than refusing to meet with people they once regarded as their brothers and sisters. They are turning their backs on Jesus Christ. They are, in symbol, treading on his blood.

There is an example of this behaviour in the tragic life of Judas Iscariot. The blood of the Passover lamb had been shed. It would have been daubed on the lintel and doorposts of the upper room. Inside was Jesus, the fulfilment of the Law – “our Passover … sacrificed for us” (1 Corinthians 5:7). And Judas walked away. He may literally have trodden on the blood of the lamb as he left the room, for that blood would have run down the doorposts and dripped from the lintel, collecting around the entrance to that place. Of course, others walked the same way a short time afterwards, with Jesus. But Judas did so alone. He turned his back on “the light of the world” (John 8:12; 9:5) and headed off into the night (13:30). And, by leaving an upper room, there was only one way for him to go: down!

The memory of Christ’s death

We remember Jesus’ death, week by week. We should remember it each day, for we are commanded to “take up [our] cross daily” (Luke 9:23). But what should this do for us? This isn’t like some vague memory of an event years ago – a holiday or a pleasant day out. It has to touch us. In Hebrews 9 we read of the offerings under the Law, and what they achieved. In this context, the apostle asked:

“how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” (verse 14).

The Law was given by God, and under it people were sanctified. But it was only a shadow. The substance is Jesus. This is key to our appreciation of what the Law did – and what it could not do.

What, then, should the blood of Jesus do? It should purge our consciences. This isn’t about the outward appearance; it’s about the heart. So, as we take the bread and the wine – as we consider what Jesus did, and how he suffered (and how God suffered) – we should try to “purge” our lives; to try and make them a little more like Jesus’ life.

The Greek word translated “purge” is katharizō. This gives us our English word ‘catharsis’. This is the process of releasing, and thereby providing relief from, strong or repressed emotions. This is one reason why we do what we do: to release certain things; to turn our backs on them. And if we do, then we benefit – and so will others. And, most importantly, God will be glorified.

Washed in blood

In Revelation 7 we read of a great multitude. John was told who they were:

“These … came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (verse 14).

Here we have a further apparent contradiction. Nothing can be washed in blood. If something were, then it wouldn’t be white! Yet spiritually, this is wholly true. We are cleansed, by grace, through the blood of Jesus, because he offered himself to God. What a privileged people we are!

When we meet, week by week, we don’t do so specifically to have our sins forgiven. If that were the case, then pity the brother who sins on Sunday evening, or the sister who is too ill to attend for three or four weeks. We meet to remember the way that such forgiveness was made possible. We meet to recall what has been done for us (1 Corinthians 11:24), to show Christ’s death (verse 26), and to examine ourselves (verse 28). And in doing so, we have to try to purge our lives. If we wish to be clad in white with him one day, then this is what’s required of each one of us.

What’s precious to you?

So, as we meet to take the bread and the wine, is this something that is “precious” to you and me? Do we long to meet together? Is it the highlight of our week? Or is it something that we do out of habit? Perhaps after so many years it has lost its power to move us – to change us. Cast your mind back to the first time you broke bread and drank wine. Was there a desperation to do so? Was it truly special? Was it “precious”? And if the passion that once existed is waning, isn’t now the ideal time to determine to do something about it?

One day – perhaps very soon – our Master will come again to call his people to him. When he does, what will he see? What does he want to see? A group of people touched by the beauty and power of Scripture. A family of believers, waiting faithfully for him, longing to see his face, regarding the truth concerning him and his death as the most wonderful, valuable thing – the most glorious thing; without question, the most precious thing of all.

title.rendered: How do we differentiate between chance and God at work in our lives?

content.rendered:
Question of the month

Since events that happen in our lives do not come with neat explanatory labels attached, we can unfortunately never know for certain this side of the Kingdom the reason why any particular thing has occurred. We might wish that we did, but we don’t. It’s also probably too simplistic to think that there is just one cause for a particular thing that happens; causality is highly complex, probably much more complex than we can imagine, and there may be different levels of causality (for instance: the physical or material; the human and the divine).

Hindsight

God certainly does not owe us an explanation for what happens, as the Book of Job makes plain, and it’s possible that, even if we were to be told the reason, we wouldn’t really understand that bigger picture, or we might struggle to agree with it (our tiny perspectives only compounding our struggles). After all, how can we with our small minds hope to fathom how the will of God and His ability to direct our lives interacts with our own free will, let alone the free wills of everyone else in the world? The problem is so complex that we can be greatly relieved that we can trust in the Lord’s sovereignty rather than having to rely on our own ability to rationalise fully causes and effects.

It is often not until afterwards – sometimes months or years later – that we can perhaps start to comprehend something of what God may have been orchestrating and achieving through the difficult circumstances of our lives. This is not always the case, but it is true that many have had this experience. We can begin to discern, even if only in shadowy outline, the purposes that God may have had which were perhaps different from our own wishes and calculations, but which have brought about a greater or different good that we did not expect. At times like this, it dawns on us that God is so much wiser than we often give Him credit for. It is a good thing that He is in charge and not we ourselves.

We could be wrong

Even in such cases, however, it’s good to remember that our later realisations are only deductions or assumptions about what God may have been doing through those difficult circumstances. He doesn’t explicitly tell us, which means that when we think along these lines we are engaged in interpretation, and we may be wrong. We may have had the experience of listening to someone tell of something that has happened in their life which they are sure represents the intervention of God, and it may sound to us as more arbitrary in nature, part of the normal ‘ebb and flow’ of life. No one can say for sure, apart from God and potentially the Lord Jesus and the angels. That doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t reflect on our lives (either in retrospect or in real time), trying to discern God’s hand. In fact it is a good idea to do so, considering our ways and what God may be teaching us. But we should remember that we could be mistaken.

Complexity

Events that take place in the world are a complex interaction of many things, including:

  • human free will and the real-world consequences of human choice
  • mechanistic laws of cause and effect (if we bang our heads against a wall for long enough, we will bleed)
  • more general principles of cause and effect and probability (socio-economic tendencies; upbringing; genetic effects (people of such-and-such genetics are more likely to suffer so-and-so); geographic and technological implications (earthquakes are more likely in some places; some technologies only generally available in some areas), and so on)
  • the overarching power and will of God; His ability to act and determine; His desire and ability to bring about His purpose.

God’s ability to intervene and override whatever other factors may be in play trumps everything; at any point, it is His prerogative to do this if He so chooses. That is part of what it means for Him to be God. But the bigger miracle is how He brings about His purposes while simultaneously generally allowing the ‘laws’ of cause and effect to operate, and while giving human beings free will and the ability to act autonomously.

All things work together

The Bible tells us that God sends the angels to minister to the saints. It tells us that God is in control; there is nothing that can happen to us that God would be powerless to prevent or override if He chose to do so. But it tells us more than that – it tells us that all things work together for good to those that love God (Romans 8:28).

We need to read this carefully. It does not tell us that ‘all things that happen to us are good’, or even that God specifically singles out and chooses every individual thing that happens to us (this may or may not be true, but this passage does not say so). But it does say that, in the purview of God’s oversight and will, all things that happen work together for good. If someone is abused, then, or mercilessly mugged; if someone is hit by a car because someone else of their own free will chose to get drunk and drive irresponsibly – we do not have to say (and nor does the passage demand that we say) that these things are somehow intrinsically ‘good’. No, they are bad and they are the result of human evil. But the passage does say that if we allow them to – and, more to the point, if we allow Him to – then even these things can be turned to good outcomes in God’s purpose. God may or may not have specifically sent them for us by way of intervention; they may or may not be the consequence of other causes and effects operating in the world. But if they occur, then certainly God has chosen not to override them, and He knows every hair on our head (there is nothing that happens outside

His will and control in that sense). And, even more certainly, God is able to work for good through even the worst things that can happen – whether it is in our own lives, or in the lives of others who are also involved in the event in some way – depending, of course, upon how we and they respond.

Good from evil

This is one of the most amazing things about God. He is able to bring good out of the very worst of human evil. We see Him doing so in the aftermath of the Holocaust, for example, and we see it paradigmatically in the crucifixion. God is able to bring about His will even through the evil or indifferent wills of others. This is a most remarkable truth, and one for which God is due great praise.

Thus we find that in the life of Joseph, twice stated, his brothers intended their actions in utter evil – and Joseph certainly paid the price. But God intended it for good, and ultimately brought out of it a greater good than the evil that they had thought to do. God brings about His will without compromising the free will of others. 1

1 This is generally true. Exceptionally, there seem to be extreme cases, like the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart, where humans have set their course with sufficient evil and stubbornness that God takes over, pushing them, as it were, further down the path on which they have set themselves – but that is a different subject.

Endlessly captivating, the Bible’s very first words establish the primacy and agency of God: “In the beginning God created …” There is a world because there is first a God; without Him there would be nothing: no time, no space, no matter, no meaning and nothing that could be meant.

Because of Him there is everything. The world comes into being because He wills it; it is of His choice, His instigation. It seems like an obvious point, but one whose implications I had not really considered until provoked by a recent book about the way in which the Bible helps us to build a godly worldview. God is under no compulsion to create or to do anything in particular; the world is a gratuitous and, in a partial sense, even a capricious act of His, an act of volition involving no external stimulus. There is no transaction taking place under which God has obligation; there is nothing causing Him to create in any binding sense outside of His own nature and desire; it is a totally free act.

Agency

There is a big truth about God in this. One of the classic mysteries about Him from later scriptures is His choosing, His calling and election. But that particular mystery is part of a bigger picture that begins in Genesis 1. God is the Agent Supreme. He acts under no binding force. His action is completely unobligated and free; He is not part of any system which imposes upon Him or compels Him; He is utterly transcendent. This is a theme of which the prophet Isaiah never tires, especially in chapters 40–66.

Knowing, as we do from later revelation, what sort of God He is (His creativity, His self-disclosing nature, His love and mercy), we may not be surprised that He has chosen to create. We may even say that the world is a logical consequence and expression of the sort of God that He is; it makes sense that such a world should exist, given that He exists. But none of that reasoning, correct though it may be, obligates God to create, or to create in this particular way. That is His choice and His instigation.

Worldview

Realising this about Him is an important key in forming a biblical worldview, one of the great tasks of discipleship. We did not come about because there was a formula that necessitated it. There was no law or set of preconditions that demanded it (contra to popular theories of ‘big bangs’ which exclude God from their account); there was no scientific or legal obligation in that sense. Nor, on the other hand, did the world come about by accident, by no one and for no one out of no-thing. It came about by the free choice of God – because He could and because He chose. Those great creative acts of goodness ushered forth from Him because He chose to display them. Getting His primacy and agency big enough in our own viewfinders is the task. Once we start to understand it, then His ability and right to elect and choose are not so surprising, because we have entered the world of grace. His ability and willingness to show grace when there was absolutely no obligation for Him to do so starts to resonate and make sense, and is there in the Bible’s very first words. Things are that way because that’s how He chooses to be. It is indescribably brilliant. This is the sort of God He is.

Because of who He is

It is at one and the same time the biggest mystery and the most logical thing in the world. If God wants to create a world, or beget a people, or create in us clean hearts, then He can and will – puzzling in one sense (Why ‘over here’ and not ‘over there’?), but completely sense-making in another (Why shouldn’t He? He can do whatever He wants).

The Book of Revelation captures the enigma: “Thou hast created all things!” (4:11) sing the living creatures, and the KJV seems to rationalise a reason: “and for Thy pleasure they are and were created.” It is tempting to understand “pleasure” in the sense of enjoyment – God creates the world because it brings Him enjoyment. This may be true (in some aspects, doubtless it is true; in others, the world brings Him deep pain in its current state). But the passage really means ‘and for / by Thy will they were created’, which re-establishes the enigma. The Book of Revelation is not saying why God created the world other than that it came about because He wanted and chose to. This is the same as Genesis: everything begins because of His action. The creation is once again rooted in His gratuitous act and character, just as salvation is rooted in His unobligated grace.

Big implications

And what of us? Does this key aspect of God’s supreme agency have any implications for how we behave?

It most certainly does, and we shall consider two. The first is that the world is about Him before it is about us. The famous quotation from Brother John Thomas points out that God’s plan is about God-manifestation before it is about human salvation, and there is an element of that truth to this theme. We are used to a highly commodified world in which goods are exchanged and traded, a market economy in which one thing is done in order for another thing to be done in return. Everything has been turned into a market in which nothing is free. God’s action to instigate and create, by contrast, is a free initiative on His part and it is all grace. He does not owe us anything and is not indebted to us in any way. Instead, He freely chooses to give us so much and to reveal Himself to us. We move beyond the transactional when we think of God; we marvel at who He is and what He has done, and we gratefully thank Him for allowing us to be a part of it. God didn’t have to do anything; yet by His grace He has chosen to do so much. What we have to do, therefore, is to make Him bigger and ourselves smaller in our thinking.

Human agency

Our second point has to do with our potential as human beings. The fact is that in some measure we are like Him, made in His image. There is a lot that might be said about what it means to be in God’s image, but one aspect of it has to do with this point about agency. We sometimes talk about human beings as ‘free agents’, which captures that very idea and is another way of talking about what it means to have a free will rather than being governed purely by instinct like an animal, or by subroutines like a robot. Of course, our creaturely instincts are powerful, but we can be more than just a collection of instincts.

“Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16, KJV)

God has given us agency. We can choose to act and the manner of our acting. Just as God chose to create a world of good things that summed to “very good”, so too we have been empowered with the ability to act, the choice to do good in the world. We don’t have to; we are not under obligation with our arms twisted behind our backs or our instincts so powerful that they cannot be resisted. But we can choose to. We can act for good, as God did. We can do this of our own free choice, just because we can – because that is the sort of person we choose to be, and that is how we choose to reveal ourselves.

This is tremendously empowering. I can be more than a victim of market forces, compelled to purchase just because advertising tells me to do so. I can be more than a victim of my appetites; I can say ‘No!’ to what is evil and choose what is good. I can be more than a cog in a transactional machine which does things only because it is first acted on by something else. I can resist tit-for-tat or merely doing something just so that I will receive something in return. I can instead choose to do and be what I believe in. I can choose to show good just because I can, to forgive because that is what He does; to seek the right because that is what I want to stand for.

These are not small things. The world that God chose to create was not small, and when He gave to us the power of agency He was not passing on a part of Himself which was small. To act freely with grace and forgiveness and to do what is right are the biggest things in the world, and God has empowered us to do them! We are not under compulsion or under duress; we don’t have to bite back just because someone first bites us. We can choose to be the Christlike and the Godlike person. It is God who has given us that tremendous capacity and who has forgiven us so great a debt out of His free choice. Now it is up to us to decide what kind of micro-world we will create in the sphere of influence that God has gifted us. Now, inspired by Him, let us find the will to act.

‘Ecclesial autonomy’ or ‘ecclesial independence’ is a great blessing enjoyed within the worldwide Christadelphian fellowship. It has various advantages, particularly when compared with models of community organisation practised by other groups – especially those with authoritative hierarchical structures or complicated bureaucracies.

It is an inferred doctrine, rather than a directly taught one, but one which emerges very clearly from the pages of the New Testament. First-century ecclesias were expected to be responsible for caring for and upbuilding one another, and also for instruction and taking disciplinary action when that was required. The letters of both Paul and Jesus make this plain (for example, 1 Corinthians 5:2-5,9-13; Revelation 2:14-16,20).

Wonderful benefits

Ecclesial autonomy is a beautiful thing with all kinds of wonderful advantages. For instance:

  • It encourages serious thought and engagement with the Word of God at the local level; it encourages us to be accountable and to develop spiritual maturity amongst ourselves, rather than relying on external ‘authorities’.
  • It demands responsible welfare and care for one another by those who know us best and are best positioned practically to help.
  • It enables the shaping of ecclesial activities to best meet the needs of the members and their circumstances and preferences (for example, the range and extent of youth activities, preaching activities of different types, Sunday school before or during the main service, and so on).
  • It allows difficulties to be addressed and support to be offered where the circumstances and needs are best understood.
  • It permits non-fundamental differences of style, emphasis and practical application and – let’s admit it – personalities to be accommodated in a way that need not compromise the overall integrity of Christ’s body (differences of language choice and level of formality, cup or cups, order of service, collections, musical accompaniment choices …).

In all this we are seeking for unity, not uniformity. God may be worshipped in spirit and in truth in ways different from the ones I may personally prefer or be used to. Anyone who goes on a CBM trip and visits a variety of ecclesias, or who takes a stroll through history, well knows this.

We are all joined together as parts of Christ’s body with our common doctrines and fellowship, but we have a measure of flexibility to take decisions and pursue initiatives that will be most edifying for us at the local level, provided those decisions don’t seriously impact the fellowship harmony of the wider community or jeopardise its position. 1

1 While it may sound unlikely, there is a risk that this can happen. What might be some examples? An ecclesia deciding to practise ‘open fellowship’ would go against our general biblical understanding and our practice as a community and cause big issues – it would, ironically, be destructive of unity. This is not the basis on which the Christadelphian community is defined and functions. Similarly, an ecclesia deciding to endorse service in the armed forces or to become politically active would jeopardise our community’s united position on military service, which has been a powerful point when we have had to testify before the authorities during periods of conscription in many different places.

A balancing principle

But good though ecclesial autonomy is, there can be a danger. Considered in isolation, as if it were the only governing principle of association, ecclesial autonomy can create an incomplete and potentially even a dangerous understanding of ecclesial relations. In a sense, it is a half-doctrine: true as far as it goes, but an understanding which needs to be balanced by a counterweight. This counterweight is a sense of ecclesial responsibility – of accountability to Christ, and to the body of Christ and the wider community. Consider Paul’s phrase “as in all churches [ecclesias] of the saints” (1 Corinthians 14:33). Ecclesias are not laws unto themselves, independent island states in an archipelago, or, worse, unconnected corks bobbing in the ocean. Each is a part of the one body of Christ, connected by living ‘tissue’ and united under our great Lord and head.

Getting this balance right – ecclesial autonomy and ecclesial responsibility to the wider body – is a delicate matter. We need to have an eye, not only on the interests of our own ecclesia, but also on what is helpful and unifying within the wider body. This will include our corporate stance on belief, behaviour and practice based on our collective understanding of God’s Word. Our love for the community and for one another, and our Lord’s desire for unity, demand no less (see his prayer in John 17).

If we push towards either extreme (ruthless unanimity on every small matter, or fiercely guarded independence on everything), it will not work, and fellowship will become impossible. We have to really want unity within the body of Christ, and to be willing to regulate our behaviour accordingly, if we are to have any hope of achieving it. This is obviously true in marriage and family life, but it is true in the ecclesial family as well. We accept constraints on our own freedom in order to experience a greater togetherness.

Autonomy with responsibility

Pushed to an extreme, autonomy can mean selfishness and a lack of responsibility to the wider body of which all ecclesias form part. It is not ‘our’ ecclesia to do as we please; it is Christ’s. Other ecclesias are also part of that body, and ought at least to be considered and respected in our decision-making, because our ecclesial actions impact on them to some degree. Ecclesial autonomy is not a licence for thinking only about the local ecclesial ‘self’ to the exclusion of other local ecclesias or the wider body. It can be a real temptation, particularly if we are frustrated with our ecclesial neighbours for one reason or another, to write them off and disregard them. The world we live in worships individualism – which makes the notion of autonomy a natural fit – but we have spiritual responsibilities to the wider body of which we are part. We should seek a harmonious and mutually edifying relationship with our local ecclesias as far as we possibly can.

Ecclesial autonomy ought not to become a form of ‘every ecclesia doing what is right in its own eyes’ – where an ecclesia decides that it will do something and, if others don’t like it, then that’s their problem. We must seek the cohesion and unity of the body and the spirit of Christ in our actions. If pursuing a particular course as an ecclesia is going to cause great concern and upset in surrounding ecclesias, and is going to mean that fellowship with those ecclesias will no longer be possible, then we should think extremely carefully before pursuing that road. Is it really what is for the best, and are we so sure that we are right when the majority evidently think otherwise? There is a delicate balance to be struck here between what we think best for our ecclesia and what may be helpful for the wider body. If we push too far down an individualistic path, then the wider fellowship could ultimately cease to exist.

Thinking responsibly

We have a responsibility, then, to think of others, not just of ourselves, in the decisions that we take. We must trust other ecclesias and give them space to make their own decisions, and they must trust us also to be striving for what is best in the Lord – rather than constantly treating each other with suspicion. We should not be holding other ecclesias to ransom, or poking our noses in on matters which are their responsibility; we should engage if there is a genuinely serious issue at stake which threatens the unity or integrity of the body and is in serious contravention of Scripture. Of course, we may not always agree on what constitutes “a genuinely serious issue”, so we need to communicate and to be prepared to explain our reasoning to one another and to listen. The Ecclesial Guide has some wise advice on this.

It is good to think about what might actively encourage or enable neighbouring ecclesias to share fellowship with us, or whether we are putting up unnecessary barriers. For example, if we stand at the door with a list of propositions which we require visitors from other ecclesias to sign before they enter, then we convey a spirit of suspicion and betray a lack of trust, making it unpalatable for others to fellowship with us. It is right, within the body of Christ, for us to trust one another that we are in the faith as our default position; if others betray that trust, then that is on them. Yet if we expect the trust of our neighbouring ecclesias, then it is incumbent on us to behave in a way that is worthy of being trusted and in the spirit of our one fellowship. It is a mutual relationship in Christ (see Paragraph 41 of The Ecclesial Guide).

Great blessings

There are many amazing benefits that flow from our fellowship in the Lord. It is a unique structure. The tension between autonomy and responsibility keeps us productively on our toes, encouraging us to consider prayerfully what is best, and to engage with the Scriptures, as we seek the unity of the body and as we “grow up into him” (Ephesians 4:15).

Our central authority is the Lord Jesus Christ – ours is a body that belongs to him as head. It is to the teachings of all the Scriptures that we turn to understand what we are to believe and how we should behave. It is to these that we look as we seek the unity of the faith. These are aspects of what it means to “[continue] stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Acts 2:42).

With the rapid increase in computing power, our world is shaken by a new kind of intelligence. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a mind-blowing technology that can predict, recognise, solve and understand problems that normally require human intelligence. AI can change every aspect of our lives – including our faith.

Even though the Bible doesn’t mention AI, God provides us with some valuable guidelines. This emerging technology is crafted by humans and can be used for better or for worse. New AI tools can assist us in improving our understanding and study of God’s Word. AI chatbots, for example, can benefit us with the translation of talks, worksheets, Sunday School material or even books. Why not use this technology to deepen your knowledge of the word of God? AI can aid you in recognising patterns in Scripture, such as chiasms, repetition and emphasis. We can also identify cross-references and analyse the Hebrew and Greek text to comprehend the true meaning of a Bible passage.

However, we need to be cautious. It’s easy to blindly trust artificial intelligence without cross-checking with God’s Word. Psalm 146:3 (Amplified Version) warns us not to “trust in princes, in mortal man, in whom there is no salvation.” Instead, Proverbs 3:5,6 encourages us to “trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.” Our focus is evident when we trust God rather than man-made technology.

AI models are only as innovative as their training data, and therefore sometimes come up with entirely wrong answers. Consequently, we need to “test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). With a prayerful approach to Bible study, God will give us guidance and insights into His inspired Word.

Will AI take over the world? While this is a common phenomenon in sci-fi movies and books, technology hasn’t advanced to a world-dominating power (yet). AI will undoubtedly replace jobs, cause ethical dilemmas and make it harder to differentiate truth from lies. Our single source of truth is the Bible. We don’t have to worry about tomorrow (Matthew 6:34), as it will take care of itself.

The God-given blessing of searching His words and seeing the Bible come to life cannot be replaced by AI. But this reverence for God’s Word can be enhanced. In addition, we can use the information to uplift and encourage others by double-checking AI text for biblical accuracy. With a healthy amount of critical thinking, prayer and discussion within our community, this new technology can benefit us in many practical ways. ν

When the word ‘meditation’ comes up in conversation, it is often equated with mindfulness, something which today has become connected to good mental health. It usually involves stopping the hectic routine of life for a moment and taking time to try and empty one’s mind of stressful thoughts and to just ‘be’. Some smart watches will even buzz to remind their owners to take some time out to do it! This type of meditation – where people try not to think, but to just be aware, be at peace, and live moments as they unfold – might indeed be helpful to some in this very busy world; but is this the meditation that is spoken about in the Bible?

Not really. This idea doesn’t occur very often in Scripture, and when it does, it doesn’t mean striving to think about nothing. On the contrary, it is always talking about reading/studying/thinking about God’s Word. We’re told in Genesis 24:63 that Isaac went out in the field in the evening to meditate – no doubt on the promises made to him through his father Abraham. It was during one of these times that his wife arrived, perhaps as an answer to questions running through his mind as he pondered how the promises would come to fruition.

In Joshua 1:8, God commands Joshua: “This book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.” Rather than trying to fill our mind with nothing, we can gather from this verse that we should be making sure that we take some time out of our busy lives to fill our minds with God’s Word.

Fourteen times the word ‘meditate’ occurs in the Psalms, and again the writers are referring to pondering God’s works or His Word. Also, just like the command in Joshua, often the time of meditation happened at night – perhaps when sleep escaped the writer due to something causing him worry or fear. Jesus often stayed up all night in prayer, no doubt asking God for the strength and wisdom to do his ministry well. Prayer can therefore become an important offshoot of meditation. What we read in the Bible causes us to yearn to be better, to want to repent from our sins, to ask for strength to carry on, to ask for wisdom and understanding – and so our meditation leads to ‘conversation’ with God about these things.

So, next time your smart watch gives you a nudge to be mindful, instead of just closing your eyes to concentrate on your breathing why not read a chapter of the Bible or think about your favourite verse? No doubt this will lead on to a heartfelt prayer of praise to our heavenly Father and will keep the wonderful hope of the promise of the Kingdom burning bright in your mind. ν

Whenever we think about disciples, our minds usually go immediately to the twelve disciples who Jesus chose to accompany him during the hardest three years of his life (Luke 6:13).

But discipleship is much broader than that. The word “disciple” (“mathetes”) occurs hundreds of times in the Gospels and in Acts, although interestingly only once outside of that (in Isaiah 8:16 – which uses the equivalent Hebrew word “limmud”).

Today we think of a disciple as being a follower of someone or something, but the word “disciple” refers to a learner or a pupil – someone who follows someone’s teachings.

It is the opposite of the word “master” or “teacher”. For example we see the two words together in Matthew 10:25, where Jesus says “it is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher”.

Not only do we read about the twelve disciples of Jesus in the Bible, but also many other disciples such as Paul, Timothy and Joseph of Arimathea as well as the disciples of John of the Pharisees.

The full scope of the word can be seen in the command of Jesus to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19), and in how the believers in general are called “disciples” in Acts (e.g. Acts 6:1).

The concept of discipleship is not exclusive to the Gospels and Acts! Although the writers of the letters in the New Testament prefer to call their fellow believers “brothers and sisters” and “saints”, being a disciple is still a clear theme.

This is clear in 1 Peter 2:21, where we read, “For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps”. The word “example” here literally means “underwriting”. We have the picture of the pupil learning to write by copying the perfect example of the teacher’s writing above.

Maybe the best way to think about a disciple is as an apprentice. In Jesus we don’t just have a teacher who tells us what to do from afar. We have someone who has done it all already and shows us what to do by leading by example. Luke 6:40 sums it up perfectly. “A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher”.

Are you a disciple of Christ? It doesn’t mean that you’ve perfectly completed every commandment. But it does mean that you’ve started the journey, you’ve committed to learning and humbly following every day in the footsteps of Jesus.

Do not go gentle into that good night,

Old age should burn and rave at close of day;

Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

Though wise men at their end know dark is right,

Because their words had forked no lightning they

Do not go gentle into that good night.

Good men, the last wave by, crying how bright

Their frail deeds might have danced in a green bay,

Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

Wild men who caught and sang the sun in flight,

And learn, too late, they grieved it on its way,

Do not go gentle into that good night.

Grave men, near death, who see with blinding sight

Blind eyes could blaze like meteors and be gay,

Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

And you, my father, there on the sad height,

Curse, bless, me now with your fierce tears, I pray.

Do not go gentle into that good night.

Rage, rage against the dying of the light.—Dylan Thomas (1914–1953)

The poet’s flame was extinguished when he was only thirty-nine. He did not “go gentle into that good night”; he drank himself to death, felled in the end by pneumonia. His poem is about resistance, rebellion and shouting down the darkness that eventually descends upon all the living. It is a keening, heartbreaking elegy on what death can feel like for people with no faith, no real hope for life beyond this life. It is the battle cry of a man of this world, a bitter meditation on lost opportunities, squandered hours, deeds undone and painful regrets.

When the world dies

People react differently on that last stretch of road that leads to their demise. A man might comfort himself with fanciful myths that provide a false sense of hope, or he might fall prey to the reactions that emerge when one feels that one’s most precious possession is being torn from one’s grasp. Today, desperate and frightened billionaires are making investments in life-extension research as the reality of their mortality sinks in. They know that their money will not render them immune to the death that they feel uncoiling itself mercilessly within their withering husks. Generally speaking, people see the final phase of their lives as a time of weakness, frailty, decrepitude, humiliation, and finally dissolution. They experience it as the time when they are at their lowest level of value and contribution, a burden to others and to themselves.

But for us, for believers, this last stage need not be characterised as a time of weakness or uselessness. We are comforted by the knowledge that death is not the end for us. We close our eyes in sleep and reopen them at the Lord’s feet, seeking his mercy and grace, being confronted with the things that we have done in our lives yet confident in his love for us, in his forgiveness and his desire for us to be in his Kingdom.

When we are at the last stage

As believers, we need to consider something we don’t often think about, our last days, with a deliberate focus on having a good death – one that does not have as its theme a caustic railing against the dying of the light. “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints”, writes the psalmist (Psalm 116:15; cp. 72:14).[1] Our death is meaningful to Him. It can be invested with meaning by us through what we do and say during that time. Once we have the opportunity to prepare for it, it need not be a mournful, regretful departure into that “good night”. For us, as it was with the Lord Jesus, it can be an exodus which we ‘accomplish’ (Luke 9:31), a fruitful final stage of life, one marked by the emergence and expression of a fully matured woman or man of faith. True, chronic pain, depression, memory lapses and other ills attendant upon the aging process might act as serious constraints on the extent to which we make something useful of that last stage. But if we have some vestige of our wits available to us, and the willingness to make our death an accomplishment rather than a defeat, then God will help us, giving purpose and focus to our last days.

In Psalm 71, David wrote, “Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth” (verse 9). God never casts off His children; but, when troubles mount, when pain is our daily companion, when loneliness and isolation can lend a dismal tint to so many of our days, we can feel abandoned by Him. It’s just a feeling, not reality. David balances this feeling with a call to action, a corrective to despondency in old age:

“My mouth shall tell of Thy righteousness, and of Thy salvation all the day … Yea, even when I am old and grayheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have declared Thy strength unto the next generation, Thy might to every one that is to come” (verses 15,18, RV).

Having a good death has, at its heart, a desire to honour God in our last days, to elevate Him above our fears, aches, pains and losses, to speak of Him to those we leave behind, and to bequeath to them a rich inheritance, one more precious than gold, silver, paper and soil – a legacy of faith humbly expressed, the articulation of the experience and memory of a life moulded by God.

Good deaths in the Bible

God’s Word gives us many examples of the godly in the last phase of life. Reflecting upon the actions taken by them, the realisations that they came to and shared, and the exhortations (or calls to action) that these elderly believers made to the generations after them, can be very helpful.

Jacob

Jacob, in Genesis 48 and 49, speaks to his sons of the work of God’s angel in his life. Raising them had not been easy, and many tragic events scarred the family. They had seen his struggles and experienced their own. In his tender moment with Joseph and his sons, Jacob says: “the God which fed me all my life long unto this day, the angel which redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads …” (48:15,16). These are the words of a brother who struggled with worry and anxiety all his life, and who, at this last stage, had come to realise the full extent of the continuous, protective and saving hand of God all through his life.

When we share with our children the impact and presence of God in our lives, a presence that we often forgot, doubted or failed to perceive, then we show them what it means to grow in faith as a believer. We encourage them to hold on through thick and thin, trusting in the presence of a loving and faithful God, a Father whose care has been demonstrated in concrete ways in the work of His redeeming angel.

In the following chapter, Jacob depicts the future of each of his sons and their descendants; and, as he does so, he discloses how they have each lived, their wrongs committed, and the shame hidden by them. He tells them, in effect, who they have been and who they are destined to become through the hand of the Lord in their lives and in the lives of their children. In doing these things, Jacob, frail and wracked with pain, shows us that having a good death does not only involve encouragement. It may also include confrontation of harm that has been done, things covered over or hidden that need to be aired so that people can move forward from them, as forgiven sinners.

Moses

Moses, in Deuteronomy 28–33, reminds the nation of God’s work with them from the beginning. He warns them about the dangers of unfaithfulness to their loyal God. He encourages them with pictures of blessedness if they obey and honour Him. Service in the community involves personal cost, and sometimes painful experiences. Yet, Moses had never abandoned them, and had remained faithful to God and to his stiff-necked brothers and sisters through all their rebellions.

He is frank about how the nation had behaved during his tenure as their leader, and makes preparation for his departure by encouraging Joshua to serve and lead Israel with strength and good courage. He knows that Joshua feels completely inadequate for the task of being his successor. As an elder passing the torch to his younger brother, Moses takes time to show Joshua that God will equip him with everything that he needs to lead the ecclesia. “Be strong and of a good courage” (31:6,7,23) becomes a clarion cry to Joshua and to all future labourers among God’s people. Moses’ good death is utterly focused on honouring God, on helping the nation with a clear view of the blessings and curses ahead of it, and on strengthening the leaders who will follow him.

David

David, in 1 Kings 1:1–2:11 and in 1 Chronicles 29, rises from a state of decrepitude, stirred up by Bathsheba and Nathan to save the monarchy and the people. As he hears about the danger that they face, he rallies physically and emotionally and counsels Israel’s faithful leaders on urgent steps to ensure that Solomon is installed securely as king, and the nation saved from another civil war. He addresses Israel as their (temporarily) rejuvenated, elderly king, recounting the unselfish action that he had taken to prepare for building a house for God, attesting to the generosity of the whole nation, praying publicly that God might direct the hearts of the people and of Solomon toward Him. The old king is at pains to note God’s ownership of everything that we imagine to be our own. This fact should have acted as a brake on the greed and covetousness that His people would engage in. Surely this continues to be relevant counsel to modern believers, immersed in the materialism of a self-indulgent society. We are only ever stewards of what is God’s property, money and possessions. It isn’t ours. David ascribes all honour and glory to God, lifting Him up in the presence of the people. He describes the shortness of human life: “our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no hope” (1 Chronicles 29:15, NASB 1995).

David directs his son to remain faithful to the Lord, and makes this the substance of his last conversation with him. He could not have imagined the direction that his son’s life would take. But Ecclesiastes 12:13 indicates that Solomon came back to his father’s wise counsel at the end of his life. David warns Solomon of painful actions that he must take with rebellious elements in Israel, a prudent cleansing of the nation that he must act on to safeguard the continuity of his rule.

Old and infirm, Brother David deeply influenced the nation’s future through the actions that he took in his last days and the words that he spoke. David’s good death addressed spiritual and practical matters that those who remained after him needed to understand to survive and avert much trouble.

Solomon

Solomon had a good death, I believe. A terse, almost cryptic comment in 2 Chronicles 11:17 gives one the hope that he did finally amend his ways: “So they strengthened the kingdom of Judah, and made Rehoboam the son of Solomon strong, three years: for three years they walked in the way of David and Solomon.” Note “the way of David and Solomon.” I draw much comfort and hope for Solomon, and for myself, from this verse. These words, added to the body of lived experience described transparently in Ecclesiastes, suggest to me that Solomon was a man who changed. His good death, drawing on Ecclesiastes, involved the sharing of painful realisations during a life of hedonistic and materialistic abandon, the acknowledgment that no comfort, no luxury that this world offers apart from God, truly satisfies us, and that real and enduring happiness is rooted in the fear and obedience of the Lord.

These men show us what it is to be useful, fruitful and productive all the way through to our final moments. Their actions and their words define what a good death can look like. May the wonderful pictures of these old brothers, serving to the very end, even with greatly depleted strength, move us to follow suit, that our loved ones may remember and be moved to serve God through our good death, and that our Father and His Son might be honoured.

(Part 1 of 2)

[1] Bible quotations are from the KJV unless otherwise stated.
